This case involved a 17-year-old Pashto-speaking female who initially presented to a community emergency department (ED) after intentionally ingesting Ortho® Orthene Fire Ant Killer. The ingestion occurred approximately two hours prior to the patient’s arrival at the ED. The patient herself admitted the ingestion to her mother shortly after it occurred. The patient’s father was called home from work and found the patient lethargic, diaphoretic, and with copious oral secretions. Emergency medical services (EMS) were called. At the time of the patient’s initial presentation, it was reported that she ingested approximately one half of the bottle (∼ 170 g). The bottle accompanied the patient to the ED via EMS and was indeed noted to be half empty (Fig. 1); however, later in her course the patient clarified that she only ingested one “spoonful."
In the ED, the patient had a temperature of 35.6 °C, blood pressure 116/67 mmHg, heart rate 129 beats per minute, and a respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. On examination, the patient was noted to be lethargic and minimally responsive to questioning. She also had copious oral secretions, generalized weakness, and muscle fasciculations. She had no bronchorrhea or bronchospasm. Laboratory studies were largely unremarkable, aside from a slight leukocytosis (13.1 K/mcl), hyperglycemia (146 mg/dL), hypokalemia (3.0 mmol/L), hypomagnesemia (1.8 mg/dL), mildly decreased serum bicarbonate (19 mmol/L), and elevated INR (1.4). Her acetaminophen and salicylate concentrations were undetectable. A comprehensive urine drug screen was also negative. A computed tomography scan of the head, electrocardiogram, and chest x-ray were also obtained and were unremarkable. Poison Control was contacted and recommended giving atropine and pralidoxime. Atropine was titrated to secretion resolution, specifically oral secretions and bronchorrhea, as a clinical endpoint. Importantly, heart rate was not used as a primary definition of atropinization. Although bradycardia is classically associated with the cholinergic toxidrome, tachycardia may predominate in OP poisoning due to stimulation of nicotinic receptors at sympathetic ganglia. As such, using heart rate as a marker of clinical improvement risks underdosing of atropine. The patient received 1 mg of atropine and then a second 1 mg dose approximately 15 min after the first. A bolus dose of 1.5 g of pralidoxime was also administered. These interventions significantly improved both the patient’s oral secretions, generalized weakness, and fasciculations. She did not require any additional treatment while at the community ED. She was then transferred to a specialized pediatric hospital with a dedicated toxicology consultation service.
Approximately 12 h after her ingestion, the patient was evaluated in the pediatric intensive care unit by our toxicology service, where she was found to be tachycardic (heart rate 115), lethargic, and with copious oral and respiratory secretions. She did not have any appreciable weakness or muscle fasciculations, but complained of nausea and generalized abdominal pain. An aliquot of 1 mg of atropine was given with almost immediate improvement in her symptoms. She was started on dextrose and potassium containing maintenance fluids. Serum and red blood cell (RBC) cholinesterase concentrations were obtained, which resulted after hospital discharge.
On reevaluation nearly 24 h after her ingestion, she had no recurrence of her cholinergic symptoms and did not require any additional atropine. She was noted to be more alert and reported feeling near baseline. However, she did have prominent tongue fasciculations. She did not have any proximal muscle or neck flexor weakness. Negative inspiratory force was normal throughout her inpatient stay. Interim labs were remarkable for ongoing hypomagnesemia (1.6 mg/dL) and a mild respiratory alkalosis (7.42/32.5/22.0/80.2). Her repeat INR and CK were within normal limits. Given her tongue fasciculations, the decision was made to administer an additional 1 g of pralidoxime as a bolus. She had no progression of her fasciculations, and by hospital day 2 the patient’s neurological exam had returned to normal. At this time, she was downgraded from intensive care and was monitored on the medical floor for an additional 24 h with no recurrence of symptoms (Fig. 2).
The patient’s initial cholinesterase concentrations, which were obtained 14 h after her ingestion, were notable for a plasma cholinesterase level of 0.2 U/mL (normal 2.9–7.1 U/mL) and RBC cholinesterase of 3.2 U/mL (normal 7.9–17.1 U/mL). A subsequent sample obtained 26 h after ingestion showed improvement of both the plasma cholinesterase (1.5 U/mL) and RBC cholinesterase (8.8 U/mL).

A 67-year-old female patient was found by emergency medical services (EMS) smoking a cigarette outside her apartment approximately 30 min after a suicide attempt involving the ingestion of multiple medications, including but not limited to: metoprolol, nifedipine, nortriptyline, venlafaxine, and temazepam, all at toxic doses (a comprehensive list of the reported medications, their dosages, and mechanisms of action can be found in Table 1). After ingestion, the patient contacted psychiatric services to convey a farewell message, leading to EMS being alerted. Her medical history was notable for depression, iron deficiency anaemia, hypertension, reduced renal function attributed to previous lithium use, and prior suicide attempts. Her estimated bodyweight was 90 kg. At EMS arrival, she was hemodynamically stable with normal vital signs.
45 min after ingestion and during EMS transport, the patient deteriorated from full responsiveness with stable vitals to decreased mental status (E2M5V2). On reassessment patient was tachycardic at 115 bpm, with a blood pressure of 86/48 mmHg, a respiratory rate of 10 breaths/min and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air.
The patient presented at the emergency department (ED) approximately one hour after ingesting the overdose. Her condition had already worsened significantly during transport and continued to deteriorate in the ED. Ten minutes after arrival, her manual blood pressure readings were nearly unmeasurable, occasionally recording 50/30 mmHg. Her heart rate declined to 65 beats per minute. Her consciousness dropped further to E1M1V1 at this stage. Despite administration of 15 L/min oxygen through a non-rebreather mask (NRBM) and the use of two nasopharyngeal airway devices, her oxygen saturation decreased from 92% to ultimately 40%. This was attributed to a combination of airway obstruction and decreased respiratory drive as a result of reduced level of consciousness, ventilation-perfusion mismatch and inadequate pulse oximetry readings due to profound hypotension.
Bag-mask ventilation was initiated and after she had been treated with two grams calcium gluconate intravenously, 5 mg glucagon, 100cc sodium bicarbonate 8.4% and 1500 mL of crystalloid fluids initially, vasopressors were started with a total of seven 50 µg boluses of phenylephrine and a norepinephrine infusion titrated up to 0.93 µg/kg/min. These interventions raised her blood pressure to 95/55 mmHg, as confirmed by invasive monitoring through an arterial line. With increasing cerebral and peripheral perfusion pressure, spontaneous ventilation returned, as well as pulse oximetry reading 92% and her consciousness improved to E1M5V2.
The first electrocardiogram (ECG) in the ED, performed 90 min after the overdose, showed a slightly prolonged QRS (109 ms). However, the ECGs later on in the intensive care unit (ICU) demonstrated an increasingly prolonged QRS (max 135 ms) with a prominent terminal R wave in aVR, suggesting sodium channel blockade. Further, with an absolute QT interval of 400 ms at an heart rate of 78 bpm, the QT nomogram indicated no increased risk of torsades de pointes. At the ED, her venous blood gas demonstrated a pH of 7.30, with pCO2 of 7.9 kPa, lactate of 2.4 mmol/L and a glucose of 5.6 mmol/L. All other laboratory results were unremarkable except for her known renal failure, indicated by an eGFR of 17 mL/min/1.73 m². Approximately 3 h after ingestion she was transferred to the ICU for further monitoring and treatment. Activated charcoal was considered; however, this was deferred because of rapidly progressive hemodynamic instability, reduced consciousness, and the absence of a definitively secured airway.
Upon arrival in the ICU her consciousness remained decreased at E1M5V2. Patient was breathing spontaneously and her oxygen saturation maintained above 90% on 15 L/min oxygen through a NRBM. Given the patient’s hemodynamic instability and ongoing requirement for high-dose vasopressor support, endotracheal intubation was deferred at this stage. The priority was initial hemodynamic resuscitation, as induction of anesthesia with additional hypnotic drugs was considered to carry a high risk of precipitating further cardiovascular collapse. A second generation supraglottic airway device (SAD) was therefore placed, which she was able to tolerate well without the need for additional sedatives. Spontaneous ventilation and oxygenation kept being adequate with low inspiratory pressures, minimal leakage and FiO2 was titrated down to 0.5. The patient hemodynamically stabilised and norepinephrine infusion was at that point decreased to 0.27 µg/kg/min.
Eight hours post-ingestion, there was a secondary decline in the patient’s condition. The level of consciousness decreased to E1M1V1. The patient was then intubated to reduce the risk of aspiration of gastric contents owing to decreased airway reflexes. Concurrently there was a marked decrease in diuresis and a lactate increase on arterial blood gas to a maximum of 4.7 mmol/L and ventilator FiO2 needed to be increased to 0.8 after intubation. This was attributed to acute progression of left sided cardiac failure, which was confirmed by severely decreased left ventricular function on echocardiography and chest x-ray indicating pulmonary congestion.
At 11 h post-ingestion, high-dose insulin euglycemic therapy (HIET) was initiated because of the progression of the toxic cardiogenic shock. Treatment consisted of an initial bolus of 80 units of insulin with 40 g of glucose, followed by a continuous infusion of insulin at 80 units/hour with concurrent glucose at 40 g/hour following the relevant guideline of the Dutch National Poisoning Information Center. Concomitant glucose supplementation was titrated to maintain euglycemia, with frequent glucose and electrolyte monitoring during treatment. Particular attention was paid to potassium levels because HIET may induce hypokalemia. The intended therapeutic response was improvement in perfusion parameters, including blood pressure, lactate clearance, urine output, and vasopressor requirement. Additionally, inotropic support with dobutamine at 5 µg/kg/min and milrinone at 0.25 µg/kg/min was initiated, while the continuous adrenaline infusion was maintained.
Despite these measures, blood pressure dropped significantly to 78/55 (MAP 57) and serum lactate remained elevated and diuresis nearly stopped. Norepinephrine infusion was increased to 0.59 µg/kg/min and argipressin at 0.01IE/min was started to treat profound vasodilation, with minimal effect. Additionally, the patient was treated with 3 g of calcium gluconate, 5 mg glucagon, 1000 mL of crystalloid fluids (totalling 2500 mL), and 100 mL of 8.4% sodium bicarbonate, administered in response to QRS rewidening (which increased to a maximum of 145 ms in ICU). At that stage, the patient was considered to have developed catecholamine-refractory shock, based on persistent hypotension with MAP < 65 mmHg, rising lactate levels indicating ongoing tissue hypoperfusion, near-anuric renal failure, worsening respiratory failure, and severely depressed left ventricular function on echocardiography, despite maximal conventional therapy including escalating vasopressor and inotropic support as described above and HIET; Given the patient's refractory cardiogenic shock, VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery was considered. In our local ICU-protocol regarding VA-ECMO, refractory cardiogenic shock is defined as persistent systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg with a cardiac index < 2.2 L/min/m² and/or a cardiac power output < 0.6 W despite treatment with two or more vasoactive agents. In the absence of other contraindications (advanced age over 70 years, severe aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, cardiac arrest with uncertain neurological outcome, a contraindication for systemic anticoagulants such as recent intracranial haemorrhage or metastasised malignancy), a consultation with psychiatry was held prior to cannulation, to consider the appropriateness of this treatment modality given the suicide attempt and the patient's medical and psychiatric history. Considering the patient's positive response to treatment of a previous episode of depression, the relapse leading to this intoxication was deemed reversible and sixteen hours after ingestion VA-ECMO was initiated. ECMO placement was percutaneously. The left femoral vein was canulated with a 25 French drainage canula and the right femoral artery was canulated with a 19** French return canula. A distal perfusion canula was placed in the right superficial femoral artery which is common practice with this VA-ECMO configuration in our institution. Invasive blood pressure was already monitored in the right radial artery and INVOS (Medtronic plc, Minneapolis, USA) monitoring was applied bilaterally on the forehead and distally on the lower limbs to possibly detect differential hypoxemia and/or a relative perfusion defect to the right lower leg. Initial hemodynamic goals in our institution are ECMO flow of 3–4.5 L/min in adults, further titrated on a target MAP> 65 mmHg, SvO2 of > 60% and a normalisation of the serum lactate, while sweep flow is titrated to achieve an arterial pH between 7.35 and 7.45. Transthoracic echocardiography is conducted daily to evaluate opening of the aortic valve and unloading/distension of the left ventricle (LV), LV function, mitral valve regurgitation, right ventricular function and pericardial effusion. Directly after connecting the ECMO circuit a bolus of 5000IE iv heparin is administered followed by a continuous infusion with 6-hourly dose titration targeted on anti Xa levels between 0.15 and 0.30 IU/mL. Initial ECMO flow was 2.7 L/min. Lactate decreased to normal levels, norepinephrine could be tapered to a minimal dose and diuresis increased slightly over the subsequent hours. Directly after cannulation, a pale and slightly colder left foot and no duplex signal distal of the femoral artery were noticed. A vascular surgeon was consulted and additional imaging studies were conducted. Thrombotic material in the external iliac artery and superficial femoral artery and an occlusion of the popliteal artery were detected, which were all effectively managed with additional intravenous heparin. In the subsequent days, vasopressor support was gradually discontinued, and transthoracic echocardiography showed recovery of the systolic function of the left ventricle and no other abnormalities. In our hospital, patients are eligible for weaning of VA-ECMO as soon as the underlying cause of cardiogenic shock has subsided, pulse pressure has increased to > 20 mm Hg for over 24 h and the earlier mentioned hemodynamic goals are met with decreasing dose of supportive inotropes (dobutamine <5 mcg/kg/h) and vasopressors (norepinephrine <0.1 mcg/kg/h). ECMO flow is then initially tapered down to 2,5 L/min and a wean trial is conducted when anti-Xa levels are 0.5IU/mL. In our institution ECMO-flow is decreased to 0.5 L/min for 15 min during this wean trial. When pre-defined hemodynamic (CVD<15 mmHg, MAP >65 mmHg, pulse pressure >30 mmHg, ScvO2 >60%, lactate <2 mmol/L, VIS score <15) and echocardiographic (LVOT VTI ≥12 cm, TSDa ≥6 cm/sec and LVEF ≥20–25%) criteria are met, the patient is eligible for VA-ECMO removal. The patient met these criteria after three days and was then successfully weaned from VA-ECMO.
During decannulation, which in our hospital is conducted in the ICU after initial percutaneous ECMO placement and canula insertion openings are routinely closed with purse-string sutures, she lost 800 cc of blood from her right common femoral artery, necessitating a secondary transport to the OR for embolectomy and surgical closure of the right femoral artery. An additional embolectomy was later performed to resolve a right popliteal artery occlusion, likely due to embolic material migrating distally during the femoral artery procedure.
Her ICU stay was further complicated by respiratory insufficiency due to ventilation associated pneumonia and a reintubation due to ICU acquired weakness (ICUAW) and atelectasis, necessitating a tracheostomy to wean her from the mechanical ventilation. Multifactorial acute-on-chronic renal insufficiency due to the hemodynamic collapse, bleeding and intravenous contrast exposure was managed with continuous venovenous hemofiltration until renal function returned to its baseline level. After 22 days in the ICU, she was transferred to the hospital's psychiatric ward primarily for observation of ICUAW. After a total of 66 days, she was discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation centre. At hospital discharge, no ongoing depressive symptoms or suicidal ideation were present, and the patient expressed regret regarding the suicide attempt together with a wish to continue living. Neurological examination showed no focal deficits, although persistent bilateral foot drop and ICU-acquired weakness which required rehabilitation. Renal function partially recovered, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 28 mL/min/1.73 m² at discharge. See Fig. 2 for an overview for the major stages of clinical deterioration and escalation of therapy.
The subsequent course remained complicated by pressure ulcers and osteomyelitis on her left heel, likely related to prolonged immobilization and use of a lower-leg splint for foot drop, ultimately requiring below-knee amputation due to insufficient antibiotics response. Several months later, the patient was readmitted with urosepsis which was treated with antibiotics and fluids. However, due to frailty and functional decline, further care was transitioned to a palliative approach, after which the patient died in the rehabilitation facility in approximal 8 months after intoxication.

Castleman disease exists on a spectrum of lymph node involvement and severity. UCD typically presents as an enlarged mass in the mediastinum, which may be visually apparent or detected incidentally. Most patients are asymptomatic, but some may present with symptoms related to compression of nearby anatomical structures. Laboratory abnormalities can include hypergammaglobulinemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and anemia. Up to 90% of UCD cases present with hyaline vascular (HV) histopathology, which is characterized by atrophic germinal centers circumscribed with concentric rings of lymphocytes in an ‘onion-ring’ pattern and containing dysplastic follicular dendritic cells; the germinal centers are penetrated by hyalinized vessels giving a ‘lollipop’ appearance.
Unlike UCD, MCD is almost always symptomatic. Patients present with multifocal lymphadenopathy and signs of systemic inflammation, most commonly fever, night sweats, fluid retention, and renal dysfunction. These symptoms can be episodic, progressive, or chronic, and in severe cases can be fatal if left untreated. Laboratory tests often reveal cytopenias, abnormal liver function tests, markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and ESR, and proteinuria. The histopathology of MCD is more varied than UCD; it may present with a hypervascular type (hyperV), the plasmacytic (PC) type, or a mixed type. The hyperV nomenclature is used to differentiate vascular MCD from HV UCD, though HV MCD and HyperV MCD are often used interchangeably by many authors. The lymph nodes in the PC type are characterized by hypertrophic germinal centers, with intrafollicular spaces populated by sheets of plasma cells and vascular proliferations; as its name suggests, the mixed type exhibit features of both the HyperV and PC types.
The etiologic agent varies for the different subtypes of MCD. Uncontrolled infection with HHV-8 is often the pathogenic driver of MCD, especially in patients who are immunocompromised due to infection with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In these HHV-8-associated MCD cases, CD20+ B cells act as reservoirs for HHV-8 infection and replication, with symptomology stemming from production of a viral homolog of IL-6 and subsequent downstream upregulation of proinflammatory human cytokines. For POEMS-associated MCD, up to 60% of cases are caused by malignant monoclonal plasma cells, which drive reactive lymph node changes with CD features. Cases of MCD which are not concurrent with HHV-8 infection or POEMS syndrome do not have a clear etiology and are considered idiopathic (iMCD). While the exact etiology remains unknown, IL-6 has been identified as a key pathological driver of iMCD. Episodes of disease flare may be marked by mild lymphadenopathy and B-symptoms, or in severe cases present acutely with extensive inflammation, organomegaly and organ dysfunction, pleural effusion, anasarca, and ascites.
Cases of iMCD in which thrombocytopenia, anasarca, renal dysfunction or reticulin fibrosis, fever, and organomegaly are present are classified as iMCD-TAFRO. Ferritin and sCD25 are only modestly elevated in iMCD-TAFRO, whereas CRP is very high (often >100 mg/L). The gamma globulins are usually low, normal or modestly elevated in iMCD-TAFRO (5–15 g/L), in contrast to iMCD-IPL (usually >35 g/L). The cytokine profile, histopathology and clinical course of iMCD-TAFRO are different from iMCD-NOS; patients often have less markedly elevated serum IL-6 and increased serum vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), the lymph nodes are often highly vascularized and demonstrate the HyperV histopathology type, and the patients typically present with acute and severe disease. Additional differences include frequently elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) without hyperbilirubinemia or transaminase elevation, and normal to mildly elevated gammaglobulin.
Differentiating iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO syndrome is challenging due to substantial overlap of signs and symptoms and lack of specific biomarkers. While the first descriptions of TAFRO syndrome by Takai and colleagues in 2010 focused on its hyperinflammation symptoms, acute onset, and rapid progression, current perspectives now acknowledge how TAFRO presents as a constellation of nonspecific symptoms that can occur concurrently with other conditions, including malignancies, rheumatologic disorders, infections, and POEMS syndrome.
Due to the heterogeneity in disease presentation, Nishimura et al. introduced the categories of probable iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO syndrome without iMCD; these designations are based on the number of diagnostic criteria met (see below). There was an open debate as to whether TAFRO was exclusively a subtype of iMCD, a distinct clinical entity, or both. A recent retrospective analysis of data collected from 11 rheumatology and hematology centers in Japan identified 104 patients with TAFRO, of which 26 (25%) did not have lymphadenopathy, confirming that TAFRO can in fact exist without CD. To date, there is no available data regarding the proportion of patients in the Western hemisphere who have TAFRO without CD. It is important to note that there is significant overlap in consensus diagnostic guidelines and treatment modalities for iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO syndrome, and it has been proposed that iMCD-TAFRO and TAFRO without proven iMCD or other underlying pathologies be considered a single clinical entity.
Diagnosing iMCD-TAFRO can be challenging due to lack of specific diagnostic biomarkers and a heterogenous clinical presentation, requiring differential workup and collaboration across multidisciplinary teams. There are currently two diagnostic frameworks for TAFRO syndrome, which differ in their dependence on lymph node biopsy and TAFRO’s relation to iMCD (Table 1). Consensus criteria for iMCD-TAFRO require an excisional lymph node biopsy with histopathology consistent with the criteria listed in Table 1. As both criteria have significant overlap, and an excisional lymph node biopsy may not be feasible (due to patient critical condition, risk of bleeding, and/or inaccessible lymph node location), both criteria should be considered to diagnose iMCD-TAFRO. When an excisional lymph node biopsy is not possible, a chest CT may be of diagnostic utility. Patients with TAFRO may have an apparent enlarged anterior mediastinum lacking a solid mass, described as ‘matted’, due to a mixture of adipose and soft tissues.
Additional criteria have been established which stratify iMCD by disease severity for the purpose of informing treatment. Severe disease is defined as having at least two of the following: Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG-PS) >2, stage IV renal dysfunction, anasarca and/or ascites and/or pleural/pericardial effusion, hemoglobin <8 g/dL, or pulmonary involvement/interstitial pneumonitis with dyspnea.
While progressive kidney failure or acute kidney injury are common in iMCD-TAFRO, evidence describing the kidney histopathology in this patient population is limited, as biopsy is often precluded by the critical nature of the disease and bleeding risk. In a case series of 7 TAFRO patients who underwent renal biopsy, all cases displayed endothelial cell swelling and glomerular basement membrane double contouring, with mesangiolysis or mesangial loosening, consistent with a membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)-like pattern with endothelial injury. All patients had acute kidney injuries at different stages and 57% of them needed kidney replacement therapy. Using electron microscopy, investigators also reported endothelial cell swelling and loss of mesangial architecture, as well as loss of endothelial cell fenestrations. Another case report described MPGN in an iMCD-TAFRO patient, with an accompanying literature search identifying 19 iMCD-TAFRO patients with renal biopsies, of which 8 (42%) were described as MPGN-like and 11 (52%) were described as thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA)-like glomerulopathy, though without fibrin thrombi in glomerular vasculature. In this report, the clinical, biological (including renal function and urinary sediment as well as IL-6 and VEGF levels), and outcome characteristics were similar between patients with MPGN and TMA-like presentation. The authors suggest there is a histopathological and likely a physiopathology continuum between TMA and MPGN, where TMA seems to appear first and gradually move toward an MPGN phenotype. Accordingly, the diagnosis may alternate based on how early the biopsies were performed. Additional review of the available literature reporting data from patients with iMCD-TAFRO/TAFRO syndrome and renal failure shows a histology pattern consistent with MPGN and TMA on kidney biopsy.
While IL-6 has been identified as a key pathological driver of iMCD, not all patients have elevated IL-6 and other factors may be involved. Whole lymph node transcriptome analysis in patients with iMCD showed upregulation of genes in the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex, complement and coagulation cascade (C4A and C4B), as well as the B cell-attracting chemokine CXCL13, and the angiogenic mediator placental growth factor (PGF, a ligand of VEGF receptor 1 [VEGFR1]). These findings were generally well aligned with another transcriptomic analysis study focusing on immune-related genes, which reported overexpressed CXCL13 and upregulated genes involved in the complement cascade, VEGF signaling, and mTOR pathway. These studies highlight the importance of angiogenesis, consistent with the hypervascularity observed in iMCD-TAFRO, as well as the potential involvement of the complement cascade and mTOR pathway in pathogenesis. Of note, complement dysregulation is the predominant mechanism of endothelial injury in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (also known as complement-mediated TMA), while mTOR dysregulation has been linked with a variety of kidney disorders including acute kidney injury, kidney fibrosis, glomerular disease, and polycystic kidney disease. These two mechanisms could potentially drive the kidney damage observed in patients with iMCD-TAFRO.
Additional analysis of the cytokine microenvironment found that IL-6 was overexpressed in interfollicular areas of affected lymph nodes in MCD (observed in 76% of cases) when compared to UCD (25%) and reactive non-CD controls (20%), particularly in CD31-positive vascular structures of endothelial or lymphatic origin. To a lesser degree, all samples showed some IL-6 expression in B cell rich mantle zones and GCs. These findings suggest that vascular cells, rather than plasma cells, are the major source of excess IL-6 in this condition. This is corroborated by a recent report of the source of IL-6 production and its transcriptional regulation across multiple iMCD subtypes, which showed that vascular endothelial cells are the major source of IL-6 in samples collected from patients with iMCD-TAFRO and that elevated serum IL-6 in these patients is secondary to upregulated cytokine storm-related genes (e.g., TNFα, IL-1R, mTOR, and VEGFA). In contrast, plasma cells were identified as the major source of IL-6 in the IPL subtype. Overall, these data may provide additional insight into the mechanisms of kidney injury in iMCD-TAFRO. One hypothesis is that kidney injury may be the result of a negative feedback loop in which increased circulating VEGF and IL-6 lead to decreased glomerular VEGF and loss of endothelial fenestrations. Another hypothesis is loss of glomerular permeability and resultant microvascular injury, in which TMA is driven by autoantibodies produced by clonal B cells, in tandem with increased serum VEGF, disrupting the glomerular VEGF gradient.
While the exact etiology of iMCD is unknown, consensus treatment guidelines focus on targeting the underlying hypercytokinemia. These guidelines do not distinguish iMCD-TAFRO from other subtypes of iMCD, but rather focus on different treatment strategies based on disease severity. There are two organizations with detailed consensus treatment guidelines for iMCD: The NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology (NCCN Guidelines®) and the International Consensus Treatment Guidelines developed by the Castleman Disease Collaborative Network (CDCN). The anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody siltuximab is the sole therapy approved by the FDA to treat iMCD and is recommended as a first-line treatment option per the CDCN and NCCN Guidelines®. The approved dosage is 11 mg/kg intravenous (IV) infusion every 3 weeks. In addition, the consensus CDCN guidelines suggest that patients diagnosed with severe iMCD who have marked organ dysfunction, poor performance status, and require intensive critical care should receive weekly siltuximab infusions (11 mg/kg) for up to 4 weeks. Patients who respond to treatment should remain on the approved treatment schedule (11 mg/kg every 3 weeks) indefinitely with tapering of corticosteroids. Alternative therapies for patients who do not respond to siltuximab include tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist), rituximab (anti-CD-20 monoclonal antibody), and/or cytotoxic chemotherapy. Corticosteroids can also be used as adjunctive therapy to anti-IL-6 agents or rituximab. If patients with severe disease do not show any response to siltuximab within 1 week or show any signs of deterioration, aggressive combination chemotherapy should be considered immediately. In a case series/report of patients with iMCD-TAFRO who were refractory to IL-6 blockade, the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus and the TNFα inhibitor adalimumab, respectively, have been shown to induce durable remission and may be considered as alternative treatment options for these patients.
There are currently no consensus treatment guidelines for TAFRO syndrome outside of the context of iMCD, and no conclusive evidence from randomized, controlled clinical trials to assess treatment efficacy. A treatment strategy for TAFRO syndrome as a separate entity from MCD was first proposed by Masaki et al. in 2015; however, treatment guidelines are based on case reports, analyses of registry data, expert opinion, and physician experience. TAFRO is treated empirically with high-dose corticosteroids, blockade of IL-6 signaling with the monoclonal antibodies siltuximab or tocilizumab, or other options such as rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors, and cytotoxic chemotherapy; these modalities can be utilized as monotherapy or as part of a combination therapy approach.
A 31-year-old white female at 16 weeks gestation with her first pregnancy presented with chest pain, fever, and dyspnea for one week. Her medical and surgical history were unremarkable. On exam, the patient had poor inspiratory effort, bilateral wheezing and rales, and required supplemental oxygen. The patient also had moderate to severe pitting edema along with pronounced cervical bilateral lymphadenopathy. D-dimer was elevated, but there was no radiographic evidence of pulmonary embolism, and screening for upper respiratory tract infections was negative. Bloodwork showed elevated white blood cell (WBC) count (23 x 109/L), elevated CRP (22.5 mg/dL), low hemoglobin (8.5 g/dL), low platelets (118 x 109/L), and serum creatinine (sCr) of 1.1 mg/mL. Fetal heart sounds were normal prior to hospitalization; however, fetal demise was diagnosed on admission. Volume overload in the patient was treated with albumin and furosemide, but she did not respond (sCr 2.2 mg/dL on day 4) and became anuric. The patient’s respiratory status worsened and required mechanical ventilation. Follow-up assessments showed worsening thrombocytopenia (31 x 109/L) with further elevation of CRP (27.5 mg/dL) and sCr (3.7 mg/dL), and no improvements of hypervolemia, anuria, and metabolic derangements. Due to the decline of her condition, the patient was placed on kidney replacement therapy, which improved her volume status and allowed her to be extubated.
A kidney biopsy showed membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with TMA and red blood cell (RBC) fragmentation (Figure 1A,B). Electron microscopy analysis of the kidney tissue showed endothelial cell swelling, loss of endothelial cell fenestrations, and expansion of the subendothelial space, confirming an acute presentation of TMA (Figure 1C).
In view of the early complex presentation, we had a wide differential diagnosis including disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), viral infection, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and secondary TMA. Additional diagnoses also were considered for work-up including hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome, gestational thrombocytopenia, autoimmune diseases and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Viral screening was negative for HHV-8, HHV-6, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and HIV, and there were no findings on rheumatology and immunology work-up. Additional screenings were negative for cytoplasmatic and perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (C-ANCA, p-ANCA), anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody (anti-GBM), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), international normalized ratio (INR), hepatitis panel, anticardiolipin, beta-2 glycoprotein, antistreptolysin O (ASO), anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), as well as a gastrointestinal panel. Moreover, aHUS genetic panel was unremarkable and flow cytometric analysis for acute leukemia was also negative. TTP was not likely as the ADAMTS 13 activity was 41%. Head and neck ultrasound showed multiple enlarged lymph nodes, and affected tissue was first collected by fine needle aspiration (yielded insufficient sample for analysis) followed by excisional biopsy of the supraclavicular lymph node (Figure 2). CD20 and CD79a markers for B-cells showed diminished follicular architecture/attenuation. The follicular architecture was retained, with CD21/CD23 staining showing an intact FDC meshwork. The features were overall compatible with follicular regression. Furthermore, a panel of CD138 stains and Kappa/Lambda in situ hybridization showed numerous interfollicular plasma cells that were associated with increased vascularity. EBV and HHV8 stains were negative within the biopsy. Flow cytometry did not detect any abnormal B-cell, T-cell, or plasma cell populations to suggest a leukemic/lymphomatous process. These findings are compatible with HHV-8 negative CD. The numerous polytypic plasma cells with interfollicular distribution associated and increased vascularity suggest a mixed histological subtype. The lymph node histopathology in conjunction with clinical features was suggestive of severe iMCD-TAFRO (Table 2). This diagnosis was further supported by elevated VEGF (198 pg/mL) and IL-6 (48 pg/mL, reference range <6.4 pg/mL).
Weekly infusions of siltuximab 11 mg/kg with high-dose steroids and sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis were started. After the first siltuximab dose, there were immediate improvements in kidney and respiratory functions, recovery of platelet count (120 x 109/L) and a reduction in CRP (5.7 mg/dL). Kidney replacement therapy was stopped after the second dose of siltuximab, with normalization of CRP (0.5 mg/dL), platelet count (197 x 109/L), and full recovery of kidney function (sCr 0.9 mg/dL). The patient was discharged with siltuximab titrated down to every 3 weeks plus a steroid taper. Prior to the third siltuximab infusion, the patient developed a mild, pruritic rash for which sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim was switched to dapsone. Given the persistent rash, siltuximab was switched to tocilizumab, which led to resolution.

The proband, a 60-year-old male, presented to our department on January 17, 2024, with a 5-year history of elevated serum creatinine (110–160 μmol/L) and persistent proteinuria (1–2+). His medical history included long-standing hypertension and gout (duration >10 years). Notably, his family history was significant, with both his father and maternal aunt succumbing to uremia (Figure 1). Physical examination was unremarkable.
The laboratory workup revealed 2+ proteinuria without hematuria, with elevated 24-h urine protein excretion of 1.1 g/24h (normal range: 0–0.15 g/24h). Serum biochemistry demonstrated normal albumin (40.5 g/L; reference 40–55 g/L), elevated creatinine (153.4 μmol/L; reference 57–111 μmol/L), and normal uric acid levels (221 μmol/L; reference 208–428 μmol/L1). Immunological profiles showed normal IgG/IgA/IgM, C3/C4 complement levels, and negative autoantibodies (ANA, dsDNA, anti-PLA2R, ANCA). Infectious disease screening was negative for HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis, HSV, and CMV, with normal hematologic, coagulation, and thyroid function parameters. Ophthalmologic examination demonstrated no anterior lenticonus or perimacular dot/fleck retinopathy, while audiometry showed no bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Renal ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with altered parenchymal echogenicity and a 2.0 × 1.6 cm right renal cyst.
On light microscopy, histopathological examination showed tubulointerstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy with cystic dilatation, and global glomerulosclerosis (53%). Immunofluorescence was negative for immunoglobulins and complement. Immunohistochemistry using anti-UMOD antibody (EPR20071; Abcam) revealed abnormal intracellular accumulation of mutant uromodulin in distal tubule epithelial cells (Figure 2a and b). Electron microscopy revealed one obsolescent glomerulus with characteristic alterations: capillary endothelial vacuolization, segmental GBM thickening (250–750 nm), and diffuse podocyte foot process effacement (>80%). The mesangium showed mild hypercellularity with rare electron-dense deposits. Tubulointerstitial findings included tubular epithelial vacuolization, focal basement membrane thickening, and mild inflammatory infiltrates. Vascular changes were limited to occasional capillary erythrocyte aggregates.
NGS revealed a novel heterozygous missense mutation in UMOD (NM_003361.4: c.1676A > G, p. Tyr559Cys), located within exon 8. This variant was absent from all major genomic databases (e.g. gnomAD, NCBI、OMIM, and others) and had been submitted to ClinVar with accession number RCV006253441.1. Bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that the affected tyrosine residue at position 559 was evolutionarily conserved across species (Figure 3, Ugene analysis).
The patient was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 3. The patient was managed with a comprehensive therapeutic regimen including valsartan (for proteinuria control), empagliflozin (for kidney protection), febuxostat (for hyperuricemia management), and sodium bicarbonate (for urine alkalization) (Table 1). At the 1-year follow-up (January 22, 2025), laboratory evaluation demonstrated stable renal function (serum creatinine 155.8 μmol/L) with significantly improved proteinuria (trace [1+] (near-normal) on urinalysis; urine protein-to-creatinine ratio 0.29).
A 36-year-old male proband presented to our department on April 7, 2024, with a 3-year history of persistently elevated serum creatinine and abnormal urinalysis. Serum creatinine fluctuated between 119 and 129 μmol/L over the past 3 years. Urinalysis demonstrated microscopic hematuria (occult blood 2+) without proteinuria. The patient had no personal history of hypertension or gout. Family history was significant for chronic kidney disease, including: (1) father with end-stage renal disease (status post renal transplantation), (2) maternal aunt with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (5-year duration), and (3) paternal grandmother who succumbed to uremia (Figure 4). Physical examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory evaluation revealed microscopic hematuria (36.2 RBCs/μL) without proteinuria, with normal 24-h urinary protein excretion (0.085 g). Serum biochemistry showed normal albumin (40.8 g/L), mildly elevated creatinine (120 μmol/L), and hyperuricemia (458 μmol/L). Comprehensive workup excluded secondary causes of nephropathy. Renal ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with altered parenchymal echogenicity and a 2.0 × 0.5 cm right renal cyst.
NGS analysis identified a heterozygous UMOD mutation (NM_003361.4: c.1499C > T: p. Ala500Val), located within exon 7. The affected alanine residue at position 500 demonstrated remarkable evolutionary conservation across species (Figure 5). This variant was recorded in ClinVar under accession number RCV005019788.2. While this variant had been submitted to the ClinVar database, it had not been comprehensively described in the peer-reviewed literature. Our case provided detailed clinical and phenotypic information for this variant.
The patient was diagnosed with CKD stage 2. The patient was managed with febuxostat for hyperuricemia control (Table 1). At the 6-month follow-up (November 12, 2024), laboratory assessment demonstrated stable renal function (serum creatinine 120 μmol/L) with resolution of proteinuria (urine dipstick negative) and minimal microscopic hematuria (20 RBCs/μL).
A 41-year-old male proband presented to our department on June 23, 2023, with a 5-year history of persistently elevated serum creatinine and abnormal urinalysis findings. His serum creatinine fluctuated between 110 and 142 μmol/L over the past 5 years. Laboratory evaluation revealed trace proteinuria without hematuria. The patient had no personal history of hypertension or gout. His father and uncle both developed ESRD (see pedigree, Figure 6). Physical examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrated trace proteinuria (24-h urinary protein excretion: 0.163 g) without hematuria. Serum biochemistry revealed normal albumin levels (40.1 g/L) with elevated serum creatinine (142.5 μmol/L) and marked hyperuricemia (531 μmol/L). Comprehensive workup excluded secondary causes of nephropathy. Renal ultrasound revealed normal-sized kidneys with altered parenchymal echogenicity and a 1.4 × 1.4 cm right renal cyst.
NGS analysis identified a heterozygous UMOD mutation (NM_003361.4: c.197T > C: p. Leu66Pro), located within exon 3. The affected leucine residue at position 66 demonstrated exceptional evolutionary conservation across vertebrate species (Figure 7). This variant had been submitted to ClinVar with accession number RCV002251377.14. Although this variant had been previously reported in a Chinese family with ADTKD, Our independent identification of this variant in a new family confirmed its pathogenicity and allowed for further observation of its phenotypic expression.
The patient was diagnosed with CKD stage 3. The patient was managed with febuxostat, combined with nephroprotective agents (Table 1). At the 6-month follow-up (September 12, 2024), laboratory assessment demonstrated stable renal function (serum creatinine: 99 μmol/L) without proteinuria and hematuria.

A 12-year-old Hispanic female with well-controlled systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) complicated by hypertension, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, and acute anterior uveitis, on biweekly tocilizumab, was referred to the nephrology clinic for persistent proteinuria. She was diagnosed with sJIA in 2022 and was in clinical remission on tocilizumab several months later. Proteinuria was first noted in 2023, 1.5 years after diagnosis of sJIA and 11 months into a state of clinically inactive disease.
She was referred to nephrology for proteinuria in 2024 with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPC) ranging from 1 to 1.5 mg/mg (normal < 0.2 g/g) and a normal albumin of 4 g/dL. She had no microscopic hematuria, and her serum creatinine was normal at 0.49 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 104.5 mL/min/1.73 m2 using the CKiD U25 equation. She was normotensive with a blood pressure of 99/70. Serologic workup was largely unremarkable aside from a positive antinuclear antibody titer (ANA) at 1:640 and a mildly low C3 level at 73 mg/dL (reference range 93–203 mg/dL). At the time of presentation with proteinuria, the patient’s sJIA was clinically inactive, with no fevers, rash, or arthritis, and normal inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP).
Initial kidney biopsy revealed mild C3GN versus latent infection-related GN. The sample contained 15–22 glomeruli, of which 1–3 were globally sclerosed. The remaining glomeruli showed mild segmental mesangial hypercellularity. Focal mild interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) were seen without significant interstitial inflammation. IF microscopy showed 5 glomeruli, 1 of which was globally sclerosed. Tubulointerstitial changes were similar to LM findings noted above. IF showed mesangial staining for C3 (1–2 +). No glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, or kappa or lambda light chains was seen. EM revealed parts of 3 glomeruli, 2 of which were globally sclerosed. A few mesangial electron-dense deposits and a single subepithelial electron-dense deposit were seen and identified as normal. The podocyte foot processes showed focal effacement. Serum C3 normalized on repeat testing one month later to 99.6 mg/dL. The C3 Glomerulopathy Complement Panel (C3G-CP) was sent to Iowa Health Care and was negative.
She was started on angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE-I) therapy for two months, yet UPC increased into the nephrotic range (2–2.2 mg/mg). High-dose prednisone (60 mg daily) was initiated for 4 weeks, resulting in mild improvement of her UPC to 1.4 mg/mg. Steroids were tapered, and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) (600 mg/m2 twice daily) was added alongside daily ACE-I. Tocilizumab was spaced to every six weeks after MMF initiation.
Despite induction immunosuppression directed at C3GN, she had persistent proteinuria with UPC of 1.75 mg/mg; therefore, a second biopsy was performed. Results showed features of membranous glomerulopathy with masked IgG-kappa deposits. LM revealed thickened glomerular basement membranes with mild mesangial hypercellularity, raising suspicion for membranous nephropathy. Jones silver stain demonstrated frequent glomerular basement membrane (GBM) spikes, and several glomeruli showed segmental sclerosis. Again, no significant IFTA was noted. Routine IF again demonstrated only granular mesangial C3 staining. Given suspicion for MGMID based on her personal history of an autoimmune disease, IF was repeated on paraffin-embedded tissue with protease digestion, which revealed IgG-kappa deposits (Fig. 1).
Retrospective paraffin IF staining of the first biopsy was negative. EM from the initial biopsy showed only infrequent subepithelial deposits, likely suggesting early disease. At this time, we elected to initiate therapy with steroids and MMF for its efficacy and relative simplicity, as it does not require routine therapeutic drug monitoring. Additionally, we aimed to avoid the potential burden of an additional infusion on her quality of life.
This patient has remained on ACE-I and MMF with progressive improvement, with UPC decreasing to 0.32 mg/mg after 7 months (Fig. 2). Creatinine at last follow-up was 0.47 mg/dL. Although it is unknown what her response would have been without intervention, we hypothesize that the continued resolution of her proteinuria is a result of time on treatment. Her kidney function remains normal, and tocilizumab infusions have been discontinued as her sJIA has been in long-term remission.

We had three cases of fetal kidneys with T2-hyperintense cortex and T2-hypointense medulla reversal of the correct appearance. In all of them, the kidneys were enlarged and hyperechoic on US of the second or third trimester, and the inverted pattern of cortex and medulla was only found on MRI. All fetuses had enlarged kidneys on MRI performed between 32 and 36 weeks (range 52–58 mm), weaker diffusion restriction in the kidneys than under normal conditions, had their bladders filled, and no oligohydramnios/anhydramnios. Figure 1 presents the MRI findings in fetus no. 1 compared with normal appearance of the fetal kidneys and with postnatal sonographic appearance.
In male case no. 1, amniocentesis was performed due to the first trimester sonographic abnormalities (tricuspid valve regurgitation, regurgitation wave A, enlarged urinary bladder). The array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) analysis of the DNA extracted from uncultured amniocytes showed the deletion at 17q12 region ~ 1.4 Mb in size encompassing the region of renal cysts and diabetes (RCAD) syndrome (OMIM 137920, ORPHA: 93111). The deletion included 15 protein-coding genes, including the HNF1B gene. So far, no parental examination has been performed to assess the origin of the deletion of 17q12. At the age of 14 months, the boy’s kidney function parameters were within normal limits.
In female case no. 2, there was postnatal appearance of bilateral multicystic kidney, so the PKHD1 gene was sequenced and no pathogenic variants were identified. As there was also a Müllerian duct anomaly (bicorporeal uterus with double cervix), microdeletion 17q12 syndrome was then suspected. The results of Multiplex Ligation-dependent Probe Amplification (MLPA; Kit P297-D1, MRC-Holland, Amsterdam) revealed heterozygous deletion in the region of the long arm of chromosome 17 including genes ZNHIT3, LHX1, AATF, ACACA, and HNF1B, which refers to the region typical for 17q12 microdeletion syndrome. The parents have declined testing themselves. At the age of 4.5 years, the girl has normal kidney function, and on US, the kidneys show increased cortical echogenicity, preserved cortico-medullary differentiation, and a few cortical cysts up to 4 mm. No more detailed examination of the reproductive system was performed.
The same 17q12 deletion as in case no. 1 was identified postnatally in male case no. 3 using the same technique (aCGH analysis of the DNA extracted from blood). The results of MLPA in the healthy young parents are pending. Up until the age of 1 month, the boy showed no biochemical abnormalities, including kidney function parameters.

An eight-month-old male infant was referred to our center with the clinical diagnosis of prenatal onset Bartter syndrome, severe polyuria, advanced CKD, and poor response to treatment with sodium chloride and potassium chloride supplements, associated with ibuprofen first or indomethacin later. Initial genetic testing for SLC12A1, KCNJ1, BSND, CLCNKA, CLCNKB, MAGED2, and SLC12A3 genes was negative. Further diagnostic work-up including a panel of additional genes associated with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (CASR, KCNJ10, SCNN1B, SCNN1G, SCN4A, CLCN5, OCRL1, HNF1B, SCNN1A, NR3C2) turned out to be also negative.
He was the 2nd child from consanguineous parents, without a record of family kidney diseases, born after cesarean delivery at 34 weeks of gestation complicated by polyhydramnios since the 29th week. He was born with normal weight and length for age (Table 1), and normal physical exam except significant hypotonia. After birth, he presented early and severe polyuria (7 mL/kg/day), associated with severe metabolic alkalosis, hyponatremia, and hypochloremia of renal origin, but normocalciuria. Other findings included remarkable hyperuricemia, mild hypercalcemia (2.84 mmol/L), and hypermagnesemia (1.28 mmol/L) associated with severe kidney dysfunction (Table 1). Initially, kidney ultrasound was reported as normal. No extrarenal manifestations were observed. He was treated with high fluids and electrolyte supplementation (up to 28.4 mmoL/kg/day of NaCl and up to 196 ml/kg/day of fluids), and transiently discharged home at 1.5 months of life with enteral feeding. He continued with polyuria and suffered from several episodes of hyponatremic, hypochloremic, and hypokalemic severe metabolic alkalosis, and progressive CKD (Table 1). Repeated ultrasound at 4 months of age showed that both kidneys were small, at the lower normal range for age, with diffuse cortical echogenicity lack of corticomedullary differentiation, without nephrocalcinosis. Patient management during the first months of life became extremely difficult due to treatment with high doses of electrolyte supplementation, feeding difficulties, prolonged hospitalization, and delayed growth and development. Prostaglandin inhibition with ibuprofen or indomethacin was ineffective and worsened patient eGFR.
Upon arriving to our center at 8 months, indomethacin was discontinued due to advanced CKD. Enteral feeding was started through a nasogastric tube first and gastro-jejunostomy later. The child had increased serum aldosterone levels and low plasma renin activity. Urinary prostaglandin E and complementary exams (echocardiogram, funduscopy, esophagogram, central nervous system magnetic resonance, and hormonal studies) were normal (Table 1). A new ultrasound revealed normal-sized but dedifferentiated kidneys without nephrocalcinosis.
Over time, we achieved better patient control and development after intensive nutrition, water, and electrolyte supplementation, which enabled discharge from hospital. Currently, he is 2 years old, with normal weight and growth. He has a severe renal salt-wasting phenotype associated with CKD 4 (eGFR Schwartz 2009 32.4 mL/min/1.73 m2; eGFR creatinine-cystatin C-based CKiD 27 mL/min/1.73 m2). He developed hypertension at 12 months of age and was treated with two drugs (carvedilol and amlodipine). He still receives salt supplementation (15 mmoL/kg/day) to maintain plasma electrolytic balance. Tubular proteinuria has been noted (β2-microglobulin 1.61 mg/L (normal value: 0–0.10); β2-microglobulin/creatinine ratio of 20,125 µg/g) with no albuminuria.
Additional genetic analyses with whole exome sequencing demonstrated a homozygous variant in the TFCP2L1 gene (TFCP2L1 (NM_014553.3):c.1279 del; p.(Gln427Serfs*18)) encoding the transcription factor CP2-like 1. This variant is predicted to lead to a frameshift transcript, resulting in either a truncated protein or non-sense mediated mRNA decay. This variant has not been reported previously, either in ClinVar or in Human Gene Mutation database (HGMD®) and it is not present in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD). Currently, this variant is classified as “likely pathogenic” according to the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG-AMP) guidelines (PVS1, PM2). However, the evidence of this gene as a monogenic cause of kidney dysplasia and salt-losing tubulopathy is limited due to the presence of only one patient with a similar clinical picture previously reported. Segregation analysis showed heterozygous carrier status of the parents.

A 77-year-old man with a history of distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction for gastric cancer presented with fever, general fatigue, and dysarthria. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed acute cerebral infarction. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus oralis, and echocardiography demonstrated vegetations on the mitral valve, leading to the diagnosis of IE.
Because the vegetation showed low mobility and mitral regurgitation was not severe, conservative treatment with intravenous antibiotic therapy was initiated. Approximately 1 month later, the patient developed lower back pain, and lumbar magnetic resonance imaging revealed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (Fig 1).
Concurrently, rapid morphological changes were observed in a previously diagnosed AAA, leading to the diagnosis of infected AAA with impending rupture (Fig 2). Inflammatory markers had normalized, and blood cultures had become negative, indicating clinical control of IE.
Semiurgent surgical intervention for the infected AAA was required. However, the adjacent untreated spinal infection was considered to pose a high risk of graft reinfection. Therefore, a single-stage multidisciplinary surgical approach was planned.
Because the patient had previously undergone robot-assisted distal gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction, the availability of the greater omentum for graft coverage was uncertain. Therefore, alternative reconstructive options, including a rectus abdominis muscle flap, were considered preoperatively.
During adhesiolysis, a viable residual omentum was identified and preserved for graft coverage.
The vascular surgery team performed complete resection of infected aortic tissue followed by in situ reconstruction using a rifampicin-soaked prosthetic graft. The graft was routed through a pathway separate from the infected spinal field, representing an infection-avoiding graft-routing strategy (Fig 3).
After extensive irrigation, the orthopedic surgery team performed L4/5 discectomy, curettage, and resection of the necrotic vertebral end plate, followed by anterior spinal reconstruction using an autologous iliac crest bone graft without instrumentation (Fig 4). The anterior vertebral periosteum was closed to the extent feasible to separate the spinal field from the vascular graft. The graft was repeatedly irrigated intraoperatively and finally covered with the omental flap.
Intraoperative cultures from the aneurysm, vertebral body, and intervertebral disc showed no growth of pathogenic organisms.
Postoperatively, the patient developed chylous ascites, which subsequently resolved with temporary abdominal drainage and conservative management. No recurrence of infection was observed, and the patient was discharged approximately 3 months after surgery with continued oral antibiotic therapy (Fig 5).

A 70-year-old male presented to the hospital with intermittent ache and swelling in his right foot. The patient claimed he had had the pain for several years and had difficulty standing and walking. The pain worsened during the night and was alleviated with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). There was no history of concomitant trauma. The pain was localized in the head of the fifth metatarsal. In physical examination, the distal diaphysis was tender and swollen without erythema and calor (Fig. 1). Range of motion (RoM) was intact, and there were no signs of neurovascular defects. Initially, standard dorsoplantar (AP) and lateral radiographs of the foot were obtained. In general, there was no sign of fracture or dislocation with normal overall alignment. In lateral view, a small cyst-like lesion was seen (Fig. 2). Further imaging of the fifth metatarsal showed subtle cortical thickening along the shaft and a small lytic lesion in the axial view of computed tomography (Fig. 3). On MRI, on a T1 weighted image, small, round, low signal lesion in the cortex (nidus) was seen (Fig. 4).
In hematological assessments, inflammatory biomarkers were negative. Bone tumor biomarkers (Ca, Phos, LDH, and PTH) and PSA were also normal. There was no trace of bence jones protein in the urine.
The patient underwent excision of the soft tissue mass along with curettage of the cyst and cauterization of the inner walls (Fig. 5, Fig. 6).
A superficial dorsolateral incision was made over the head of the fifth metatarsal. The soft tissue cyst was excised along with its capsule (Fig. 7). At that point, the nidus and the site of the cyst were curetted. Then, the skin tissues were sutured. Pathological inspection of the excised mass revealed a ganglion cyst with an osteoid osteoma of the head of the fifth metatarsal (Fig. 8). Within 10 days after the operation, clinical symptoms resolved thoroughly (Fig. 9).

A 32-year-old woman presented with a two-year history of progressively worsening bilateral lateral calf pain associated with dysesthesia. The symptoms were exertional in nature, initially occurring after prolonged walking but gradually progressing to occur after walking distances as short as approximately 90 meters. The patient also reported symptom exacerbation with prolonged standing. Symptoms were consistently relieved with rest.
The patient had no significant past medical or surgical history. There was no family history of neuromuscular, connective tissue or peripheral nerve disorders. She denied lower back pain, lower limb trauma and previous lower limb surgery. There was no history suggestive of vascular claudication.
Clinical examination demonstrated altered sensation over the anterolateral aspects of both lower legs. Motor examination revealed no weakness and there was no evidence of foot drop. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were palpable and symmetrical bilaterally. No palpable masses were identified in either calf at rest.
Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits and were not contributory to the diagnosis.
Given the exertional nature of the symptoms and their distribution, neurogenic claudication secondary to lumbar spinal pathology was initially suspected. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated no evidence of spinal canal stenosis, intervertebral disc herniation or nerve root compression.
Due to the persistence of symptoms and normal lumbar imaging, further evaluation was undertaken. MRI of both calves was performed on a 1.5-T MRI system using axial and coronal T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences. Imaging demonstrated bilateral focal defects measuring approximately 5-8 mm in the deep fascia of the lateral compartments. Through these defects, the peroneus longus muscles were seen to herniate into the subcutaneous tissues. At the level of the fascial defects, the superficial peroneal nerves were visualized in close proximity to the herniated muscle and appeared compressed (Fig. 1A–D).
No alternative cause of superficial peroneal nerve compression was identified. Specifically, there was no evidence of lipoma, peripheral nerve sheath tumor, ganglion cyst, venous malformation, venous engorgement or vascular compression.
These imaging findings were considered consistent with bilateral superficial peroneal nerve compression secondary to peroneus longus muscle herniation and correlated closely with the patient’s symptoms.
Initial management consisted of activity modification, physiotherapy, and analgesia over a period of six months. Due to persistent symptoms, multidisciplinary discussion was undertaken and the patient underwent bilateral targeted fasciotomy with decompression of the superficial peroneal nerves. The procedure was performed without complication.
At postoperative follow-up, the patient reported complete resolution of symptoms, including both pain and dysesthesia. She was able to return to normal activities without limitation. Postoperative imaging was not performed because complete clinical resolution was achieved and there was no clinical suspicion of recurrent nerve compression or postoperative complications.

A 62 years old man was referred to the Interventional Radiology Department for an internal/external biliary drain exchange, on a background of unresectable duodenal adenocarcinoma. The locally invasive neoplasm involved the first part of the duodenum (D1) and extended into the common bile duct and the right hepatic duct, thus requiring a palliative internal/external biliary drain.
The procedure was performed under fluoroscopy with a plan for routine exchange of an indwelling 8.5 French Cook internal/external biliary drain (Cook Medical, Bloomington, IN). A control image was obtained to assess the position of the indwelling drain. An Advantage Glidewire with a hydrophilic tip (Terumo Corp., Somerset, NJ) was placed through the indwelling drain into the duodenum and the internal/external drain was removed over the wire. A new 8.5 French drain was subsequently placed over the wire with its distal tip in the duodenum (Fig. 1). During the procedure, the distal locking pigtail loop appeared to be mispositioned in the third part of the duodenum (Fig. 2) and proximal retraction of the drain was performed. Increased resistance was felt during retraction, and retraction was halted to allow a repeat contrast injection to assess the drain position which was then appropriately positioned in the second part of the duodenum. Subsequent contrast injection demonstrated a 3 cm filling defect within the third part of the duodenum with evidence of obstruction of contrast flow beyond this area, the features of which were recognized as an intussusception (Fig. 3). The intussusception was presumed to result from traction of the catheter tip on the inner mucosa during proximal positioning. Notably, the mechanism of this case differs from typical antegrade intussusception, as the tip of the catheter pulled the distal bowel proximally.
The intussusception was promptly treated by rapidly instilling a combination of saline and contrast into the duodenum through the internal/external drain while screening with fluoroscopy. Using a 50 mL syringe, a mixture of 50:50 saline and contrast was manually injected over 20 seconds in firm boluses. The contrast allowed real time fluoroscopic visualization of intraluminal pressure changes and reduction of the intussusception (Fig. 4). Injection was performed steadily, with the operator keeping alert to signs of perforation. No prophylactic antibiotics were used. No sedation was necessary beyond standard procedural analgesia, and bowel rest was not required. Following procedure, cross sectional imaging with computed tomography (CT) was performed to confirm that the intussusception had completely resolved. The patient remained well and was discharged later that day.

A 2-year-old Nauruan girl with known beta-ketothiolase (T2) deficiency presented to our institution with acute metabolic decompensation and encephalopathy.
Seventeen months before the current admission, at the age of approximately 7 months, the patient had been hospitalized at an overseas center with an episode of depressed consciousness following an upper respiratory tract infection. At that time, she was noted to have tachypnea and decreased responsiveness. Laboratory evaluation revealed severe metabolic acidosis with markedly elevated anion gap and strong ketonuria; lactate was not significantly elevated. An inborn error of metabolism was suspected.
Because of concern for infectious or inflammatory encephalitis or demyelinating disease, a brain MRI was obtained. That MRI demonstrated normal brain parenchyma, without abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, no restricted diffusion, and no abnormal enhancement. There was no evidence of encephalitis, demyelination, or a primary metabolic leukoencephalopathy. No basal ganglia, brainstem, or cerebellar signal abnormalities were identified at that time (Fig. 1A-D).
Given the unexplained severe ketoacidosis and normal structural MRI, a comprehensive metabolic and genetic evaluation was pursued. Urine organic acid analysis showed a pattern consistent with an organic acidemia; subsequent extended genetic testing identified homozygosity for the I323V mutation in the acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1 (ACAT1) gene. This I323V variant has been well established as a pathogenic mutation causing beta-ketothiolase deficiency. Based on the biochemical and molecular findings, a diagnosis of beta-ketothiolase deficiency was made. The patient was started on dietary management, including avoidance of prolonged fasting and moderate protein restriction, together with carnitine supplementation, and she remained clinically stable until the current episode.
At 2 years of age, the patient was admitted to our hospital with a 1-day history of vomiting and diarrhea, leading to moderate dehydration. Initially, she was alert but irritable. Intravenous fluids were administered, and gastrointestinal symptoms improved.
Within 12 hours of admission, she developed progressive respiratory distress with wheezing and increased work of breathing. On hospital day 3, she acutely deteriorated neurologically: her Glasgow Coma Scale score fell to 8 (E2V2M4), with poor eye opening, incomprehensible sounds, and withdrawal to pain only. She was tachypneic and tachycardic, with borderline hypotension and persistent signs of dehydration. Laboratory evaluation at this time revealed: Severe euglycemic metabolic ketoacidosis on central venous blood gas: pH 6.91, bicarbonate 3.4 mmol/L, and base excess −29. Strongly positive urine ketones. Lactate within normal limits. Leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, with preserved renal function (Fig. 2).
These findings were consistent with an acute metabolic crisis due to BKTD, triggered by intercurrent gastrointestinal illness.
Subsequently CT scan was done to rule out metabolic related Brian disease and brain edema. Noncontrast CT of the brain (Fig. 3A-D) demonstrated bilateral, symmetric hypodensity of the globus pallidus, with mean attenuation of approximately 20 HU and no evidence of hemorrhage. In the setting of severe metabolic acidosis, this appearance was considered suggestive of early microcystic degeneration secondary to metabolic injury. A small additional hypodense focus was noted in the right parietal white matter, while the remainder of the brain parenchyma was unremarkable. There was no mass effect, midline shift, generalized cerebral edema, or hydrocephalus.
Because of ongoing clinical deterioration, a follow-up non-contrast CT was obtained during continued metabolic instability (Fig. 4A-D). This study showed clear interval progression, with extension of the hypodensity from globipallidi to involve both putamina, resulting in more extensive lentiform nucleus involvement. In addition, new, symmetric hypodensities were identified in the bilateral cerebral peduncles and asymmetric hypodensity in the bilateral frontal lobe. This progressive, highly symmetric pattern indicated that the metabolic insult was not static and suggested that deep gray injury could propagate along myelinated white-matter pathways when metabolic derangement persisted. After correction of the metabolic acidosis, the patient’s level of consciousness improved and laboratory parameters normalized, and she was referred overseas for MRI and further management.
Subsequent MRI demonstrated corresponding chronic and acute changes. Within the basal ganglia, the bilateral globus pallidi were T2- and FLAIR-hyperintense and T1-hypointense. There was no diffusion restriction in the globipallidi on DWI/ADC maps. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) revealed punctate foci of hypointensity within both globipallidi, compatible with microhemorrhages (Fig. 5A-F). Taken together, these features were interpreted as microcystic cavitary degeneration with associated microhemorrhage, representing irreversible basal ganglia injury and closely resembling the chronic stage described in prior BKTD reports. In contrast, the bilateral cerebral peduncles and adjacent brainstem showed T2-hyperintense, T1-hypointense signal with corresponding diffusion restriction (DWI hyperintensity and low ADC) (Fig. 6A-D), in keeping with acute/subacute tract injury temporally related to the recent metabolic crisis. Additional small, scattered T2/FLAIR hyperintense foci were present in the subcortical and deep white matter of the bilateral frontal lobes and the right parietal lobe and temporal lobe, more prominent on the right, without diffusion restriction, suggesting subacute–chronic gliotic white-matter changes rather than acute infarction (Fig. 7A-D). Finally, there was generalized decrease in brain volume, with prominence of the ventricles and cortical sulci, compatible with diffuse cerebral atrophy (Fig. 6, Fig. 7A-D). Together, the CT and MRI findings support a pattern of irreversible pallidal degeneration with microhemorrhage, superimposed on acute/subacute peduncular tract injury and more diffuse white-matter and global brain involvement following severe metabolic decompensation in beta-ketothiolase deficiency.
The patient was managed with aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, sodium bicarbonate infusion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and metabolic stabilization with high-calorie, glucose-based nutrition and protein restriction. After correction of the acidosis, her neurological status gradually improved. She was discharged on carnitine supplementation, strict dietary protein/isoleucine restriction, and close metabolic follow-up. Interval neuroimaging was planned to monitor basal ganglia and tract-related sequelae.
Initial CT showed globus pallidus hypodensity, mirroring the pallidal-predominant pattern described on MRI in O’Neill’s case, but identified on CT due to lack of immediate MRI, (Fig. 4). Follow-up CT revealed progression to involve both putamina and the cerebral peduncles, demonstrating that the injury is dynamic and may propagate beyond the pallidi during ongoing metabolic stress (Fig. 5).
Subsequent MRI showed chronic-stage globus pallidus lesions—T2/FLAIR hyperintense, T1 hypointense, nonrestricting, with punctate SWI hypointensities suggestive of microhemorrhage—fully consistent with microcystic cavitary degeneration and irreversible basal ganglia damage described in the chronic phase of BKTD (Fig. 6).
Increasingly, BKTD is recognized to involve extra-basal ganglia structures. Guo et al. reported a 10-month-old girl with severe BKTD whose MRI showed T2/DWI hyperintensities affecting the caudate nuclei, lentiform nuclei, bilateral cerebral peduncles, and mesencephalon (periaqueductal region). Over time, diffusion restriction resolved and basal ganglia lesions evolved to liquefactive cavitation and atrophy, while brainstem lesions fully regressed. Al-sawadi and Hussain reported combined basal ganglia and cerebellar involvement with multiple cerebellar hypodense foci on CT and T2/FLAIR hyperintensities on MRI that partially regressed but left the patient ataxic. Zhang et al. described additional pediatric cases with both basal ganglia and cerebellar abnormalities.
In our patient, extra-basal ganglia involvement is clearly demonstrated on CT progression from globus pallidus hypodensity to new hypodensities in the cerebral peduncles, suggesting early tract involvement (Fig. 5). MRI confirm bilateral cerebral peduncle lesions that are T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense with diffusion restriction, indicating acute/subacute insult (Fig. 6).
Additional nonrestricting T2/FLAIR hyperintense foci in the rightfrontal and right parietal white matter, together with generalized cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, indicate more diffuse brain involvement, likely from repeated or severe metabolic stress (Fig. 7).
This constellation—irreversible pallidal degeneration, acute/subacute peduncular lesions, and widespread white matter abnormalities—is highly concordant with severe BKTD as described by Guo et al. and underscores that BKTD can produce both focal (deep gray and tract) and diffuse (white matter and global atrophy) brain injury.
The basal ganglia, especially the globus pallidus and putamen, have high metabolic demands and are particularly sensitive to fluctuations in oxidative metabolism and pH. In BKTD, impaired ketone body utilization and accumulation of organic acids lead to energy failure and oxidative stress in these regions. The extension of lesions along internal capsules, corticospinal tracts, and cerebral peduncles likely reflects a combination of direct metabolic susceptibility of highly myelinated long tracts and secondary Wallerian degeneration propagated from primary basal ganglia injury.
Differential diagnosis, the differential diagnosis of symmetric basal ganglia lesions in a child includes other organic acidemias (methylmalonic, propionic, and isovaleric), pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, urea-cycle disorders, hypoxic–ischemic injury, carbon monoxide poisoning, Wilson’s disease, and neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, among others. However, in this case, the known ACAT1-related BKTD, age, severe euglycemic ketoacidosis with normal lactate, highly symmetric nonvascular distribution, and temporally normal prior MRI strongly support BKTD as the etiology. In a child with severe ketoacidosis and acute encephalopathy, bilateral globus pallidus hypodensity on CT should prompt consideration of BKTD and other inborn errors of metabolism. Interval extension of lesions to the putamina and cerebral peduncles indicates ongoing metabolic injury and parallels patterns of tract involvement described on MRI in severe BKTD. MRI demonstrating T2/FLAIR hyperintense, T1 hypointense, nonrestricting globus pallidus lesions with SWI microhemorrhages, plus diffusion-restricting peduncular lesions—helps differentiate irreversible basal ganglia damage from acute tract injury. A previously normal MRI is invaluable for confirming that these findings are acquired and temporally related to the metabolic crisis. Early radiologic recognition should trigger urgent metabolic evaluation and treatment to prevent further irreversible brain injury.

Table 1 shows the characteristics of the 5 patients, including the location of the lesion, medical history, and imaging findings. For case 1, 2, and 4, the lowest apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value was obtained at solid part.
A man in his 60s had swelling in his left inguinal region up to the left breech for 7 years since noticing the mass for the first time, which had grown rapidly for the past 3 months. His medical history included appendicitis, a subarachnoid hemorrhage, and hypertension. Marginal excision under general anesthesia was performed at a previous medical facility. Histopathological examination confirmed that the mass was a squamous cell carcinoma, and the surgical margin was positive. Therefore, the patient was referred to our hospital, and additional wide resection were performed.
