Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from the previous hospital demonstrated a multilocular cystic tumor measuring 11 × 7 cm from the left inguinal region to the left breech. Most lesions showed a high signal intensity on T2-weighted images (T2WI), with low signal intensity nodular lesions observed along the wall (Fig. 1A). The nodular lesions appeared as iso-intensity signal to muscle on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and demonstrated contrast enhancement (Figs. 1B and C). On diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and ADC map, the entire lesion exhibited a high and low signal intensity, respectively (Figs. 1D and E).
The pathological findings of the resected tumor reveal squamous cell carcinoma with marked keratinization is observed. The tumor appears to extend along the cyst wall and is surrounded by fibrous tissue. Tumor nests are also found within the surrounding fibrous tissue in some areas, suggesting invasion.
A man in his 60s had a mass in his right breech that had gradually grown over 10 years. Owing to pain in the same area, the patient consulted a previous medical provider. He had no relevant medical history. At the previous medical facility, he had been diagnosed with a subcutaneous cystic tumor, and marginal excision was performed under general anesthesia. On histopathological examination, the lesion was diagnosed as a squamous cell carcinoma arising from an epidermal cyst, and the surgical margins were found positive. Therefore, the patient was referred to our hospital, and additional wide resection were performed.
Preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a cystic tumor measuring 13 × 6 cm at his right breech. A nodular lesion was observed on the cyst wall (Figs. 2A-C). MRI at the time of recurrence revealed a cystic tumor measuring 10×4 cm at his right breech. A cystic tumor was observed predominantly within the subcutaneous adipose tissue with multiple nodular lesions visible on the wall and showing low signal intensity on T2WI (Figs. 2D and E). Most lesions appeared as iso-intensity signals to muscle on T1WI (Fig. 2F), and the nodular lesions exhibited substantial contrast enhancement (Fig. 2G). The nodular lesions exhibited restricted diffusion (Fig. 2H and I).
The pathological findings of the resected tumor reveal a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with marked keratinization, extending from subcutaneous tissue to skeletal muscle. The tumor is near the deep margin and may represent residual disease from a previous excision, as it is found adjacent to scar tissue and surgical sutures.
A man in his 50s consulted a physician for a mass in the posterior left thigh that had gradually grown. He had an injury to the posterior left thigh caused by a weed cutter 18 years previously. His medical history included infiltrating urothelial carcinoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia. At another hospital, the patient was diagnosed with a cystic tumor, and marginal excision was performed under general anesthesia. On histopathological examination, the lesion was diagnosed as a squamous cell carcinoma arising from an epidermal inclusion cyst, and the surgical margins were positive.
Preoperative MRI performed at another hospital revealed a cystic tumor measuring 7 × 6 cm at his posterior left thigh. The tumor showed heterogeneous intensity on T2WI (Figs. 3A and B) and iso-signal intensity to muscle on T1WI (Fig. 3C). On contrast-enhanced T1WI, the wall of the cyst and nodular lesion on the wall were well-enhanced (Fig. 3D). He was referred to our hospital, where additional wide resection and radiation therapy were performed. The resected specimen revealed a cystic lesion measuring approximately 7 cm.
Histologically, the lesion exhibited squamous cell carcinoma with keratinization, chromatin clumping, and eosinophilic cytoplasm proliferating within a cystic structure, with minimal invasion into the underlying skeletal muscle. Inflammatory cell infiltration was also noted in the surrounding tissue.
A man in his 80s presented with a tumor on his left shoulder. The size of the tumor was approximately 5 cm and had not changed for 60 years; however, it rapidly expanded in the past 1 year.
Preoperative MRI at a previous hospital revealed a subcutaneous tumor measuring 25 × 12 cm on his left shoulder. The tumor showed a heterogeneous signal with a dendritic low-signal area on the tumor wall on T2WI (Figs. 4A and B). The tumor edges were smooth. On T1WI, the tumor showed iso-intensity to muscle (Fig. 4C), and contrast-enhanced T1WI fat saturation showed partial enhancement at the dendritic low-signal area (Fig. 4D). DWI exhibited entirely low signal and low area in ADC map was observed corresponding the contrast enhanced area (Figs. 4E and F).
Needle biopsy revealed squamous cell carcinoma arising from the epidermis. Based on this diagnosis, the tumor was resected. The surgical margins were negative, indicating complete removal of the malignant tissues.
A 60s male presented with 2 contiguous bilobed cystic tumors measuring 9 × 5 cm and 7 × 7 cm on his left buttock. These tumors had been monitored for over a decade and showed no significant changes. The patient had no significant medical history.
Prior to surgery, a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed, which identified a well-demarcated bilocular mass measuring 13×4 cm in the left buttock area with a density of 26 HU, suggestive of an epidermal cyst. Thirteen years after the onset, owing to a recent increase in tumor size and discomfort, the patient underwent surgical intervention. Marginal excision of the tumors was performed under general anesthesia.
Histopathological examination revealed an epidermal cyst with a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma on the wall. The surgical margins were negative, indicating complete removal of the malignant tissues.

A 23-year-old unmarried woman with regular menstrual cycles presented with a painless swelling in the left axilla that had been gradually increasing over the past 5 months. She denied any history of trauma, infection, or previous breast or axillary surgery. Her medical, surgical, and family histories were unremarkable.
On physical examination, a well-defined, mobile, nontender mass was palpable in the left axillary region. The overlying skin showed no erythema, dimpling, or tethering, and there was no nipple retraction or discharge. Examination of both breasts was otherwise unremarkable, with no palpable masses or lymphadenopathy on the contralateral side.
On ultrasound, the left axillary lesion was an oval, heterogeneously hypoechoic mass located 3-4 mm deep to the skin and oriented parallel to the skin surface. The margins were macrolobulated with an angular upper margin, and no posterior acoustic features were present. A central echogenic line within the lesion initially raised the possibility of an enlarged lymph node. Taking these features together with interval growth over 5 months and the atypical axillary location, the lesion was categorized as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy was performed to establish a definitive diagnosis and exclude nodal pathology (Fig. 1). Two additional nodules were noted in the breast, at the 1 and 4 o’clock positions. Both were well-circumscribed, hypoechoic, and avascular, in keeping with incidental probably benign fibroadenomas, and both have remained stable in size on follow-up, consistent with a benign course.
A core needle biopsy of the axillary mass was performed. Histopathological analysis demonstrated compressed ducts lined by benign ductal epithelium within a fibromyxoid stroma, with focal areas of ductal proliferation features consistent with FA.
Following multidisciplinary team discussion, surgical excision of the left axillary mass was undertaken under local anesthesia through an elliptical incision. The lesion was completely excised, and the wound was closed in layers. Subsequent histopathological examination of the excised specimen confirmed the diagnosis of FA (Fig. 2). The postoperative course was uneventful, with satisfactory wound healing and no recurrence on follow-up.
The postoperative course was smooth, and the surgical wound healed by primary intention without complications. The patient remains asymptomatic and continues regular annual follow-up, with no evidence of recurrence or new lesions at 17 months.

An 8-year-old child presented to Nauru Medical Center with cough and failure to thrive. The child was born to a 36-year-old G3P3 mother via normal vaginal delivery after a previous cesarean section. Shortly after birth, the infant developed neonatal cyanosis, which initially resolved but later recurred, resulting in a 3-month admission to the neonatal intensive care unit, where oxygen therapy was required. At the age of 3 months, a CT scan of the chest suggested the presence of only a functioning left lung.
During early childhood, the patient was considered medically fragile and required home oxygen therapy until the age of 2 years. Despite early concerns regarding possible long-term disability, the child achieved all developmental milestones appropriately.
Since the age of 2 years, the patient has remained clinically stable, with no hospital admissions and only 1-2 minor respiratory illnesses per year, which were managed in the outpatient department. The child currently attends regular school and is in Grade 2.
The parents reported a history of recurrent respiratory infections since infancy, occasionally associated with symptoms suggestive of cardiac failure. These episodes required hospitalization on 1 occasion for 1 month, during which the patient was treated conservatively. Before the arrival of a new medical team from GMSS, Nauru Medical Center did not have specialist medical services available.
The parents denied any history of tuberculosis, hepatitis, or other chronic infectious diseases. They also denied any drug or food allergies. There was no history of chills, vomiting, diarrhea, or convulsions.
On physical examination, the child appeared comfortable at rest. Oxygen saturation on room air was 88%, likely reflecting chronic adaptation to long-standing hypoxemia. The most notable finding was digital clubbing involving the toes. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated hemoglobin level of 17.6 g/dL, above the normal range, likely to represent secondary polycythemia due to chronic hypoxemia. Other laboratory parameters were within normal limits, including white blood cell count, red blood cell count, neutrophil count and percentage, lymphocyte ratio, and platelet count. Additional investigations, including liver function tests, renal function tests, and immunoglobulin levels, were also normal.
The patient was referred to the radiology department for further cardiac evaluation and underwent transthoracic echocardiography. Echocardiography demonstrated marked cardiac displacement to the right side hemithorax with preserved normal leftward apex orientation and situs solitus (cardiac dextroposition), along with right ventricular hypertrophy and dilation of the right atrium and IVC (Fig. 1). About 8 mm in size an ASD was also identified, showing a bidirectional shunt more form right to left consistent with advanced pulmonary vascular disease.
There was a large PDA and a dilated main pulmonary artery with pulmonary HTN measuring 44 mmHg. The PDA demonstrated bidirectional flow on color Doppler imaging.
The left pulmonary veins drained into the left atrium, but the right pulmonary veins were not visualized draining into the left atrium. Instead, they appeared to course inferiorly and join the IVC, raising strong suspicion for anomalous pulmonary venous return with complex congenital cardiac anomalies and advanced pulmonary hypertension resulting in Eisenmenger syndrome.
A chest radiograph was subsequently performed. This showed a significant reduction in right lung volume with rightward mediastinal shift and relative hyperinflation of the left lung. The cardiac silhouette was difficult to delineate clearly due to the marked dextroposition and right lung hypoplasia (Fig. 2). In view of the suspected complex pulmonary venous anomaly, CT angiography of the chest was obtained for detailed anatomical assessment.
CT angiography revealed a severely hypoplastic right pulmonary artery and a markedly enlarged main pulmonary artery, with an increased pulmonary-to-aortic diameter ratio (2.89/1.55 = 1.9) (Fig. 4, Fig. 5), consistent with severe pulmonary hypertension. The right lung was hypoplastic, associated with rightward mediastinal shift and compensatory hypertrophy of the left lung (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). The pulmonary venous anatomy was abnormal: All the right pulmonary veins drained anomalously into the IVC above the diaphragm rather than into the left atrium (Fig. 5). In addition, the right lung received systemic arterial supply from branches arising directly from the abdominal aorta just superior to the celiac trunk, coursing upward to supply predominantly the entire right lung (Fig. 5).
The CT angiogram also demonstrated a large PDA (Type B, short, and wide configuration), with dilation of the main pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary artery (Fig. 4, Fig. 5). There was marked enlargement of the right atrium and right ventricle with myocardial hypertrophy, reflecting long-standing pressure overload (Fig. 1, Fig. 4). These findings, together with the right-to-left shunt at the atrial level (Fig. 1) and severe pulmonary hypertension and hemoglobin level of 17.6 g/dL and physical finding of differential clubbing, are consistent with Eisenmenger physiology.
Three-dimensional volume-rendered CT angiography images (Fig. 5C and D) provide a comprehensive overview of the vascular anomalies. They show: an aberrant systemic artery arising from the abdominal aorta and coursing superiorly to supply the right lung (blue arrow). A markedly hypoplastic right pulmonary artery (circle). The anomalous scimitar vein (star) descending along the right cardiac border and draining into the inferior vena cava.
Overall, the constellation of findings confirmed the diagnosis of severe, complex Scimitar syndrome with Eisenmenger syndrome, characterized by right lung hypoplasia, anomalous pulmonary venous drainage to the IVC, systemic arterial supply to the right lung, severe pulmonary arterial hypertension, and associated congenital cardiac defects.
Following confirmation of the diagnosis, the patient was managed conservatively with supportive treatment. Given the complexity of the congenital anomalies and the presence of Eisenmenger physiology, definitive management would require specialized multidisciplinary care. After consultation with a pediatric cardiologist and a cardiac surgeon, the decision was made to continue conservative management because of the advanced stage of the disease.

A 58-year-old man presented with recurrent bleeding from a permanent ileal conduit urostomy. His medical history was notable for bladder and prostate cancer treated with cystoprostatectomy and ileal conduit urinary diversion 2 years prior to presentation. Additional comorbidities included obesity (BMI 37 kg/m²), chronic kidney disease stage 3, prior venous thromboembolism on anticoagulation, and cirrhosis secondary to metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with ongoing alcohol use.
The patient experienced multiple hospital admissions over an 18-month period for recurrent episodes of gross hematuria via the urostomy, resulting in symptomatic anemia requiring repeated blood transfusions. He described steady, nonpulsatile bleeding from the stoma associated with fatigue and dyspnea. Social history was significant for continued alcohol consumption of approximately 3-6 beers daily with heavier intake on weekends.
On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable (blood pressure 127/79 mmHg, heart rate 84 bpm). The urostomy appliance contained gross blood. There was no ascites, jaundice, or hepatic encephalopathy. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL), preserved hepatic synthetic function (albumin 3.9 g/dL, INR 1.1), and chronic kidney disease (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL). The Model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) score was 12, and Child–Pugh class was A.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated hepatic steatosis, mild splenomegaly, and prominent stomal venous collaterals extending from the right superficial inferior epigastric vein to the ileal conduit, consistent with stomal varices (Fig. 1). Transhepatic portal venography confirmed portal hypertension with a portosystemic pressure gradient of 12 mmHg and demonstrated stomal varices draining into superficial abdominal wall veins (Fig. 2).
Endoscopic evaluation of the ileal conduit revealed mucosal congestion and vascular ectasia consistent with portal hypertensive enteropathy (PHE), as well as small grade I varices approximately 2 cm from the stoma without high-risk stigmata (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Correlation of imaging, venography, and endoscopic findings established the diagnosis of urostomy-associated stomal variceal bleeding secondary to portal hypertension.
Initial management consisted of direct percutaneous puncture of the stomal varices under fluoroscopic guidance. Venography confirmed variceal anatomy, and embolosclerotherapy was performed using 2 cc of sodium tetradecyl sulfate (STS) mixed with 6 cc of air, followed by Gelfoam slurry. This resulted in transient hemostasis.
Bleeding recurred after 4 weeks, with active hemorrhage visualized at the urostomy stoma. A transhepatic portal venous approach was subsequently pursued, and embolization of the stomal varices was performed using 0.018-inch detachable coils and Gelfoam (Fig. 5). Despite technical success, bleeding again recurred 6 weeks later.
Given prior evidence recommending carvedilol for treatment of increased hepatic vascular resistance, nonselective beta-blockade with carvedilol 6.25 mg twice daily was initiated for 6 weeks. Despite achieving adequate heart rate reduction (66 bpm), intermittent bleeding persisted. Due to the failure of local and embolization-based therapies, portal decompression was pursued.
A TIPS was placed via a transjugular approach, reducing the portosystemic gradient from 15 mmHg to 9 mmHg (Fig. 6). Following TIPS placement, the patient developed hepatic encephalopathy 1 week postprocedure, requiring hospitalization and initiation of lactulose and rifaximin. Symptoms resolved within 48 hours, and the patient was discharged home.
At 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up, Doppler ultrasound demonstrated a patent TIPS with normal flow velocities, and the patient reported no further episodes of urostomy bleeding.

A 62-year-old man visited his local physician with a 2-day history of persistent headache and nausea. Neurological examination revealed no focal deficits. Plain computed tomography (CT) of the head showed subarachnoid hemorrhage and subcortical hemorrhage predominantly in the left frontal lobe (Fig. 1A), and he was transferred to our hospital under the careful management of blood pressure. Three-dimensional CT angiography showed dilated cortical veins with varix extending from the left olfactory fossa to adjacent to the hematoma (Fig. 1B). Cerebral angiography of the left external carotid artery showed a cortical vein with a varix draining into the superior sagittal sinus via the facial and ethmoidal arteries, forming a shunt at the olfactory fossa (Fig. 2A-C). We diagnosed anterior cranial fossa dAVF, with the bleeding point considered to be the varix. Right internal carotid angiography also showed severe stenosis of the middle cerebral artery with the developed moyamoya vessels (Fig. 2D and F). Left internal carotid angiography showed stenosis from the terminal portion of the internal carotid artery to the M1 and A1 segments, with the development of moyamoya vessels in the surrounding area (Fig. 2E). The patient had vascular risk factors associated with atherosclerosis, including hypertension and diabetes mellitus. However, thin-slice T2-weighted MRI demonstrated shrinkage of the outer vessel diameter in the bilateral middle cerebral arteries and the terminal portion of the right internal carotid artery, findings that have been regarded as characteristic of moyamoya disease (Fig. 2G). No other cause of arterial stenosis, such as vasculitis, was identified. Furthermore, the patient had no known conditions associated with moyamoya syndrome, including neurofibromatosis type 1, Down syndrome, thyroid disease, or prior cranial irradiation. Accordingly, the patient fulfilled the current Japanese diagnostic criteria for moyamoya disease rather than moyamoya syndrome. Concomitant adult moyamoya disease was therefore diagnosed. No prior clinical episodes suggestive of transient ischemic attack (TIA) or imaging findings indicative of cerebral ischemia were identified. On hospital day 2, disconnection of the draining vein with unilateral left frontal craniotomy was performed to prevent rebleeding. Endovascular treatment was not selected because of the technical difficulty of catheter access, the low curative rate, and the potential risk of inadvertent embolic material migration into the ophthalmic artery. Care was taken to avoid intraoperative hypotension and hypocapnia in discussion with the anesthesiologist. Cerebral angiography on postoperative day 12 showed obliteration of shunt flow (Fig. 3). Because the patient was asymptomatic with respect to moyamoya disease and no old ischemic lesions were detected on neuroimaging, conservative observation was chosen. Genetic testing for RNF213 mutations was not performed. One month postoperatively the patient was discharged without any neurological deficit. As of 3 years postoperatively, no recurrence of dAVF has been seen and moyamoya disease has remained asymptomatic. Magnetic resonance angiography at follow-up revealed no interval changes, including no progression of arterial stenosis or development of new collateral channels related to craniotomy site (Fig. 4).

We present the case of a 45-year-old female with a past medical history of asthma and lactose intolerance who presented with bilateral hand numbness, migraines, neck pain, and left upper extremity pain. The patient described the neck pain as a sharp pain radiating down the left arm into the hand. The left upper extremity pain was positional and got worse at night. This started gradually but had been going on for about 5 months. On physical exam, the patient had upright posture with no visual deformity on inspection. There was tenderness on the cervical spine with limited flexion and extension of the neck. A positive Spurling test was observed on the left side. A positive Tinel sign was noted on median nerve compression testing bilaterally. The patient had a positive Adson and Roos test concerning for thoracic outlet syndrome as well as a positive Cozen’s test on the left elbow signifying lateral epicondylitis. Radiographic imaging of the cervical spine demonstrated fusion anomalies and hemivertebrae in the lower cervical and upper thoracic spine (consistent with a type II Klippel–Feil deformity) with mild superimposed degenerative changes (Fig. 1).
MRI of the cervical spine was obtained to better characterize the neurovascular structures associated with the fusion anomalies and to identify a focal source for the thoracic outlet syndrome symptoms. MRI clarified the anatomical relationships of the fusion anomalies and hemivertebrae. Specifically, there was a left C7 hemivertebra and a right T1 hemivertebra with an oblique vertebra extending from C7 on the right to T1 on the left (Fig. 2). Additionally, the images demonstrated an atypical relationship of the posterior arches. Specifically, the pedicle of the left C7 hemivertebra is connected to the right C7 portion of the oblique vertebra, and the pedicle of the right T1 hemivertebra is connected to the left T1 portion of the oblique vertebra. There were mild superimposed spondylodegenerative changes with disc protrusions at C3-C4 and C6-C7.
Additionally, there was a pseudoarthrosis between the left T1 and T2 ribs with associated compression of the left T1 nerve root. CTA imaging was performed to evaluate for vascular compression. The fusion anomalies and hemivertebrae were similar to prior imaging, but there was no evidence of vascular compression (Fig. 3). This pseudoarthrosis provides a plausible structural correlate for the patient’s left upper extremity symptoms.
Radiographs identified the initial cervicothoracic segmentation anomalies and prompted cross-sectional evaluation. MRI better characterized the complex vertebral anatomy, posterior arch relationships, disc protrusions, and relationship of the congenital anomalies to adjacent nerve roots. CTA confirmed the osseous configuration and demonstrated patency of the left subclavian artery without fixed vascular compression. Together, these modalities helped distinguish structural nerve root irritation from arterial thoracic outlet syndrome.
Overall, the imaging demonstrated a complex cervicothoracic congenital segmentation anomaly with left C7 and right T1 hemivertebrae, an oblique vertebral segment extending from C7 to T1, elongated lower cervical and upper thoracic block vertebrae, and pseudoarthrosis between the first and second left ribs. MRI demonstrated narrowing and compression of the adjacent left T1 nerve root, while CTA confirmed patency of the left subclavian artery without fixed arterial compression.
Symptomatic management involved bilateral wrist splints, physical therapy, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug gel 2-3 times daily. For her migraines, she was prescribed Rimegepant. Botox and epidural injections were discussed as options for her cervical radiculopathy. A nerve conduction study was performed, which demonstrated evidence of right carpal tunnel syndrome but normal left median nerve conduction which was unexpected given the left hand symptoms (Fig. 4). Later, electromyography demonstrated left C4 radiculopathy, which may have been related to the C3-C4 disc protrusion. However, the C6 and C7 conduction studies were normal.

A 71 year old male with a past medical history of atrial fibrillation, mild nonobstructive coronary artery disease, hypercholesteremia, prediabetes, no smoking history, and severe symptomatic aortic valve stenosis with an ejection fraction of 60%, a valve area 0.8 cm², a mean gradient of 40 mmHg, and peak velocity of 4.5 m/s, presented with progressively worsening dyspnea on exertion for evaluation for transcatheter valve replacement (TAVR). He denied chest pain, syncope, palpitations, however endorsed activity fatigue and dyspnea. He had a history of radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation and the placement of a permanent pacemaker. Family history was noncontributory for congenital or premature cardiovascular disease. Patient medications included aspirin, apixaban, and pravastatin. On a physical exam, blood pressure was 144 / 85 mmHg, heart rate was 76 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 95% on room air. There was additionally presence of a systolic murmur on auscultation, with the remainder of the exam within normal limits. Routine laboratory evaluation was not contributory.
Due to the symptomatic aortic stenosis, the patient underwent a chest CT angiogram for pre-procedural evaluation for TAVR. On TAVR CTA, a bicuspid aortic valve was identified, along with a 4.3 cm ascending aortic aneurysm and a 4.4 cm sinus of Valsalva aneurysm involving the noncoronary sinus. Most notably, CTA imaging demonstrated an incomplete membranous band in the left atrium along the interatrial septum/fossa ovalis, consistent with cor triatriatum sinister (Fig. 1). Anomalous coronary venous drainage additionally was identified with the left ventricular vein, great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, and small cardiac vein draining into the coronary sinus, which demonstrated drainage into the left atrium rather than the right atrium (Fig. 2). Three dimensional volume rendered reconstructions further delineated the anomalous venous anatomy and the adjacent cardiac structures (Fig. 3).
Following evaluation, the patient underwent successful transcatheter aortic valve replacement with implantation of a bioprosthetic aortic valve. Post procedural transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated appropriate prosthetic valve function without evidence of procedural complications. The examination also noted suspected cor triatriatum sinister without evidence of pulmonary venous flow restriction. At a 30 day follow up, the patient remained clinically stable and without concerns.

A 17 year old boy presented with chief complaints of poor urinary stream, straining, intermittency and overflow incontinence for 2 months. The boy had no prior history of hematuria or lower urinary tract symptoms. Examination revealed a palpable bladder that failed to recede completely following voiding. The external genitalia were normal and neurological examination didn’t reveal any abnormality. The initial ultrasound (USG) examination showed thick walled urinary bladder with significant post-void residual urine. The upper urinary tract was normal however a pedunculated polypoidal mass measuring 3×4cm was documented on the posterior bladder wall near neck (Fig. 1). The color doppler study revealed vascularity within the lesion and demonstrated its descent into prostatic urethra on voiding maneuver. Retrograde urethrography revealed a normal urethra with a smooth filling defect near the bladder neck. On voiding cystourethrography the same filling defect was seen to migrate into the posterior urethra (Fig. 2). Patient was planned for cystoscopic examination under general anesthesia. Cystoscopy revealed a polypoidal growth (4×3cm) with long stalk arising from the bladder neck on left side and completely blocking the bladder neck. A 16Fr non continuous resectoscope was introduced and the polyp was resected piecemeal with Monopolar cutting electrode (Fig. 3). Procedure was uneventful and patient had complete resolution of symptoms. Histopathology revealed polypoidal structures with broad based non-branching fronds lined by benign urothelium. The urothelium showed mucosal invaginations, nests of urothelial cells and glands in lamina propria consistent with cystitis glandularis (Fig. 4).

A 76-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prediabetes, and presented as a trauma transfer after a rollover motor vehicle collision. Initial evaluation at an outside hospital revealed bilateral rib fractures, a T10-T12 ligamentous injury with associated fluid collection, bilateral pneumothoraces requiring chest tube placement, and significant agitation requiring endotracheal intubation. He was subsequently transferred to our facility for higher-level neurosurgical care.
Upon arrival, the patient was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit for management of a 6 mm subdural vs epidural hematoma, thoracic spine injury, and respiratory failure. He remained intubated and sedated and was hemodynamically stable. On hospital day 3, ultrasound-guided right subclavian vein access was attempted using a standard 18-gauge introducer needle, and a 0.035-inch guidewire was advanced. Following placement of a 7F triple-lumen central venous catheter, arterial-appearing blood return was noted, and transduction confirmed arterial waveforms. Given the presence of a large-bore catheter within a noncompressible arterial location, the catheter was left in place to tamponade the arteriotomy and avoid uncontrolled hemorrhage. Computed tomography angiography of the chest confirmed direct cannulation of the lateral aspect of the distal brachiocephalic (innominate) artery, with the catheter tip extending into the aortic arch and a moderate mediastinal hematoma. No pseudoaneurysm or active extravasation was identified (Fig 1, A).
Given that the catheter entry site was located on the lateral aspect of the artery approximately 1 cm proximal to the carotid-subclavian bifurcation, simple catheter removal with manual pressure would be at high risk of uncontrolled hemorrhage into the mediastinum. Achieving an adequate endovascular seal would require covered stents deployed in a “kissing” configuration. The measured diameters of the proximal subclavian, common carotid, and innominate arteries were 12 , 8 , and 16 mm, respectively (Fig 1, B). To guide stent sizing, we applied a bifurcation formula based on Finet's law, originally derived from quantitative analysis of coronary artery bifurcations, which relates the diameter of the parent vessel to the sum of its daughter vessels: Dinnominate artery = 0.68 × (Dsubclavian stent + Dcarotid stent). Although this relationship has not been validated for supraaortic vessels, it provides a standardized framework to estimate combined branch diameters in the absence of established formulas for large bifurcations such as the innominate-carotid-subclavian junction. Proportional sizing of the branch stents helps optimize wall apposition and minimize gaps that could predispose to endoleak. Similar applications of fractal-based bifurcation sizing have been described in the common femoral artery, supporting the conceptual utility of this approach beyond coronary anatomy. In addition to applying this formula, we considered modest oversizing based on the direct vessel measurements and used careful balloon molding to further enhance seal and ensure durable exclusion of the arterial defect. Using the measured innominate diameter of 16 mm, this corresponded to a combined target stent diameter of approximately 24 mm for the subclavian and carotid branches. Based on these calculations, a fully endovascular approach was feasible only with a combination strategy: a Gore iliac extender stent-graft delivered via a brachial approach (eg, 16 mm proximally, 14.5 mm distally) paired with a 9-mm VIABAHN stent-graft.
The patient was brought to the hybrid-operating suite and placed under general anesthesia. Ultrasound-guided right common femoral artery access was obtained, and a 9F shuttle sheath was advanced into the aortic arch. A right brachial artery cutdown was performed, and a Rosen wire was advanced through the subclavian artery into the arch under fluoroscopy. Arch aortography confirmed a right subclavian venous catheter traversing the distal innominate artery near the carotid-subclavian bifurcation. A wire was advanced from the femoral access across the carotid origin, and a 9 × 50-mm VIABAHN stent-graft was positioned in the proximal carotid artery. Concurrently, a 14.5 × 70-mm Gore iliac limb endograft was advanced via the brachial access from the subclavian origin across the innominate artery, spanning the catheter entry site. Both devices were deployed simultaneously in a kissing configuration.
To enhance distal seal, an additional 9 × 50-mm VIABAHN was deployed in the carotid artery. Owing to the differences in radial force between the VIABAHN and the Excluder limb, proximal reinforcement of the carotid stent was performed using a 9 × 39-mm Omnilink balloon-expandable bare-metal stent (Abbott Vascular Inc.), with 3 to 4 mm protruding into the aortic arch to optimize apposition. Final kissing balloon molding was performed using the Omnilink delivery balloon and a Gore molding and occlusion balloon.
After adequate balloon molding and confirmation of stent apposition, the malpositioned central venous catheter was carefully withdrawn. Systemic anticoagulation was not administered given the presence of intracranial hemorrhage. To mitigate thrombotic risk, all sheaths were periodically flushed with heparinized saline, device exchanges were minimized, and wire and catheter manipulation within the aortic arch and supra-aortic vessels was performed with meticulous technique. Completion angiography demonstrated brisk, unobstructed flow through the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries, with no evidence of extravasation (Fig 2). The femoral access site was closed using a Perclose device (Abbott Vascular), and the brachial artery was repaired with the preplaced purse-string suture. The procedure concluded with a palpable radial pulse and no immediate complications. Postoperative computed tomography angiography confirmed widely patent carotid and subclavian stents with complete wall apposition within the innominate artery (Fig 3). Given the patient's intracranial hemorrhage, initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy was deferred. The patient was managed with aspirin 81 mg once deemed safe by the neurosurgical team after repeat computed tomography of the head demonstrated stable intracerebral hemorrhage, with close neurologic and imaging surveillance. At 1-month follow-up, the patient remained on aspirin 81 mg and a statin. Duplex ultrasound study demonstrated continued patency of the carotid and subclavian artery stents without evidence of elevated velocities. The patient remained neurologically intact, with plans for repeat duplex imaging at 6 months.

A 40-year-old female presented with productive cough, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, and fever. She reported a long history of recurrent respiratory symptoms beginning at the age of 17 years, characterized by repeated episodes of productive cough requiring multiple courses of antibiotics, which resulted in temporary improvement followed by recurrence within two to three months. The patient also reported a history of primary infertility, with no prior successful pregnancies despite prolonged periods of unprotected intercourse. There was no history suggestive of chronic sinusitis or imaging findings to suggest sinusitis (Fig. 4).
The patient had not previously been diagnosed with Kartagener syndrome or primary ciliary dyskinesia. Prior management consisted of repeated courses of antibiotics and symptomatic treatment for recurrent lower respiratory tract infections at various healthcare facilities. Despite longstanding respiratory symptoms beginning in adolescence, no prior investigation for an underlying ciliary motility disorder had been performed. The current presentation at 40 years of age represented the first recognition of the constellation of findings suggestive of Kartagener syndrome.
Computed tomography of the chest revealed dextrocardia with complete situs inversus (Fig. 2A-C). There was bilateral bronchiectasis predominantly involving the middle lobe and lingula, associated with bronchial wall thickening and mucus impaction. In addition, multiple areas of tree-in-bud nodularity were noted, consistent with small airway inflammation, along with patchy ground-glass opacities in the adjacent lung parenchyma (Fig. 3A-D). The constellation of imaging findings, in conjunction with the clinical history of recurrent respiratory infections and infertility, was highly suggestive of an underlying ciliary motility disorder consistent with an atypical presentation of Kartagener syndrome.
Following diagnosis, the patient was treated for the acute respiratory exacerbation with antibiotic therapy, bronchodilator treatment, and airway clearance measures. She was counseled regarding the chronic nature of the disease and referred for pulmonary follow-up for long-term management of bronchiectasis. Recommendations included regular airway clearance therapy, vaccination against respiratory pathogens, and prompt treatment of future respiratory infections. Further evaluation for primary ciliary dyskinesia using specialized diagnostic testing was recommended if resources became available. Counseling regarding the association between primary ciliary dyskinesia and infertility was also provided.

A 52-year-old man with a history of arterial hypertension and chronic respiratory failure due to combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema (CPFE) syndrome, on home oxygen therapy for 1 year, presented to the Emergency Department of the Military Hospital of Tunis, Tunisia with sudden-onset right brachial monoparesis, faciobrachial paresthesia, and slurred speech lasting for 2 days. He had a 52 pack-year smoking history and a previous ischemic stroke in 2022, for which he had been prescribed aspirin but discontinued it on his own.
The patient was admitted to the Department of Neurology of the Military Hospital of Tunis, Tunisia.
On neurological examination, the patient had dysarthria, right brachial monoparesis, and cerebellar ataxia. The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 5. The modified Rankin Score (mRS) was 3 at admission.
A non-contrast brain CT revealed sequelae of a prior right superficial middle cerebral artery infarct and spontaneous hyperdensity of intracranial vessels (Fig. 1). Brain MRI with MR angiography showed an acute left paramedian pontine infarct without evidence of atherosclerosis (Fig. 2). Echo-Doppler of the supra-aortic trunks revealed a dominant right vertebral artery.
Laboratory investigations confirmed polycythemia: red blood cell count was 6.99 million/µL (reference: 4.00-5.70), hemoglobin 20.8 g/dL (reference: 13.5-17.0), and hematocrit 62.5% (reference: 37.0-50.0). White blood cell count was 13,800/µL, and platelet count was 263,000/µL. Peripheral blood smear was normal. His arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2: 56 mmHg, PaCO2: 49 mmHg, and pH: 7.38, consistent with chronic compensated respiratory failure. Vitamin B12 was 258 pg/mL, and homocysteine was elevated at 22.58 µmol/L. Testing for the JAK2V617F mutation, thrombophilia screening, and autoimmune markers was negative, except for a positive rheumatoid factor.
Transthoracic echocardiography and troponin levels showed no embolic source. C-reactive protein (CRP) was within normal limits. Serum erythropoietin was elevated (78.2 mIU/mL), supporting a diagnosis of secondary polycythemia due to chronic hypoxia.
A noncontrast CT scan showed sequelae of right superficial middle cerebral artery infarct and spontaneous hyperdense intracranial vessels (Fig. 1). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with angio MR revealed an acute left paramedian pontine infarct without atherosclerosis (Fig. 2). The supra-aortic trunk echo-Doppler showed a dominant right vertebral artery. Lab tests confirmed polycythemia: His red blood cells were 6.99 m/cumm (normal range: 4.00-5.70 m/cumm), hemoglobin was 20.8 g/dL (normal range: 13.5-17.0 g/dL), and hematocrit was 62.5% (normal range: 37.0%-50.0%), white cell count was 13,800 and thrombocyte count was 263,000. Blood film was normal. Vitamin B12 (258 pg/mL) and homocysteine (22.58 µmol/L) were measured. JAK2V617F mutation, thrombophilia screening, and autoimmune markers were negative, except for rheumatoid factor positivity.
Transthoracic echocardiogram and troponin showed no embolic source. His C-reactive protein (CRP) level was normal. The final diagnosis was multiple thromboembolic strokes due to secondary polycythemia from chronic hypoxia.
The patient was started on aspirin (100 mg/d) and atorvastatin (40 mg/d). Hematology consultation recommended therapeutic phlebotomy. He underwent 6 phlebotomy sessions, each removing 200 mL of blood, performed every other day over a 2-week period. This reduced his hematocrit to 48.7%. Neurological symptoms improved significantly within 4 days of initiating phlebotomy and supportive care. During hospitalization, he developed an acute exacerbation of COPD complicated by heart failure, which was managed successfully. At discharge, the modified Rankin Score had improved to 1. He was discharged on aspirin, statins, and maintenance therapy for CPFE syndrome and heart failure.

A 21-year-old male presented with complaints of progressive behavioral changes over the preceding several months. According to his family, the patient developed increased irritability, mood swings, social withdrawal, and decline in academic performance, which were markedly different from his baseline personality. He also exhibited psychiatric manifestations, including emotional instability and inappropriate behavior, for which he initially sought psychiatric consultation. Over the following weeks, the patient developed tremors involving both hands, more pronounced during voluntary movements and fine motor tasks such as writing and eating. The tremors were insidious in onset and gradually progressive. There was no history of seizures, loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficits, headache, or visual disturbances. The patient reported generalized fatigue and reduced appetite but denied jaundice, abdominal distension, hematemesis, melena, or pedal edema. There was no history of alcohol intake, illicit drug use, or exposure to hepatotoxic medications. Past medical history was unremarkable, and there was no similar illness in family members. Preliminary investigations elsewhere revealed altered liver function tests, prompting referral for further evaluation.
On general physical examination, the patient was conscious and oriented, with stable vital signs. Mild scleral icterus was noted. There were no stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider nevi, palmar erythema, or ascites. Slit-lamp examination revealed bilateral Kayser–Fleischer rings. Neurological examination revealed bilateral upper limb tremors, predominantly action and postural tremors. Mild dysarthria was noted. Muscle tone and power were normal in all limbs, with intact deep tendon reflexes. No focal motor or sensory deficits were identified. Gait examination showed mild unsteadiness. Psychiatric evaluation revealed behavioral abnormalities with impaired judgment and emotional lability. Abdominal examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were within normal limits.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrated bilateral symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in head of caudate nucleus, lateral aspect of bilateral putamen, posterior limbs of internal capsules, lateral aspect of bilateral thalami, superior and middle cerebellar peduncles and pons. There is symmetrical hyperintensity in bilateral globus pallidi. There is relative T2 hyperintensity in red nucleus and substantia nigra giving “ bright eyes of panda” sign, which is hypo intense on FLAIR giving “ face of giant panda” sign. On diffusion weighted imaging, there is diffusion restriction seen in bilateral red nuclei, globus pallidi and thalami, with no restriction seen in bilateral putamen (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5).
Laboratory investigations showed elevated serum transaminases and a markedly reduced serum ceruloplasmin level of 8 mg/dL. Twenty-four-hour urinary copper excretion was elevated (>100 µg/d), supporting increased body copper burden.
Based on the Leipzig scoring system, the patient had a cumulative score of 6 (serum ceruloplasmin <10 mg/dL, neurological involvement, and elevated urinary copper excretion), strongly diagnostic of Wilson disease. The diagnosis was further supported by characteristic neuroimaging findings and clinical improvement following initiation of chelation therapy with D-penicillamine.

A previously healthy 4-year-old boy presented to the emergency department with intermittent abdominal pain and episodic non-bilious vomiting of several weeks’ duration. The pain was colicky, recurrent, and poorly localized. There was no history of fever, weight loss, trauma, prior abdominal surgery, or exposure to livestock or unpasteurized dairy products.
On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable. The abdomen was mildly distended but soft, without guarding or rebound tenderness. No palpable mass was identified.
Laboratory investigations were largely unremarkable. The white blood cell count was within normal limits without leukocytosis. Mild anemia was noted on subsequent testing. Platelet count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Tumor markers (AFP and β-hCG) were normal. Echinococcus serology was negative.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a left paracolic gutter fluid collection with multiple well defined internal components which could represent daughter cysts.
Additional findings included reactive mesenteric lymph nodes (largest approximately 1 × 0.8 cm), displacement of adjacent bowel loops without evidence of obstruction, and mild surrounding inflammatory changes. No definite communication with adjacent bowel loops was identified on CT. Based on these imaging features, hydatid disease was initially suspected. (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).
Follow-up MRI demonstrated interval migration of the lesion from the left paracolic gutter to the right lower quadrant, indicating lesion mobility. The lesion showed heterogeneous signal on both T1- and T2-weighted images with multiple internal floating rounded components. Focal internal calcification was present.
Post-contrast images demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement with adjacent mesenteric stranding and persistent mild intraperitoneal free fluid. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed no definite restricted diffusion.
The interval positional change raised strong suspicion for bowel-related pathology rather than a fixed peritoneal cyst (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, Fig. 7).
The patient underwent surgical exploration. An inflamed Meckel’s diverticulum arising from the ileum was identified and resected.
Enterolith formation surrounding the foreign body.
The presumed daughter cysts on imaging corresponded to inflammatory debris and enterolith fragments within the fluid-filled diverticulum.

A 58-year-old woman with a past medical history of uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis treated medically in the past and remote caesarean section, presented to the emergency department with 3 days of left lower quadrant pain. An imaging and interventional overview of the patient’s hospital course can be reviewed in Fig. 5.
An IV contrast enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis in portal venous phase with coronal and sagittal reconstruction was obtained, employing iterative dose reduction technique (CECT). This demonstrated acute perforated sigmoid diverticulitis without abscess. The patient was admitted for IV antibiotics, fluids and pain control, and discharged the next day. However, the patient continued to have gradually increasing pain, and prompted by new fecal urgency, returned to ED 2 days after discharge. On examination, the patient was tender to palpation in the LLQ without rebound, and afebrile with white cell count (WCC) of 10. Portal venous phase CECT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a 3 cm collection contiguous with inflamed sigmoid diverticula, involving the ovary and a gas-filled serpiginous structure, the left fallopian tube (Fig. 1). This was consistent with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with abscess and the rare finding of pneumosalpinx. The patient was admitted to surgery.
Interventional radiology was enlisted to drain the collection on the day of admission. Nonenhanced CT biopsy was conducted. A narrow window was identified between the broad ligament ovarian vessels and the iliac artery and vein was identified, whereupon an 18-gauge Chiba needle advanced inferior to the broad ligament until the needle tip was within the collection and 10 cc purulent material was aspirated. Passed via wire, a 10 French cope loop drainage catheter was placed in the collection with near complete resolution (Fig. 3).
IV broad spectrum antibiotics were continued. WCC trended down over subsequent days and patient tolerated a diet, but began to require increasing pain control, prompting CECT of the abdomen and pelvis on day 5 of admission. This revealed resolution of the drained abscess but interval progression of multiple abscesses in the region of the sigmoid and mesentery (Fig. 4). Monitoring continued.
Due to persistent elevated WCC, unremitting pain and progression of collections, patient was taken to OR day 6 following admission. Robotic sigmoid colectomy, end colostomy (Hartmann's procedure), and drainage of intra-abdominal abscesses was performed by general surgery. Hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (THBSO) was performed by gynecologic surgery. Intraoperatively the left adnexa was noted to be adherent to a pelvic collection and to a portion of sigmoid colon, with fistulous communication. IR drain was removed. A Blake drain was placed in the largest collection in the right lower quadrant and removed before discharge following an unremarkable postoperative course. OR wound cultures obtained on antibiotics were positive for candida albicans and fluconazole was added to the outpatient regimen.
Surgical pathology confirmed fallopian tubes showing florid bilateral salpingitis with abscess, and fibrinous adhesions with pyogenic material (Fig. 6).
Robotic assisted colostomy reversal (reversal of Hartmann's) was performed successfully 4 months following the surgery.

A 51-year-old male with a complex medical history including common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), hepatic steatosis, and prior total parenteral nutrition (TPN) use, presented for evaluation of chronic liver enzyme elevation and imaging findings concerning for cirrhosis. Abdominal CT and MRI revealed nodularity of the hepatic surface and cirrhotic morphology, prompting further assessment to determine the underlying etiology (Fig. 1). The differential diagnosis included metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), CVID-related hepatopathy, and TPN-associated hepatic injury. Based on recommendations from hepatology, a liver biopsy was performed to obtain tissue for diagnosis.
An ultrasound-guided random liver biopsy targeting the left hepatic lobe was performed in the interventional radiology suite (Fig. 2). Moderate sedation was administered using fentanyl and midazolam, along with local lidocaine anesthesia. The procedure was technically successful, with placement of an 18-gauge coaxial biopsy needle and retrieval of 3 core samples. Minimal blood loss was observed (<15 mL), and no immediate procedural complications were noted. Postprocedural tract embolization was performed with Gelfoam slurry to minimize bleeding risk.
However, within minutes of biopsy completion, the patient developed severe epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by chills and clinical signs of jaundice. A postprocedural CT scan was performed in the portal venous phase, demonstrating cirrhotic liver morphology with heterogeneous enhancement of the left hepatic lobe in the biopsy region. The observed heterogeneous left lobe enhancement was interpreted as a transient hepatic attenuation difference (THAD) reflecting compensatory arterial inflow in response to focal portal venous obstruction, rather than true parenchymal ischemia or infarction (Fig. 3). On portal venous phase imaging, a subsegmental portal venous filling defect in segment 3 was identified, consistent with acute thrombosis. No evidence of active bleeding or perihepatic hematoma was present. The patient was admitted for intravenous pain control and further evaluation.
During hospitalization, repeat CT imaging on postoperative day 1 showed persistent thrombosis of the segment 3 portal venous branch along with a new filling defect in the left main portal vein, consistent with proximal thrombus extension (Fig. 4). Imaging did not demonstrate embolic material within the main portal vein; thus, Gelfoam migration remains a hypothesized rather than confirmed contributing mechanism. Laboratory studies revealed marked transaminitis, with AST and ALT exceeding 900 U/L, hyperbilirubinemia peaking at 13.7 mg/dL, and thrombocytopenia (Table 1). No evidence of hemoperitoneum, abscess, or biliary obstruction was present on imaging. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed no bile duct abnormalities or hemobilia (Fig. 5).
Anticoagulation was initiated with an intravenous heparin drip, later transitioned to oral apixaban upon stabilization. Consultations with interventional radiology, hepatology, and urology were obtained, with hematuria deemed likely related to anticoagulant therapy. The patient underwent serial laboratory monitoring and repeat imaging to evaluate disease progression and therapeutic response (Table 2).
The patient's liver function tests and bilirubin levels improved on postoperative day 2 with anticoagulation, and his abdominal pain gradually resolved. No signs of intestinal ischemia or worsening thrombosis were noted on follow-up imaging during the index hospitalization. He was discharged home on apixaban with plans for at least 2 months of therapy. Outpatient follow-up was arranged with hepatology, urology, and immunology services. On review of the liver biopsy pathology, hepatic parenchyma exhibited mild steatosis, portal chronic inflammation with ductular proliferation, and absence of significant fibrosis, a finding discordant with the preoperative imaging impression of cirrhotic morphology, as discussed below. No further interventional procedures were required, and the patient's status returned to baseline without recurrence of hematuria. No dedicated postdischarge cross-sectional imaging was performed at our home institution to assess portal vein recanalization status.

A 38-year-old man originally from Mozambique and living in Portugal for several years, with known HIV and HBV infections under regular follow-up, presented with a 2-month history of painless gross hematuria. He denied dysuria, flank pain, fever, weight loss, recent travel to endemic areas, or prior urologic procedures, and there was no known history of urolithiasis or tuberculosis.
On physical examination, vital signs were stable and abdominal and genitourinary examinations were unremarkable. Baseline laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin, leukocyte, and platelet counts, with preserved renal function. Urinalysis confirmed hematuria and leukocyturia without significant proteinuria.
Multiple urine specimens were examined for Schistosoma ova using standard microscopy, and all were negative. A Schistosoma-specific PCR assay on urine was also negative. Because hematuria persisted in an at-risk individual and the initial laboratory work-up was inconclusive, cross-sectional imaging was requested. Although ultrasonography is often used as an initial examination in endemic settings, CT was selected in this patient because it offers superior characterization of mural calcification and distal ureteral involvement, which were the main diagnostic considerations after nondiagnostic laboratory results.
Noncontrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis (Fig. 1) demonstrated striking circumferential calcification of the entire bladder wall, extending into both distal ureters, resulting in an “eggshell” pattern of mural calcification. Mild bladder wall thickening was present, but there was no intraluminal mass, hydronephrosis, or renal calculi. In the clinical and epidemiologic context, the radiologic appearance was considered highly suggestive of chronic urinary schistosomiasis despite the negative urine microscopy and PCR findings.
Cystoscopy showed multiple irregular yellowish plaques and nodular lesions involving large areas of the bladder mucosa, with chronic inflammatory change and decreased bladder compliance. Targeted biopsies of these areas were obtained.
Histopathologic examination revealed numerous calcified S haematobium ova embedded in the urothelium and submucosa, surrounded by chronic inflammatory infiltrates and extensive stromal calcification. No dysplasia or malignancy was identified (Fig. 2). These findings confirmed chronic urinary schistosomiasis with calcified tissue eggs, indicating longstanding inactive disease rather than active transformation of eggs into other parasitic stages.
The patient was treated with praziquantel 40 mg/kg as a single dose and counseled regarding possible long-term complications, including obstruction and bladder malignancy risk. At 3-month follow-up, hematuria had completely resolved, renal function remained normal, and no new urinary symptoms were reported. No follow-up imaging had yet been performed at the time of writing, but clinical and urologic follow-up was planned. The key clinical events from symptom onset to follow-up are summarized in Table 1.

A 55-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department complaining of a right inguinal bulge, acute onset right lower quadrant pain, and nausea for 1 day after mild physical activity. She denied any history of hernia or surgery in the past.
On admission, the patient was noted to be in acute distress, but was afebrile with a normal heart rate and rhythm. Abdominal exam revealed right upper and lower quadrant tenderness with guarding. No rebound or peritonism was elicited. A small mass was felt in the right inguinal area without overlying skin changes. Complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and urinalysis were unremarkable. Differential diagnosis at this time included intra-abdominal perforation, acute appendicitis, and colitis.
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast was ordered. Examination revealed a right groin soft tissue mass with surrounding fat inflammation (Fig. 1). Further evaluation demonstrated that this mass originated from the cecum (Fig. 2) and was located medially to the femoral vein (Fig. 3), confirming that this was an inflamed appendix herniating into the femoral canal. The appendix was dilated to 8 mm and contained intraluminal fluid. The hernia sac also indented the right femoral vein near the inguinal ligament. Subcentimeter reactive right inguinal lymph nodes were seen. Ultrasound was not performed for this patient.
General surgery was consulted, and the patient underwent laparoscopic appendectomy and open right femoral hernia repair. Final pathology confirmed acute suppurative appendicitis with periappendicitis and an incidentally associated round ligament lipoma.

A 55-year-old Native American woman initially presented at age 33 to an outside emergency department for abdominal pain. CT imaging at that time demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse bony sclerosis (images not available, noting these images were obtained over 2 decades ago). Blood work revealed thrombocytopenia. The patient was referred to our facility for further evaluation.
At our center, the patient had a reported history of osteoporosis and degenerative joint disease of the hips, status post bilateral total hip arthroplasties (THA), the first performed as a teenager and the second as a young adult. No surgical pathology reports are available from these THA procedures performed at an outside hospital over 3 decades ago.
At our institution, the diagnosis of adult-onset osteopetrosis was established based on clinical history, imaging findings, bone marrow core biopsy results, and peripheral blood smear results. CT and radiographs demonstrated dense marbled appearance of the long bones and pelvis, sclerotic changes of the medullary space, and vertebral body deformities (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Analysis of the bone marrow core biopsy was difficult due to poor sampling secondary to sclerotic bone; however, pathologic evaluation reported foci of hematopoiesis consisting of erythroid precursors, maturing myeloid elements, scattered megakaryocytes, and plasma cells. Peripheral blood smear was more consistent with a myelophthisic process, demonstrating leukoerythroblastosis, occasional teardrop and nucleated red blood cells, mild granulocytic left shift, and normal platelet count with occasional large forms which can be seen in states of increased peripheral platelet turnover. Although the peripheral smear supported an underlying myelophthisic process related to osteopetrosis, the episodic isolated thrombocytopenia with preservation of other cell lines raised concern for a concomitant immune-mediated thrombocytopenia.
The patient’s platelet counts dropped as low as 3-4 × 10^3/µL multiple times, but each time, these counts responded to periodic treatment with a 4-day course of dexamethasone. Additional testing and consideration at this time included negative viral testing (including hepatitis C, HIV, and Epstein-Barr Virus), liver function testing within reference ranges, absence of thrombocytopenia inducing medications, and negative autoimmune markers (limited to antinuclear antibody or ANA). The patient was also relatively healthy with oral medications limited to calcitriol and losartan. Unavailable from our records include bleeding time results, antibody platelet testing, and nuclear platelet tracing to further evaluate for locations of platelet sequestering. These tests would have been desirable to establish a diagnosis of exclusion but were not performed. Given the information and data collected, a splenectomy was ultimately performed at an outside hospital at the age of 37 for presumed ITP. In the nearly 2 decades since the splenectomy, the patient has had platelet counts within reference range, further supporting the etiology of her isolated severe thrombocytopenia as ITP as opposed to a complication of osteopetrosis or hypersplenism. The patient does, however, continue to have mild anemia with evidence of a left shift consistent with progression of osteopetrosis.
Over the subsequent two decades, the patient experienced additional osteopetrosis-related complications, such as periprosthetic hip fractures and two right-sided periprosthetic joint infections, all requiring revisions and further surgical intervention. The patient is now 55 years old and has undergone a total of four right and two left hip surgeries to address infections and periprosthetic fractures. This complex fracture management related to osteopetrosis can be visualized in Fig. 5, Fig. 6, noting the differences in prosthetic hardware compared to prior imaging (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4). The patient has also undergone bone scintigraphy to evaluate for periprosthetic fractures, as radiographs were inconclusive for new fractures. Bone scans demonstrated diffusely increased uptake of technetium-99m (Tc-99m) methylene diphosphonate throughout the bones, particularly the lower extremities, with minimal soft tissue uptake and renal excretion (Fig. 7A and B). The increased uptake at the end of the long bones of the lower extremities corresponds to the metaphyseal flaring seen on radiographs; both are imaging manifestations of dysregulated bone formation/resorption. Bone scans also demonstrated a possible left greater trochanteric fracture; however, the patient was not experiencing any clinical symptoms that correlated with this finding. Scintigraphy, although not required for the diagnosis of osteopetrosis, demonstrates a unique but characteristic uptake pattern of osteopetrosis. The patient is currently undergoing a formal genetic evaluation with buccal mucosal testing for osteopetrosis, which was not previously performed.

A 24-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus on insulin therapy had been under ophthalmology follow-up for approximately 6 months due to diplopia. At her most recent visit, she reported a 1-week history of headache in addition to persistent diplopia. Clinical examination revealed papilledema, confirmed on fundoscopy, and left abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) palsy. No other focal neurological deficits were identified.
Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable. Glycemic control had been well maintained, with glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) values ranging from 34 to 41 mmol/mol, making uncontrolled diabetes a less likely primary contributor to her neurological presentation. Therefore, the patient was referred for neuroimaging for further evaluation.
Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated a small hypodense focus within the right frontal centrum semiovale, consistent with a chronic ischemic change (Fig. 1), with no evidence of mass effect, hydrocephalus, or other signs of raised intracranial pressure. CT angiography revealed a diffusely small-caliber petrous segment of the right internal carotid artery compared with the contralateral side (Fig. 2). No prominent collateral vessels were identified. Bone-window evaluation of the skull base demonstrated narrowing of the right carotid canal measuring approximately 3.5 mm, compared with 5.1 mm on the left (Fig. 3).
MRI of the brain demonstrated multiple chronic ischemic changes involving the right frontal centrum semiovale. The lesions exhibited T1-hypointense, T2/FLAIR-hyperintense signal characteristics without evidence of diffusion restriction or enhancement, confirming a diagnosis of chronic infarction with gliosis (Fig. 4, Fig. 5).
The patient was started on dual antiplatelet therapy for secondary ischemic prevention. During hospitalization, her headache improved, with partial resolution of diplopia. No new neurological deficits developed. She was discharged in stable condition with instructions for outpatient follow-up and interval MRI surveillance. However, the patient did not attend subsequent follow-up appointments, and long-term clinical and imaging follow-up data were therefore unavailable.

A 38-year-old woman initially presented with bloating and abdominal pain and was found to have large bilateral ovarian masses on outside imaging. She underwent resections at an outside institution resulting in mature teratomas. Her symptoms returned 3 years later with recurrent right ovarian lesion at an outside institution. Right salpingo-oophorectomy resulted in recurrent teratoma. Follow-up imaging at the outside institution showed multiple peritoneal masses that were biopsied and found to be strumosis without atypia. The timeline of important clinical events is outlined in Fig. 1.
Four years after her initial symptoms, she presented to our institution for additional workup and treatment due to relocation. MRI of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple enhancing peritoneal and abdominal wall masses and a homogenously enhancing structure in the left adnexa which was favored to represent the ovary (Fig. 2). The abdominal wall masses were biopsied and demonstrated follicular thyroid tissue without atypia. At this time, the patient had a markedly elevated thyroglobulin level of 4326 ng/mL (normal range 1.6-50 ng/mL). An I-123 whole body scan utilizing 1.2mCi of I-123 was administered to the patient, who was placed on a low iodine diet prior to the exam. The 24-hour uptake scan showed significant uptake in the thyroid, but no significant uptake in the multiple peritoneal and abdominal wall lesions. This finding may have been due to the uptake of the majority of the radiotracer by the thyroid gland (Fig. 4A).
Five years after her initial presentation, the patient underwent a round of cytoreductive surgery in the abdomen and pelvis, resulting in a lowering of the thyroglobulin level of 335.5 ng/mL. Several months after the cytoreductive surgery, she underwent total thyroidectomy, which further lowered the thyroglobulin level to 205 ng/mL. She then underwent a second round of cytoreductive surgery in the abdomen and pelvis with removal of multiple peritoneal masses including a mass in the left ovary. Pathological examination demonstrated well-differentiated follicular thyroid tissue (Fig. 3). The patient was reimaged using 3.4 mCi of I-123 (Fig. 4B), and a 24-hour uptake scan showed uptake in the remnant thyroid tissue in the thyroid bed. Shortly thereafter, given patient’s persistent elevated thyroglobulin levels, patient underwent radioiodine therapy with 128 mCi of I-131 with 7-day post ablation imaging demonstrating I-131 uptake within multiple sites in the abdomen and pelvis (Fig. 4C).
Over the next two years, her thyroglobulin levels decreased substantially with mild interval fluctuations, with the most recent level at 57.4 ng/mL. However, the most recent follow-up surveillance MRI showed small enhancing foci suspicious for early recurrent disease within the peritoneal cavity. There has been no post-surgical MRI or CT demonstrating a confirmed disease-free state during surveillance follow-up.

A 12-year-old girl with no significant past medical history presented with a two-year history of asymmetric joint pain affecting the ankles, knees, shoulders, wrists, and metacarpophalangeal joints, associated with myalgia. Laboratory studies showed positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and elevated inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), consistent with a diagnosis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Two years after the onset of articular symptoms, she developed a progressive, painless, bilateral proptosis. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed bilateral intraconal pseudotumoral orbital tissue infiltration, isointense on T1-weighted sequences with marked homogeneous enhancement following gadolinium administration (Fig. 1). The lesions were hypointense on T2-weighted sequences, with preserved optic nerve morphology and signal on CISS sequences (Fig. 2). FLAIR sequences showed hypointensity without diffusion restriction (Fig. 3). These findings were consistent with grade III bilateral proptosis, more pronounced on the left, with preserved extraconal fat.
Orbital biopsy demonstrated dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates interspersed with collagen bundles, confirming a chronic inflammatory process consistent with orbital inflammatory pseudotumor (Fig. 4). The patient was treated with corticosteroids, resulting in significant clinical improvement and complete resolution of ocular symptoms.

A 63-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute retrosternal pain after emotional stress. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I was elevated at 617 ng/L, decreasing to 545 ng/L after 2 hours. Electrocardiography showed no T-wave changes. An initial point-of-care echocardiogram performed in the emergency department suggested possible apical hypokinesia with moderately reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. A repeat transthoracic echocardiogram performed at the cardiology department clarified the pattern as predominantly midventricular hypokinesia (Movie 1).
Photon-counting detector coronary CT angiography (PCD-CCTA) was performed to exclude obstructive coronary artery disease. The examination was performed on a first-generation dual-source photon-counting CT scanner (NAEOTOM Alpha, Siemens Healthcare GmbH, Forchheim, Germany) using retrospective ECG-gating with ECG-based dose modulation. The average heart rate during acquisition was 71 beats/min. Before image acquisition, the patient received 2 doses of sublingual nitroglycerin for coronary vasodilation. No beta-blocker was administered. Coronary arteries were nonobstructive (Fig. 1). Multiphase functional analysis demonstrated a left ventricular ejection fraction of 48%, with akinesia predominantly involving the anterior midventricular wall and mild residual akinesia of the inferior midventricular wall, while basal and apical segments contracted normally. The combined anterior and inferior involvement accounted for the circumferential midventricular hypokinesia pattern on the polar map (Fig. 2). Cine reconstructions (Movie 2) clearly depicted these wall-motion abnormalities. A representative 2-chamber and 3-chamber reconstruction were added to show the basal and apical sparing and the midventricular wall-motion abnormality in a static format (Fig. 3). The patient received conservative management with temporary escalation of heart failure therapy, which was maintained until follow-up cardiac MRI. Follow-up cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging performed 1 month later (Movie 3) demonstrated complete resolution of wall-motion abnormalities, confirming the transient nature of the disease.

A man in his 50s presented to the emergency department with worsening anterior chest pain. He had intermittently experienced anterior chest pain for approximately 4-5 years. Ten days before presentation, the pain became persistent, and on the day of admission, the pain acutely worsened, prompting emergency department evaluation. The pain was described as a pressing sensation and became more severe with physical activity. There was no radiation of pain or associated dyspnea. He denied fever, sore throat, cough, or rhinorrhea.
The patient had a history of hypertension and hyperuricemia identified during routine health checkups. Although antihypertensive therapy had been initiated previously, he had discontinued follow-up and treatment. The patient did not recall any prior symptoms suggestive of early symptomatic syphilis, such as chancre, rash, fever, or malaise, and was unaware of any possible history of syphilis infection.
Height: 180 cm; weight: 77 kg. Body temperature was 36.6°C. Pulse rate was 84 beats/min with regular sinus rhythm. Blood pressure was elevated at 189/108 mmHg. Respiratory rate was 21 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed regular heart sounds without murmurs. Pulmonary auscultation demonstrated no wheezes, crackles, or stridor. Bilateral radial pulses were symmetric and regular, with no pulse deficit.
Serologic testing for syphilis was positive, with a rapid plasma reagin level of 130 R.U. and a Treponema pallidum latex agglutination level of 5800 T.U.. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction testing for COVID-19 was also positive. Tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. C-reactive protein (CRP) was mildly elevated at 3.54 mg/dL, serum IgG level was within the normal range, although serum IgG4 level was not assessed.
Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a descending thoracic aortic aneurysm measuring 70 mm in diameter. The aortic wall showed circumferential thickening. The intimal layer exhibited poor enhancement, whereas the outer medial and adventitial layers demonstrated ring-like enhancement on delayed-phase imaging, producing a characteristic double-ring sign suggestive of inflammatory aortitis (Fig. 1). Gallium scintigraphy demonstrated no abnormal uptake in the descending thoracic aorta or other sites suggestive of active systemic inflammatory disease (Fig. 2A). Based on imaging findings and serologic results, syphilitic aortitis was strongly suspected. Chest CT showed no pulmonary findings suggestive of COVID-19 pneumonia.
Antihypertensive therapy and intravenous penicillin treatment were initiated. Chest pain resolved rapidly under blood pressure control. Follow-up CT performed during hospitalization showed no significant interval change in aneurysm size (Fig. 2B-C). Surgery was deferred until resolution of active COVID-19 infection to reduce perioperative complications while strict blood pressure control was maintained because no imaging findings suggestive of impending rupture were observed, and gallium scintigraphy demonstrated no evidence of active aortic inflammation. After confirmation of COVID-19 resolution, elective descending thoracic aortic replacement was performed on hospital day 29.
Intraoperative inspection revealed diffuse whitish intimal thickening without mural thrombus formation (Supplemental Video 1). The intimal surface demonstrated a characteristic wrinkled or “tree-bark” appearance, suggestive of syphilitic aortitis (Fig. 3).
Histological examination revealed infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells in the media, adventitia, and around the vasa vasorum. In addition, endothelial cell swelling and fibrosis were observed (Fig. 4). Although spirochetes were not identified, these findings were consistent with syphilitic aortitis.

A 46-year-old man presented to our institution for evaluation of a splenic mass that had been incidentally detected 10 months earlier.
