At the time of initial detection, he reported mild, intermittent left upper quadrant discomfort that resolved spontaneously within approximately one hour, without associated gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms.
His medical history included hypertension, hyperuricemia, and previous repair of a right inguinal hernia. Physical examination on admission was unremarkable, with no abdominal tenderness or palpable mass. Laboratory tests showed mild elevations in several inflammatory markers, including fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. Liver enzyme levels, albumin, and creatine kinase were slightly below the reference ranges, and tumor marker levels were normal.
Initial ultrasonography showed a hypoechoic mass in the spleen with an irregular but relatively well-circumscribed margin and scant internal vascularity on color Doppler imaging (Fig. 1). On unenhanced CT, the lesion appeared heterogeneous and hypoattenuating (Fig. 2); unlike its sonographic appearance, lesion margins were indistinct from the adjacent splenic parenchyma, likely owing to the limited attenuation difference between the tumor and surrounding parenchyma on unenhanced images.On contrast-enhanced CT, the mass showed avid but heterogeneous enhancement in the arterial phase, with focal hypoenhancing areas (Fig. 3).Enhancement decreased mildly in the venous phase but remained heterogeneous (Fig. 4).
Because the imaging findings were indeterminate and primary splenic malignancy could not be excluded, laparoscopic splenectomy was performed. The resected spleen measured approximately 15 × 7 cm. Histological examination showed loosely arranged spindle-to-oval tumor cells within a fibrous stroma, accompanied by a prominent inflammatory infiltrate composed mainly of lymphocytes and plasma cells (Fig. 5). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positive expression of the follicular dendritic cell markers CD21 and CD23 in the tumor cells (Fig. 6). CD20 staining was negative in the tumor cells while showing strong positivity in the surrounding background lymphocytes, confirming their B-cell nature and highlighting the neoplastic population by contrast (Fig. 7). In situ hybridization for Epstein–Barr virus–encoded RNA showed diffuse nuclear positivity in the tumor cells (Fig. 8).

A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. Notably, she has a personal history of TSC and seizures. She has a family history of TSC with multiple siblings and father diagnosed with the condition; however, they were not afflicted with an arterial pathology. On physical examination, there were multiple hyperpigmented macules, ash leaf spots, fascial fibromas, and extremity fibromas. The abdomen was diffusely tender with focal peritonitis along the midline with an obvious pulsatile mass. Vital signs showed tachycardia to 120 beats per minute, hypertension (180/90 mm Hg), and adequate oxygenation on room air. Her vascular examination was intact with bilateral palpable femoral, radial, and pedal pulses. Axial and coronal computed tomography angiography demonstrated an isolated 7.2-cm retroperitoneally contained a ruptured I-AAA (Fig 1, Fig 2, Fig 3). Impulse control was promptly initiated to lessen further exsanguination risk and the patient was transported emergently to the operating room for open repair of the ruptured I-AAA.
Laparotomy revealed a 7.2-cm purely I-AAA with contained rupture into the retroperitoneum. A transperitoneal approach was undertaken given the left lateral retroperitoneal nature of the rupture. This strategy allowed appropriate aortic control distal to the bilateral renal arteries before aortic transection. Transperitoneal infrarenal aortic and bilateral common iliac artery control were obtained swiftly. The patient was heparinized in the standard fashion. Aortotomy, lumbar artery ligation, and appropriate hemostasis were performed. Notably, the radiographically identified posterior left lateral rupture site was easily confirmed on examination of the aneurysmal aortic wall (Fig 4).
The infrarenal to aortic bifurcation was then reconstructed with an 14-mm diameter tubular polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) graft tailored to an appropriate length for optimal interpositioning. Moreover, we anticipated the need for a long-term and slightly oversized graft option that would be suitable for decades of use. As such, after expert discussion, we elected to use the PTFE tubular graft platform to perform our aortic reconstruction. Although Dacron (Invista) is certainly a reasonable option, we believed that PTFE would afford the patient a more durable repair. The graft was sewn in place and buttressed with felt pledgeting proximally and distally. Graft felt pledgeting was used to reinforce anastomoses because we knew these anastomoses would certainly evolve and potentially degenerate with normal adolescent development. The aortic aneurysm sac was further closed around the graft. The patient was noted to have palpable femoral and pedal pulses before closing the abdomen in the standard fashion. The patient was then admitted to the surgical intensive care unit postoperatively.
The patient was extubated within 24 hours postoperatively and experienced a largely uneventful hospital course, with discharge to the neighboring children's hospital on postoperative day 4. Repeat computed tomography angiography was performed before discharge, which demonstrated an intact I-AAA repair without major surgical concern. She was ultimately discharged home on postoperative day 7. At the 3-month postoperative follow-up visit, she was noted to have recovered well from surgery and planned for 6-month interval imaging. Patient consent for publication was obtained per institution protocol.

A 52-year-old male with a history of native bicuspid aortic valve with prior aortic valve replacement (25 mm Edwards Carpentier valve, in 2008) for group B streptococcal endocarditis presented to outpatient cardiology with 1 week of worsening shortness of breath. He also reported chest tightness the day before presentation, but denied fever, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, or constitutional symptoms. On examination in the clinic, he was noted to have a new systolic murmur and was sent to the emergency room for further assessment. Upon admission, vital signs were stable. His examination revealed a loud systolic murmur but no signs of decompensated heart failure. Laboratory workup showed elevated high-sensitivity troponins (86 pg/mL; repeat after 2 hours: 88 pg/mL) (reference normal range <20 pg/mL), brain natriuretic peptide (693 pg/ml; reference range 6-100 pg/ml), and d-dimer (1539 ng/mL; reference range 215-499 ng/mL). His electrocardiogram showed nonspecific ST-T wave changes (T-wave inversions in leads I, aVL, and V4-V6), which were new compared with the prior ECG (Fig. 1). The patient was admitted with a diagnosis of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and a left heart catheterization was performed, demonstrating normal coronaries (Video clip 1). Chest X-ray and computed tomography pulmonary angiogram revealed bilateral pleural effusions and patchy ground-glass opacities but no pulmonary embolism. The patient was admitted with a suspected NSTEMI and was on a heparin drip.
Further workup with transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed left ventricular hypertrophy with mid-range left ventricular ejection fraction (45%-50%). TTE showed a new intra-valvular leak of the bioprosthetic aortic valve compared with TTE a year prior, significant worsening of prosthetic aortic valve gradients (peak/mean 55/33 mmHg [26/17 mmHg 1 year prior]; aortic valve maximum velocity of 3.7 m/s, dimensionless velocity index of 0.27, and aortic acceleration time of 130 ms), and a dilated inferior vena cava (Video clip 2). Subsequently, the TEE revealed Doppler parameters suggestive of worsening of prosthetic aortic valve stenosis and new moderate to severe eccentric aortic valve transvalvular regurgitation, with possible valve ring dehiscence/peri-valvular abscess near the left coronary artery take off in mid-esophageal aortic valve short axis window, and a 1.3 cm mass suspicious for vegetation attached to the noncoronary cusp (Video clip 3, Fig. 2). These TEE findings were also reported during intraoperative TEE at the higher center, where the patient underwent redo thoracotomy and valve replacement surgery (only report available for review).
A normal left heart catheterization and subsequent significant transesophageal echocardiographic findings changed the course of treatment. Two sets of blood cultures and other atypical causes of infective endocarditis were ordered. The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics with vancomycin and cefepime, and an infectious disease specialist was consulted. Two sets of blood cultures (1 hour apart, from different peripheral venipuncture sites), showed no growth. Extensive microbiological investigations, including Bartonella serology and PCR, Cryptococcus antigen, serum beta-d-glucan levels, Brucella serology, Coxiella serology and PCR, Q fever, urine Legionella antigen, and serology, all returned negative. The patient was transferred to a higher-level center for emergent surgical evaluation for redo-thoracotomy and intervention. An emergency valve replacement was planned. The valve was replaced with an Edwards Inspiris resilia aortic bioprosthetic valve (model 11500A), and the pathology specimen was sent for culture and analysis. Notably, intraoperative findings did not indicate vegetations or endocarditis, as assessed by infectious disease specialists and the cardiothoracic surgeon, and given that the old bioprosthetic valve was presumed to be degenerative.
A postprocedural echo showed bioprosthetic valve leaflets moving well, a well-seated valve with no perivalvular leak. Since intraoperative findings were not concerning for endocarditis and intraoperative specimen cultures were preliminary negative (48 hours) with no preceding symptoms suggestive of infection, the vegetations were thought to be solely degenerated valve and antibiotics were discontinued 2 days after surgery. The patient was discharged 3 days after valve replacement without antibiotics. His valve debris pathology only reported a degenerated valve and surrounding tissue without any pathognomic findings of infective endocarditis. After discharge, one of the 3 operative samples from the aorta grew C. acnes. An infectious disease specialist reached out to the patient and discussed the findings. The patient completed 6 weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily (Table 1). He had an excellent recovery, with symptom resolution, return to work, and normal valve function on follow-up echocardiography.

The patient is a 74-year-old woman who presented with a 1-month history of vaginal flatus and fecal-like discharge. She reported no prior abdominal surgery, pelvic inflammatory disease, or malignancy. Physical examination demonstrated mild lower abdominal tenderness but no palpable masses. The patient denied recent trauma and reported no systemic symptoms, including fever, worsening abdominal pain, or unintentional weight loss. Blood tests revealed elevated inflammatory markers, and vaginal microbiota analysis showed alterations in the microbial flora and acidic environment.
Transvaginal ultrasound (Mindray endocavitary probe) demonstrated an anteverted uterus with well-defined margins and normal dimensions. Multiple gas-like hyperechoic foci were visualized within the uterine cavity, extending from the fundus to the internal cervical os (Video Editing S1 and S2). The myometrium in the left uterine wall exhibited a focal discontinuity, forming a 3 mm wide tract communicating with the adjacent sigmoid colon; the margins of this communication were ill-defined. Dynamic observation revealed passage of intestinal gas through the tract into the uterine cavity, creating a mobile gas-fluid interface (Fig. 1 and Video Editing S3). Color Doppler imaging showed a flickering signal within the fistula tract and rich intestinal blood flow, suggesting local inflammatory changes. Ultrasound impression: Abnormal uterine–intestinal communication, suspicious for colouterine fistula.
CT and MRI findings‌: CT demonstrates thickening of the sigmoid colon wall and an irregular soft tissue mass at the mid-to-lower segment, with an involved length of approximately 7 cm, infiltrating the anterior wall of the uterus. Gas is observed within the uterine cavity (Fig. 2). MRI further confirms that the sigmoid colon tumor has penetrated the left anterior superior myometrium and left lateral myometrium, forming a fistula with indistinct boundaries, indicating local invasion (Fig. 3). Imaging staging: T4bNxMx and EMVI (+).
Operative and follow-up summary: Intraoperatively, a tumor measuring approximately 5 cm in diameter was identified in the distal sigmoid colon. It was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, with local tissue destruction forming a fistula. Radical resection was not performed due to tumor invasion of the left ureter and iliac vessels. Instead, a double-barrel transverse colostomy was conducted. Pathologic examination confirmed adenocarcinoma (Stage T4N1M0). Postoperatively, the patient developed incisional fat liquefaction and infection, which were successfully managed with antibiotics and local wound care. The patient recovered well with normal stoma function. Following discharge, she received adjuvant chemotherapy. At the 6-month follow-up, there were no signs of recurrence.

This is a 42-year-old male who was involved in a motor vehicle collision. At the scene, he was found in respiratory distress with a deep, irregular respiratory rate of twenty breaths per minute and a low Glasgow coma scale (GCS) score, likely due to alcohol intoxication. Consequently, he was intubated at the scene and transported to the trauma room. Upon examination in the trauma room, he had a GCS score of 2T/15, which indicated severe impairment, and bilateral 3 mm reactive pupils, suggesting initially intact brainstem function despite the severe condition. Under the effects of a muscle relaxant and sedation, the chest examination revealed decreased air entry on the left side, while the FAST exam was negative. A CT scan showed multiple left-sided rib fractures with underlying pulmonary contusions, mild hemothorax, and pneumothorax, with no abnormalities in the head CT scan (Fig. 1), abdomen, and pelvis. The ethanol level was 65.1 mmol/l, reflecting significant intoxication at the time of the incident. He was subsequently admitted to the trauma ICU. A follow-up CT head the next day (Fig. 2) revealed a small extra-axial hematoma, a few scattered small hemorrhagic contusions, and minimal subarachnoid hemorrhage. Due to persistent low GCS, an MRI on day 3 showed a diffuse axonal injury grade 3. The patient was started on DVT prophylaxis and maintained on levetiracetam 500mg, initiated at admission. A subsequent CT scan the next day showed no significant changes. Due to persistently low GCS, he underwent percutaneous dilatation tracheostomy on the seventh day of his admission.
Over the following week, his GCS improved to E3M6Vt. He was tolerating a tracheal mask. Over the next 10 days, his conscious level improved further, with a GCS of E4M6 Vt. On the 19th of his admission, in the evening, he suddenly became unresponsive with fixed dilated pupils with no corneal reflex but preserved cough reflex. There was no witnessed or suspected fall, and no abnormal behavior or agitation before the incident.
The patient underwent emergency CT head showing newly developed right-sided cerebral convexity SDH with diffuse edema, with midline shift of 7.5 mm toward the left side and crowding at the foramen magnum with tonsillar herniation (Fig. 3). He underwent emergency right decompressive craniectomy and evacuation of acute SDH (Fig. 4). The presumed source of the hematoma was the cortical vein, which was identified and coagulated. After returning from the operating room, on examination, his pupils were fixed and dilated, with no corneal or cough reflex. He underwent a follow-up CT scan of the head that showed findings suggestive of multiple foci of ischemic changes, diffuse edema, and brainstem hemorrhage. The next day, the patient was polyuric with a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. As he lost the brain stem reflexes, the brain stem testing confirmed brain death on the third day of the event.

A 70-year-old female, never-smoker, with a history of Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), harboring MYD88 (p.L265P) and CXCR4 (p.S338Ffs*6) mutations, and previously treated with dexamethason rituximab, cyclofosfamide and on relapsed disease with rituximab and bendamustine about 10 years prior, to the current presentation was evaluated by her hematologist for several weeks of fatigue and bloating. She has noted furthermore slightly higher body temperature and about 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory tests revealed slightly elevated but stable IgM level, a newly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (667 U/L, rising to 1122 U/L). A Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) scan was ordered to rule out transformation to malignant lymphoma or other malignancy. Bone marrow biopsy was also obtained and subsequently Prednisolone and Rasburicase were started.
The FDG-PET scan demonstrated diffuse, marked bone marrow uptake of FDG, multiple lytic lesions, and mediastinal, left sided hilar, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (Fig. 1).
Bone marrow pathology revealed an epithelial malignancy positive for TTF1. Further molecular analysis by Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) identified EGFR exon 19 deletion (c.2235_2249del, p.E746_A750del) in combination with a nonsense mutation in TP53 exon 9 (c.949C>T, p.Q317*).
Careful review of the chest CT and PET imaging showed a possible primary tumor in the left upper lobe (LUL) (Fig. 1).
Treatment with osimertinib was initiated, resulting in a complete metabolic response of FDG-PET scan (Fig. 2). The LUL lesion was evolved into a small, vague ground-glass opacity. Osimertinib was well tolerated. At the latest follow-up, approximately 13 months after starting osimertinib, the patient remained still in complete remission with no signs of disease progression.
A 55-year-old Asian woman, who had never smoked, presented with slightly enlarged right-sided cervical lymph nodes. Aside from fatigue, she had no other symptoms at presentation and was still able to exercise 4 times a week.
A thoracic CT scan revealed a subpleural mass in the left upper lobe. An FDG-PET scan showed intense FDG uptake in the pulmonary mass, moderately increased uptake in several cervical lymph nodes, and diffuse, inhomogeneous, intense FDG uptake with sclerosis throughout the bones of the entire axial skeleton (Fig. 3).
Lymph node biopsies confirmed adenocarcinoma with strong TTF1 positivity, negative P40, and PD-L1 negativity (TPS < 1%). The tumor harbored an EGFR exon 19 mutation (NM_005228.5:c.2236_2250del, p.(Glu746_Ala750del), VAF 28%), and a TP53 co-mutation (NM_000546.6:c.455C>G, p.(Pro152Arg), VAF = 21%).
Her fatigue worsened significantly during the first week following the initial biopsy. She developed anemia (hemoglobin 5.8 mmol/L) and thrombocytopenia (28 × 10^9/L). A bone marrow biopsy also revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma. Osimertinib was initiated at the standard dose, which resulted in rapid clinical improvement, with performance status improving from 2 at baseline to 0. The patient was able to resume jogging at her previous level. A CT scan of the chest showed reduction in the size of the left lung tumor after about 5 weeks of osimertinib treatment. Platelet counts normalized after 9 weeks of treatment. No significant toxicity related to osimertinib was observed.

A 37-year-old male presented with progressive weakness in the lower limbs, which commenced two months before admission and later affected the upper limbs. He reported observing a distinct mass in the right inguinal region. On dermatologic examination, the only cutaneous abnormality identified was a newly developed erythematous papular lesion consistent with a red mole in the left axillary region, which had appeared about one month prior to admission.
Neurological imaging indicated a normal brain MRI, whereas the spinal MRI showed a lytic lesion in the L1 vertebral body extending into the left pedicle (Fig. 1). Moreover, there was notable thickening and contrast enhancement of the spinal nerve roots, especially in the cauda equina region and conus medullaris (Fig. 2). The chest CT findings were unremarkable. Abdominopelvic CT scan demonstrated multiple enhancing right inguinal lymphadenopathies and several lytic and sclerotic bony lesions (Fig. 3). It also has demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly (Fig. 4). Ultrasound examination of the right inguinal region revealed multiple lymph nodes in the right iliac chain and inguinal canal, exhibiting oval morphology, vascular stalks, and occasional mild hypoechogenicity. The maximum short-axis diameter (SAD) recorded was 30 mm. The ultrasound-guided biopsy of the inguinal lymphadenopathy confirmed the diagnosis of Castleman disease (mixed type). The immunohistochemical analysis of the lymph node biopsy demonstrated CD20 positivity in germinal centers, signifying B-cell proliferation. CD3 exhibited positivity in parafollicular lymphocytes, indicating the presence of T-cell zones. CD21 exhibited positivity in expanded follicular dendritic cells, aligning with the characteristics of follicular hyperplasia. CD5 negativity aids in the exclusion of specific T-cell lymphomas, while CD138 positivity in germinal centers indicates plasma cell infiltration.
Electrodiagnostic studies, comprising electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies (NCS), indicated subacute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with significant secondary axonal degeneration.
Laboratory investigations indicated mild hypoalbuminemia (53.6 g/L), slightly below the normal range, and elevated alpha-1 and alpha-2 globulin fractions, which suggest an acute phase response or underlying inflammatory activity (Fig. 5). The complete blood count indicated mild anemia, characterized by a reduced red blood cell count of 4.16 M/µL, hemoglobin level of 13.6 g/dL, and hematocrit of 41.4%. The platelet count was elevated at 489,000 /µL, suggesting potential reactive thrombocytosis. The white blood cell count and differential fell within normal limits, exhibiting a balanced distribution of neutrophils, lymphocytes, and monocytes. The findings indicate a chronic inflammatory or reactive process. VEGF testing, which could have provided additional biochemical support for POEMS syndrome, was not performed because this assay was not routinely available in our laboratory.
Following confirmation of POEMS syndrome associated with mixed-type Castleman disease, the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary team including neurology, hematology–oncology, and radiation oncology for clone-directed therapy and supportive care. Because of multifocal osteosclerotic and mixed lytic–sclerotic bone lesions, systemic therapy was favored over isolated radiotherapy. He received induction chemotherapy with lenalidomide (10 mg) on days 1-21 of a 28-day cycle plus weekly dexamethasone (days 1, 8, 15, and 22), one cycle every 28 days for a total of 12 cycles. Upon presentation, the patient demonstrated extremely weak extremities, a condition known as quadriplegia. In the upcoming follow-up visits, the patient has shown gradual, although not complete, neurological recovery along with partial restoration of motor function at the joints of both the upper and lower extremities, resulting in less severe residual quadriparesis.

A 25-year-old woman presented for a routine fetal ultrasound examination at 18 weeks gestation. Maternal medical history was unremarkable, with no known risk factors or medication exposure during pregnancy.
Ultrasound examination was performed using a 5 MHz curvilinear transducer with sagittal and axial imaging planes. Color Doppler imaging was used to assess fetal venous flow patterns.
Imaging demonstrated normal anatomical relationship between the inferior vena cava (IVC) and aorta. In the sagittal plane, the aorta coursed parallel to the spinal column, while the IVC followed a similar course to the level of the renal vessels. Beyond this level, the IVC deviated anteriorly from the aorta, producing the IVC Takeoff Appearance (Fig. 1). Axial views supported this anatomical relationship, while color Doppler demonstrated normal venous within the IVC.
This case illustrates the typical appearance of the IVC Takeoff Appearance, supporting normal fetal systemic venous anatomy and serving as a practical educational landmark during prenatal ultrasound evaluation.
A 35-year-old primigravida presented for a late fetal anomaly scan at 28-weeks gestation. Maternal history was unremarkable, with no known risk factors or medication exposure during pregnancy. Ultrasound examination was performed using a 5 MHz curvilinear transducer with sagittal and axial imaging planes supplemented by color Doppler evaluation.
Examination demonstrated dextrocardia and a right-sided descending aorta, while the remainder of the fetal anatomical survey was unremarkable. The IVC Takeoff Appearance was absent, and a double vessel sign was identified, with the azygos vein coursing parallel to the aorta (Fig. 2). Color Doppler demonstrated absence of normal flow within the expected IVC region, with compensatory venous drainage through the azygos vein.
The posthepatic IVC segment drained only the hepatic veins into the right atrium.
No additional major congenital anomalies were identified.
Fetal situs was otherwise normal, with no sonographic evidence of heterotaxy spectrum disorder.
Postnatal imaging, including echocardiography and abdominal ultrasound, confirmed interrupted intrahepatic IVC with azygos continuation, supporting the prenatal ultrasound findings. The pregnancy resulted in uncomplicated delivery, and the neonate remained clinically stable postnatally.
This case demonstrates how absence of the IVC Takeoff Appearance, combined with the double vessel sign, may serve as a useful educational clue during prenatal ultrasound evaluation, promoting further assessment and counseling regarding fetal IVC anomalies.

A 51-year-old male presented with complaints of abdominal pain for the past 1 month, which had progressively increased in severity and was not relieved by medications. The pain was associated with nausea and vomiting. He was a known case of hypertension for 1 year and diabetes mellitus for 5 years with a history of occasional alcohol intake over the past 20 years. The patient also reported episodic headache, palpitations, and weight loss.
Routine blood investigations revealed elevated serum amylase (∼725 U/L) and serum lipase (∼583 U/L), along with raised total leukocyte count (∼19.9 × 10³/µL). A diagnosis of acute pancreatitis was made, and the patient was referred to the radiology department for contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to assess for complications of pancreatitis.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen performed on a 64-slice scanner revealed multiple cystic lesions in the liver, pancreas, and bilateral kidneys. Imaging revealed near-complete replacement of pancreatic parenchyma with multiple variable-sized cystic lesions. The entire left adrenal gland was replaced by a multiloculated cystic lesion with a small enhancing solid component. In addition, features of pancreatitis were present, including peripancreatic, perirenal, and bilateral paracolic gutter fat stranding with a few loculated collections in the lesser sac and perisplenic region. Mild prominence of the pancreatic duct was noted without evidence of pancreatic calcification.
A provisional radiological diagnosis of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis with walled-off necrosis was made in the background of suspected VHL, with an associated mixed solid-cystic left adrenal lesion, likely representing a cystic pheochromocytoma.
Biochemical evaluation was performed and revealed mildly elevated plasma-free normetanephrine levels (526.9 pg/mL) with normal plasma-free metanephrine levels.
Owing to its atypical predominantly cystic appearance and the need for definitive tissue diagnosis, CT-guided biopsy of the left adrenal lesion was performed under appropriate hemodynamic precautions, with emergency support and interventional radiology backup readily available.
Histopathological examination revealed nests (zellballen pattern) of polygonal tumor cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma. Areas of cystic degeneration and hemorrhage were identified, correlating with the imaging appearance. Immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin, confirming the diagnosis of cystic pheochromocytoma.

A 90-year-old woman presented to our hospital with acute abdominal pain. She underwent emergency EVAR for an impending rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 63 mm in maximum diameter. Because the left CIA was severely calcified, she underwent AUI-EVAR with deployment of an Endurant II AUI device (32 × 102 mm, Medtronic, Santa Rosa, CA) from the infrarenal aorta to the right CIA, along with placement of a GORE Excluder contralateral leg component (16 mm × 9.5 cm, W. L. Gore & Associates, Newark, DE) as a right iliac extension. Femoro-femoral crossover bypass was performed, and the left CIA was embolized using a 14-mm Amplatzer Vascular Plug II (AVP II; Abbott Medical, Santa Clara, CA). Thereafter, the aortic aneurysm diameter gradually increased. Three years and 4 months after the surgery, an aortic cuff (28.5 mm × 3.3 cm, GORE Excluder Aortic Extender, W. L. Gore & Associates) was placed on the proximal side of the stent graft owing to suspicion of a type Ia endoleak. Subsequently, contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed an endoleak through the vascular plug in the left CIA (Fig. 1). The patient was referred to our department for transcatheter embolization of the endoleak. A 4 Fr sheath (Terumo, Tokyo, Japan) was inserted via the left superficial femoral artery under ultrasound guidance. Retrograde left iliac arteriography revealed blood flow into the aneurysm through the vascular plug (Fig. 2A). Using a microguidewire with a heavy tip load (Astato xs 9-12, Asahi Intecc, Aichi, Japan), a highly penetrating microcatheter (Corsair Armet, Asahi Intecc) was inserted into the plug through the mesh of the plug (Fig. 2B). Because it was impossible to access the proximal portion of the left CIA, the parts inside and around the vascular plug were embolized with metallic coils. However, the endoleak proximal to the vascular plug remained after coil embolization, and a type II endoleak via the left iliolumbar artery branching from the left internal iliac artery and the left fourth lumbar artery was found (Fig. 3). Using a triple coaxial system, a microcatheter was inserted into the endoleak cavity and then into the proximal portion of the left CIA via the collateral pathway (Fig. 4A). The proximal portion of the left CIA, the endoleak cavity, and the left lumbar artery were embolized with 20% n-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate (NBCA; Histoacryl, B. Braun, Melsungen, Germany)—Lipiodol (Guerbet, Villepinte, France) mixture (Fig. 4B). The endoleak disappeared after embolization (Fig. 5).

A 65-year-old Iranian female arrived with stomach bloating, heaviness, and constipation as her early symptoms. Symptoms such as anorexia, nausea, vomiting, pain, or weight loss were notable absences. The patient exhibited no significant past medical, surgical, or familial history and was otherwise in good health. Furthermore, the individual denied any use of tobacco, alcohol, recreational drugs, or any relevant psychosocial history. The clinical examination revealed that the vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed no masses or tenderness. Blood tests, including a full blood count, urea and electrolytes, and liver function tests, were performed and yielded unremarkable results within normal limits.
The workup included an abdominal ultrasonography that reported normal abdominal organs. Other Imaging work-up of MRI with rectal-pelvic protocol revealed a well-circumscribed iso to high T1W and intermediate T2W in the ischioanal space, which seemed to be intramuscular without invasion to adjacent structures such as the rectum (Fig. 1). Additional Chest x-ray revealed normal. A possible diagnosis based on imaging studies was the first solitary fibrous tumor and neurogenic tumors or EGIST could be other possibilities.

A 38-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of vague intermittent left flank pain. There was no history of fever, dysuria, hematuria, urinary tract infection, or nephrolithiasis. Laboratory investigations, including renal function tests and urinalysis, were within normal limits.
Initial transabdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a large well-defined cystic lesion within the left renal sinus, suggestive of gross hydronephrosis (however the narrow infundibulum visible on the Fig. 1A was missed on initial USG). No renal calculi or obvious obstructive lesion was identified. In view of suspected hydronephrosis without a definite obstructive cause, contrast-enhanced CT urography was performed for further evaluation.
Early venous phase CT images revealed a well-defined cystic lesion adjacent to the left renal pelvis and upper pole major calyx, without evidence of ureteral dilatation. No obstructing calculus or mass lesion was identified (Fig. 2). Delayed excretory phase imaging obtained at 15 minutes demonstrated faint layering of excreted contrast material within the lesion. Additional delayed imaging acquired at 1 hour and 20 minutes (Fig. 3) showed more prominent opacification of the cavity confirming communication with the pelvicalyceal system and establishing the diagnosis of a calyceal diverticulum.
Based on the large size and communication with the renal pelvis and upper pole major calyx, the lesion was consistent with a type II calyceal diverticulum.
There was no associated calyceal blunting, proximal ureteric dilatation, significant cortical thinning, or significant mass effect to suggest obstructive hydronephrosis. The patient was managed conservatively because symptoms were minimal and renal function was preserved.

A 30-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency department for acute hemoptysis and dyspnea that appeared during the fourth month postpartum. The patient was nonobese, with no previous cardiac history, and presented with signs of congestive heart failure on admission.
Her family history was negative for thrombotic disorders. Regarding her past medical history, she had no previous miscarriages, no episodes of deep vein thrombosis, and no history of prolonged bed rest or hospitalization.
On physical examination, she was tachycardic (119 beats/min) and polypneic (25 breaths/min). Cardiac auscultation revealed a diastolic murmur at both the mitral and aortic foci, with clinical signs of right heart failure. Peripheral vascular examination was unremarkable.
A chest X-ray demonstrated cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic index = 0.65) with blunting of the right costophrenic angle. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), and secondary repolarization abnormalities.
Given the high clinical suspicion of pulmonary embolism, a CT pulmonary angiography was performed. It confirmed a bilateral pulmonary embolism involving the apical branches, associated with bilateral pleural effusion (moderate on the right, minimal on the left), cardiomegaly, and an apical thrombus in the left ventricle. The abdominal cuts revealed foci of renal and hepatic infarction (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).
Before initiating anticoagulation, the patient’s main laboratory parameters were as follows: erythrocytes 4.27 × 10⁶/µL, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, hematocrit 40%, platelets 259 × 10³/µL, D-dimers positive, and INR 1.19. Renal and hepatic function tests were within normal limits (Table 1).
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a dilated left ventricle with severely depressed systolic function (LVEF = 20%, Simpson’s method) due to global hypokinesia. A mobile, echogenic apical thrombus measuring 35 × 19 mm was visualized. The right chambers were also dilated, with severe right ventricular dysfunction (fractional area change = 29%, TAPSE = 14 mm, S′RV = 7 cm/s). Pulmonary artery systolic pressure was estimated at 30 mmHg. Valvular assessment revealed moderate aortic regurgitation and moderate mitral regurgitation (Fig. 3).
In search of the thromboembolic source and to exclude occult malignancy, venous and abdominal ultrasound examinations were performed. Venous Doppler of the lower limbs ruled out deep vein thrombosis.
An ischemic or embolic etiology was investigated. The patient had no history of angina or myocardial infarction, and echocardiography showed no regional wall motion abnormalities suggestive of coronary artery disease. Therefore, the cardiomyopathy was considered nonischemic.
Given the occurrence of multiple thromboembolic events in a young woman without traditional cardiovascular risk factors, a thrombophilia screening was conducted to identify a potential underlying hypercoagulable state. The investigation included testing for protein C and S activity, antithrombin III levels, prothrombin gene mutation (G20210A), and Factor V Leiden mutation. The results confirmed the presence of a heterozygous Factor V Leiden mutation, responsible for resistance to activated protein C (APC), thereby predisposing the patient to recurrent venous and systemic thromboembolic events.
During hospitalization, the patient developed a transient neurological deficit with dysarthria and central facial palsy. Brain MRI angiography demonstrated an ischemic lesion (Fig. 4).
Therapeutic anticoagulation was started with enoxaparin and continued later with rivaroxaban. Since our patient was hemodynamically stable, there was no indication for systemic thrombolysis.

A 38-year-old man diagnosed with testicular embryonal carcinoma via right testicular mass biopsy. His medical history was significant for chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, prior incarceration, and history of intravenous drug use. Importantly, the patient owned 2 dogs that were primarily kept outdoors and frequently hunted small animals including rabbits and rodents. Preoperative serum tumor markers showed elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG). A baseline chest CT showed an indeterminate right lower lobe 3 mm nodule. He underwent radical orchiectomy with pathology confirming embryonal carcinoma.
FDG PET/CT was performed 1 week after orchiectomy (approximately 2 weeks after the baseline chest CT) for staging (Fig. 1). The previously noted indeterminate 3 mm right lower lobe nodule on the baseline chest CT was not well visualized on the low-dose CT component of the FDG PET/CT. The study demonstrated intensely hypermetabolic retroperitoneal (aortocaval and pre/para-aortic) and right retrocrural lymph nodes consistent with nodal metastatic disease. Moderately hypermetabolic right common iliac and right external iliac lymph nodes were also noted, with differential considerations including reactive or post-surgical changes versus nodal metastasis. No suspicious FDG uptake was identified in the chest, and the lungs were clear without evidence of pulmonary metastatic disease. No pelvic lymph node involvement was identified. Subsequently, the patient was initiated on BEP chemotherapy. Approximately 2 and a half weeks after the first dose of chemotherapy, the patient presented to the emergency department with tachycardia, nausea/vomiting, and acute kidney injury. Chest CT (Fig. 2A) revealed numerous bilateral new pulmonary nodules. The nodules ranged from 5 to 15 mm in diameter, demonstrated poorly marginated, ill-defined borders with a peribronchovascular distribution throughout both lungs and no zonal predominance. While the 2-month interval from the staging PET/CT was sufficient for the potential development of new metastatic disease, particularly given the aggressive biology of embryonal carcinoma, the close temporal relationship between chemotherapy initiation and the onset of respiratory symptoms and new pulmonary findings also raised significant concern for either BIP toxicity or an infectious process. Bilateral pleural effusions were also present. Follow-up chest CT performed 1 week later (Fig. 2B) demonstrated stable size of the numerous pulmonary nodules with increased bilateral pleural effusions. There was also questionable minimal cavitation of 1 nodule. Serum tumor markers were checked which were not elevated. This finding argued strongly against active metastatic disease, as serum tumor markers are highly sensitive indicators of disease activity in nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. The discordance between the appearance of new pulmonary nodules and normalized tumor markers was a critical clinical finding that prompted further investigation for alternative diagnoses. Bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), though contamination was considered possible. Acid-fast bacilli smears and cultures were negative. Tuberculosis PCR was negative. Fungal studies were negative. F. tularensis serology showed positive IgG and IgM antibodies. The positive tularemia serology, combined with the patient’s exposure history of owning outdoor dogs that hunted small animals, raised strong suspicion for pulmonary tularemia. Serology is the most common method for confirming tularemia diagnosis. The patient resided in Missouri, one of the highest-incidence states for tularemia in the United States. CT-guided lung biopsy was performed targeting one of the larger pulmonary nodules. Histopathologic examination revealed small areas of nodular fibrosis with mildly increased alveolar macrophages and no evidence of malignancy. Based on the positive tularemia serology and epidemiological exposure, the patient was treated with oral ciprofloxacin for 10 days. Bleomycin was permanently discontinued from the chemotherapy regimen given the initial concern for bleomycin-induced pulmonary toxicity.
Serial chest CT imaging documented the temporal evolution of the pulmonary findings. Follow-up chest CT obtained 2 weeks later showed slight decrease in size of the pulmonary nodules, and ciprofloxacin therapy was initiated at this time. Follow-up chest CT approximately 1 month after the initial presentation and 2 weeks after starting ciprofloxacin (Fig. 2C) demonstrated markedly decreased size of bilateral pulmonary nodules with resolution of the left pleural effusion; however, the right pleural effusion persisted, associated with focal pleural thickening and round atelectasis. Subsequent follow-up CT at approximately 2 and a half months after the initial presentation confirmed complete resolution of the right pleural effusion.

A 51-year-old man presented to our vascular surgery outpatient clinic with a post-traumatic plantar AVF and a large venous aneurysm that had undergone multiple treatments with coil embolization. According to his medical history, the patient sustained a penetrating knife injury to the plantar aspect of his left foot extending to the bone at the age of 16. The wound was initially managed with simple suturing. Two years later, he developed persistent pressure and nonspecific pain in the sole of the injured foot. Over the subsequent 25 years, progressive unilateral leg swelling occurred, accompanied by ongoing discomfort and increasing paresthesia of the foot during weight-bearing. Finally, a plantar AVF and a large venous aneurysm were diagnosed when the patient was 47 years old. The venous aneurysm was treated in a minimally invasive manner with coil embolization. Due to persistent symptoms, the procedure was repeated twice. However, foot function continued to deteriorate, as constant pressure in the sole of the foot led to marked impairment of daily activities. On examination, prominently visible veins were observed on the dorsum of the foot, with a palpable thrill upon warming of the overlying skin (Fig 1). Duplex ultrasound examination detected a venous aneurysm with a maximal diameter of 22.5 mm and a flow of 800 mL/min. Angiography demonstrated persistent perfusion of the coiled venous aneurysm via the hypertrophic lateral plantar artery, while perfusion through the anterior tibial artery remained normal (Fig 2).
Given persistent symptoms and incomplete thrombosis, surgical excision of the AVF was indicated. The patient underwent surgical excision of the AVF via an extensive medial approach to the lateral plantar artery under bloodless conditions using an Esmarch bandage. The bandage was removed after wrapping the foot up to the ankle, leaving the proximal portion in place as a tourniquet. The large venous aneurysm was completely resected, including removal of all previously placed coil embolization material, and the arterial connection was closed from within using a simple suture technique (Fig 3).
Postoperatively, after primary wound healing and a period of temporary offloading, the patient experienced complete resolution of symptoms with full regression of leg swelling (Fig 4). Computed tomography angiography demonstrated partial preservation of the lateral plantar artery, with no residual aneurysm and maintained foot perfusion via the anterior tibial artery (Fig 5). At 60 months postoperatively, the patient remains symptom free and is able to ambulate without restrictions, including long distances.

The patient was a 63-year-old woman who had no previous known medical history and recently travelled to our state via a cross-country airplane ride. She presented to our Level 1 trauma center following 2 days of intermittent pain and weakness in her right lower and upper extremities. The emergency department initially considered diagnoses of stroke, venous thromboembolism, and lower limb ischemia, so she was sent for emergent computed tomography (CT) scan of the head, chest, abdomen, and lower-extremity runoff. There was no acute intracranial process, but a large right breast mass was noted on CT (Fig 1), along with thrombus in her common hepatic artery, as well as a splenic infarct (Fig 2). At this point, there was concern that the breast mass could be a malignancy and discussion to complete an oncologic workup, including a biopsy, was proposed. However, given the presence of acute lower limb ischemia, the workup of this mass was deferred until the life-threatening pathology was addressed first. The CT also demonstrated a pulmonary right upper lobe suprahilar irregular nodule with soft tissue attenuation measuring 2.0 cm, along with an adjacent peripheral nodule measuring 2.4 cm. This was among several other small pulmonary nodules. The initial CT scan of the chest did not mention findings of a mitral valve lesion on the final read. Although this was not a gated study and increased contrast burden on the left-sided chambers, there was not a clear visualization of a vegetation.
On return to the emergency department, she had increasing right leg and right arm pain, decreased right foot motion, and was noted to have absent Doppler signals in her right leg. Review of the CT scan showed right common femoral artery occlusion (Fig 3). Vascular surgery was consulted, and she was diagnosed with acute Rutherford 2B ischemia to both her right arm and right leg. On physical examination, her abdomen was soft and nontender, and ischemic right upper and lower extremity findings were confirmed. The patient was started on heparin and emergently taken to the operating room. Embolectomies successfully re-established blood flow via right groin and right antecubital incisions. Fasciotomies were then performed in the right calf. Because her serum lactate was normal, no abdominal exploration was performed at that time.
During her intensive care unit stay the next day, heparin anticoagulation was continued. Her electrocardiogram showed no atrial fibrillation. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was performed. It was considered technically difficult, but a nodular, thickened surface on the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve was noted. The patient then started developing abdominal pain, and vascular surgery took her back to the operating room for abdominal exploration and hepatic revascularization. An embolectomy of the common hepatic and gastroduodenal arteries was performed, along with a cholecystectomy. The embolectomies were performed using a single arteriotomy of the common hepatic artery just proximal to the gastroduodenal artery takeoff. Using a combination of 2F and 3F Fogarty catheters, embolectomies were performed of the common hepatic artery, gastroduodenal artery, proper hepatic artery, right and left hepatic arteries separately, and the celiac artery. Given the identification of hepatic and gallbladder ischemia on workup, these were the only embolectomies considered during this index mesenteric revascularization procedure. Postembolectomy Doppler ultrasound examination of the liver parenchyma show arterial signals throughout and inspection of the liver demonstrated a well-perfused appearance.
The largest size of the clot retrieved through the embolectomies was 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm; however, this was sent as a conglomerate of the embolectomies from the multiple mesenteric sites. The clot was acute appearing with a homogenous appearance throughout. The borders of the clot were unable to be accurately assessed due to the use of a Fogarty catheter for embolectomies.
The abdomen was then packed open and the patient taken back to the intensive care unit for supportive care. Over the next several days, she was taken back to the operating room for abdominal closure as well as fasciotomy closures. The hematology, oncology, infectious disease, and cardiology services were consulted and extensive laboratory studies were ordered. Over her hospital course, all blood cultures and other laboratory studies such as antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant were negative for infection, prothrombotic, or rheumatologic disorders. Blood cultures included fungal cultures and workup also included a respiratory panel, which were all negative. Postoperatively, the patient had return of sensory function in the form of intact sensation to touch, temperature, and pain and slowly improving motor function over the course of 4 weeks. Her extremities were able to be salvaged, and amputation during her hospitalization was avoided. The patient required physical and occupational therapy due to the significant physiological insult from multiple surgeries and her underlying pathology. Per American Society of Hematology recommendations for patients with thromboembolic events and presumed breast cancer, she was discharged on oral apixaban to an inpatient rehabilitation facility.
The patient was readmitted approximately 1 week later with significant fatigue and a workup for sepsis ensued. Her temperature was 37.8°C, with a white blood cell count of 22,000, hemoglobin of 6.6, and lactate of 4.9. CT of her chest was performed showing bibasilar ground-glass and consolidated opacities concerning for aspiration or infective bronchiolitis. The previously noted right breast mass and right-sided pulmonary lesions remained unchanged, and there were no pulmonary emboli. All previous and repeated blood cultures remained negative. Group B Streptococcus pneumonia was diagnosed and treated with eventual clinical improvement.
She also underwent biopsies and was diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast with metastases to the lymph nodes and lung. Her final cancer diagnosis was an estrogen receptor/progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal stage 4 breast cancer. Extensive hematologic workup for a hypercoagulable state and infective endocarditis was performed and all studies were negative. Pathology on all previous embolectomy specimens showed organized thrombus without evidence of inflammation or bacterial clumps. A repeat TTE during her second admission showed a 2.1 cm × 1.6 cm mass on the mitral valve (Fig 4). This was confirmed on a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE), along with significant mitral regurgitation (Fig 5). The final diagnosis per hematology was NBTE secondary to a hypercoagulable state due to invasive and metastatic breast cancer. She was started on letrozole for the cancer and was eventually discharged to an inpatient facility.
The patient was readmitted 1 month later with signs of congestive heart failure. Both palliative care and hospice were consulted, and she declined aggressive treatment of her breast cancer. She was discharged after a 4-week hospital stay. Before discharge, the patient agreed to publish case details and images for educational purposes. However, after discharge, she never followed up with multiple scheduled clinic visits and contact with her and family has been unsuccessful. Therefore, her long-term functional status could not be assessed.

An 11-month-old, intact male English Setter was presented to the Parasitic Diseases Unit of the Department of Veterinary Medicine, University of Bari “Aldo Moro” (Apulia, Italy), for the evaluation of cutaneous lesions affecting the metacarpal and metatarsal regions (Day 0). General physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Dermatological examination identified two round, alopecic lesions located on two distinct limbs: one on the metacarpal region of the right forelimb and the other on the metatarsal region of the right hindlimb. The alopecic skin appeared mildly (hind leg) to moderately (fore leg) erythematous, with fine scaling on its periphery (Fig. 1a–b). Pruritus and pain upon palpation were not evident. The patient was up to date with vaccinations and, one month prior to presentation, had received a canine leishmaniosis vaccine. The dog was kept exclusively outdoors, with restricted garden access. The patient cohabited with another 12-year-old English Setter that shared the same environment. Both dogs were undergoing outdoor field training for hunting, involving frequent and prolonged exposure to soil, vegetation, and diverse environmental substrates. The cohabitant dog did not show any similar dermatological lesions. The initial differential diagnosis included dermatophytosis, superficial bacterial pyoderma and demodicosis.
At the time of the clinical assessment (Day 0), the patient underwent tape-strip cytology, a trichogram, a skin scraping, and a dermatophyte culture. Samples were collected using a tape strip and stained using a Diff-Quick stain. Microscopic findings at 100x magnification showed only sporadic extracellular coccoid bacteria. Plucked hairs collected from the margins of the lesions were examined at 10x magnification and showed a good proportion between the anagen and telogen phases, a normal hair shaft shape, and an absence of ectoparasites and fungal elements. Skin scrapings were collected using a no. 10 scalpel blade. The affected cutaneous areas were cleansed with 70% isopropyl alcohol to minimize the surface bacterial contamination. Hair shafts, skin scrapings, and scales were collected from the margins of the lesions. For direct examination, a portion of the samples were placed on glass slides, suspended in a 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) solution, and gently heated to accelerate tissue clearing. Under a light microscope at 40× magnification, no fungal structures or ectoparasites were observed. Given the lesions’ clinical appearance, a dermatophyte culture was performed on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) supplemented with chloramphenicol (0.05 mg/mL) [Liofilchem®, Italy] and on Mycobios selective agar (MYC) (Biolife®, Milan, Italy). Cultures were incubated aerobically at 25°C and inspected daily for 21 days. Considering the clinical appearance of the lesions compatible with dermatophytosis, a new sample was taken after 48 hours (Day +2).
After 7 days of incubation (Day +7), fungal growth was observed in all cultures. Importantly, cultures obtained independently from each of the two lesions—one on the right forelimb and one on the right hindlimb—were both positive for dermatophyte growth. In addition to these colonies, other fungal growth was also present. The dermatophyte colonies were macroscopically characterized by a whitish color and feathery margins. To further characterize these isolates, subcultures were established on MYC and SDA and incubated at room temperature to assess the production of pigments and reproductive structures. By Day 21, the colonies macroscopically demonstrated rapid growth, presenting as flat, dense, and conspicuously granular-to-powdery in texture (Fig. 2). The obverse surface was characterized by a distinct cream-to-tan or pale buff coloration at the center, surrounded by a prominent, white downy-to-floccose peripheral zone with irregular, radiating borders (Fig. 2a–c). Notably, mature colonies exhibited active metabolic guttation, with the accumulation of small, clear exudate droplets across the granular surface matrix (Fig. 3). Examination of the reverse side on both the SDA and MYC (Fig. 2b–d) media revealed an intense, deep dark-brownish to black central pigmentation that gradually diffused into a warm golden-yellow or amber hue towards the advancing periphery. Micromorphological analysis revealed abundant macroconidia arising directly from septate vegetative hyphae, borne either terminally or laterally on short, non-branched conidiophores. The macroconidia occasionally displayed a slight apical tapering or blunt distal ends, and were predominantly elongated, spindle-to cigar-shaped, and smooth; they possessed distinctly thickened double cell walls, with multiple regular transverse septations, consistently dividing each individual conidium into 5 to 9 distinct internal cells. Conversely, microconidia were sparse, small, and inconsistently distributed throughout the examined fields, confirming a highly specialized macroconidial-dominant phenotype (Fig. 4).
Genomic DNA was extracted from young mycelia harvested from pure cultures using the commercial DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), strictly adhering to the manufacturer's instructions for filamentous fungi. Molecular identification was achieved by targeting the nuclear ribosomal ITS region. Polymerase chain reaction amplification was performed using the universal fungal primer pair ITS1 (5′-TCCGTAGGTGAACCTGCGG-3′) and ITS4 (5′-TCCTCCGCTTATTGATATGC-3′), following previously established protocols. The resulting PCR products were enzymatically purified to remove residual primers and dNTPs, and subsequently subjected to bidirectional automated Sanger sequencing. The raw forward and reverse electropherograms were chromatographically evaluated, trimmed, and assembled into a consensus sequence using AliView software (version 1.28). To establish identity, the consensus sequence was compared against reference nucleotide datasets available in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank and the MYCOBANK databases using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLASTn); this comparison demonstrated a 99% query coverage, a non-significant E-value of 0.0, and a 100% sequence identity match with validated reference strains of A. uncinatum (syn. T. ajelloi).
The resulting consensus nucleotide sequence was deposited in the GenBank database and assigned the accession number PZ567627.
Following the initial consultation (Day 0), while awaiting the culture results, the patient was started on a daily basis on a topical antiseptic (Betadine®, povidone-iodine), 1:10 dilutions. Following the macroscopic and microscopic identification of a dermatophyte (Day 21), topical treatment with a 1% clotrimazole cream (Canesten®, Bayer) was started, applying a thin layer on the affected areas twice daily for 3 weeks. While on the Canesten treatment, a definitive diagnosis of A. uncinatum was confirmed molecularly. After 3 weeks of treatment (Day +42), the patient was rechecked and, given the complete resolution of the clinical lesions, the topical treatment was discontinued. A further follow-up took place 2 weeks later (Day +56), during which no flares were observed, alongside the ad integrum restitution of the hair coat (Fig. 5). To confirm a mycological cure, a dermatophyte culture with a hair pluck technique was performed. No growth was observed 21 days post-incubation (Day +77).

A 15-year-old male presented to the Internal Medicine Clinic of the Thalassaemia and Congenital Blood Diseases Center (Sulaymaniyah, Kurdistan Region, Iraq) on September, 2021 with complaints of colicky abdominal pain, episodic severe dysentery (>10 times a day) for a period of 6 years, and fatigue for 2 months. He had been receiving regular blood transfusions since he was diagnosed with thalassemia major at 1 year of age. Chelation therapy had been required since the age of 5 years. When the patient was 8 years of age, he experienced intermittent abdominal pain, dysentery and weight loss. A general stool examination (GSE) was performed at that time and revealed Entamoeba histolytica (E. histolytica) infection. The patient received metronidazole. However, 4 years thereafter, the patient was diagnosed with growth failure and treated with growth hormone (GH) replacement therapy for 1 year, although there was no response to the treatment.
Clinical findings. Upon a physical examination, he had a typical thalassemic face (frontal bossing and flattened nasal bridge), jaundice, tachycardia (110 bpm) and a slightly distended abdomen.
Diagnostic assessment. Blood analyses revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin level, 50 g/l), an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level (265 mg/l), a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/h) and a negative Coombs test. He had an infection with E. histolytica according to the GSE, and the fecal calprotectin level was elevated (>1,000 µg/g). The patient was referred to a pediatric gastroenterologist, who performed a colonoscopy and obtained biopsies. The histopathological analysis of the specimens confirmed the diagnosis of CD (data not shown as images could not be retrieved).
Therapeutic intervention. The patient was treated with mercaptopurine (25 mg/day), mesalazine (2 g/day, suppository) and prednisolone (20 mg/day). After 1 month, the patient developed cholestatic jaundice, and the use of mercaptopurine was terminated; however, the patient's condition worsened. A magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography scan revealed sclerosing cholangitis (Fig. 1), and he was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid (13-15 mg/kg/day, divided into 2-3 doses for a lifetime duration).
Follow-up. The patient remained under follow-up for the monitoring of cholangitis. The frequency of diarrhea decreased to three to five episodes per day, and the hemoglobin level increased to 80 g/l. Unfortunately, the patient's cholangitis progressively worsened, leading to jaundice and sepsis. Despite treatment, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and the patient succumbed ~2 years after the initial presentation.
A 13-year-old female patient presented with thalassemia major to the Thalassaemia and Congenital Blood Diseases Center (Sulaymaniyah, Iraq) on September, 2021 with severe dysentery (more than 8 times/day), colicky abdominal pain, fatigue and increasing pallor. The patient had been on regular transfusions since 3 months of age and commenced chelation at the age of 3 years. At the age of 11 years, she was diagnosed with growth failure and underwent 1 year of GH replacement therapy without significant improvement. She reported a history of intermittent abdominal pain, weight loss and bloody diarrhea for 3 years. On each occasion, GSE tested positive for E. histolytica, for which she had been prescribed antibiotics by a gastroenterologist. Recently, the patient's condition had begun to deteriorate further.
Clinical findings. A physical examination revealed that she had a typical thalassemic facial appearance characterized by frontal bossing, a flattened nasal bridge and jaundice.
Diagnostic assessment. Blood analyses revealed severe anemia (hemoglobin level, 55 g/l), elevated CRP (360 mg/l) and elevated serum ferritin (4,800 µg/l) levels, with a negative Coombs test. A GSE confirmed an infection with E. histolytica. Furthermore, the fecal calprotectin level was high (>1,000 µg/g). A colonoscopy was performed, biopsy samples were obtained, and histopathological analysis was performed on 5-µm-thick paraffin-embedded sections. The sections were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin at room temperature for 24 h and subsequently stained with hematoxylin and eosin (Bio Optica Co.) for 1-2 min at room temperature. The sections were then examined under a light microscope (Leica Microsystems GmbH). The histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of UC (Fig. 2).
Therapeutic intervention. The case was managed with prednisolone (20 mg/day), mesalazine (500 mg tablet, 1x3) and mercaptopurine (50 mg/day). The chelation therapy was switched to Desferal (deferoxamine) due to the exacerbated diarrhea of the patient caused by Exjade.
Follow-up. The patient responded well to the treatment course. Her diarrhea decreased to one to two times/day without containing blood, resulting in an increase in her hemoglobin level to 88 g/l. Stool calprotectin and serum ferritin levels decreased to 75 µg/g and 3,083 µg/l, respectively.

A 16-year-old female with no previous comorbidities presented with dyspnea, odynophagia, and hemoptysis-associated cough. She was from a rural area in Maranhão, a state of autochthonous OROV transmission located near the Brazilian Amazon region, and denied recent travel. She sought emergency care, two days after onset of symptoms, where a chest X-ray suggested pneumonia, resulting in her hospitalization. Her condition progressively worsened on the next day, with increased dyspnea and cough accompanied by headache and right-sided chest pain. Orotracheal intubation was performed on the third day of illness, when massive bleeding through the endotracheal tube was identified. The patient had a hemodynamic worsening, and subsequently died.
The autopsy revealed a bilateral large serosanguineous pleural effusion totaling approximately one liter. The lungs exhibited a purplish color with hemorrhagic spots; cut surfaces showed congestion and hemorrhage; petechiae were diffusely distributed in the pericardium, along with mild cerebral edema and tonsillar herniation. Microscopic findings showed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and pulmonary edema (Fig. 1). The kidneys showed acute tubular necrosis with vascular congestion. The liver exhibited only vascular congestion.
Samples were collected for reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction testing for arboviruses and respiratory viruses. Results were positive for OROV and H1N1. For the complete list of infectious agents tested, see Table 1. For the other infectious agents, the results were negative.

An 8-year-old male was referred with a painless penile swelling noted by his parents over several years. The lesion had remained stable for an extended period but showed a gradual, progressive increase in size over the preceding 12 months, prompting surgical evaluation. He had undergone routine neonatal circumcision on the seventh day of life without documented intraoperative or postoperative complications. There was no history of penile trauma, local infections, or prior interventions. The patient was entirely asymptomatic with respect to urinary function, with no dysuria, hematuria, or voiding dysfunction.
General examination was unremarkable for his age. Focused genital examination revealed a well-circumscribed, smooth-surfaced, dome-shaped cystic mass measuring approximately 1.5 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm on the dorsolateral aspect of the distal penile shaft, within the subcutaneous tissue beneath intact overlying skin. The overlying skin showed no erythema, sinus tracts, puncta, or scarring. The mass was soft, non-tender, fluctuant, and freely mobile over the underlying corpora cavernosa. The urethra was clearly uninvolved. There was no inguinal lymphadenopathy, and both testes were fully descended (Fig. 1).
Routine hematological and biochemical investigations were within normal limits. High-resolution B-mode ultrasonography revealed a well-defined, thin-walled, hypoechoic to anechoic cystic structure within the subcutaneous tissue superficial to Buck's fascia on the dorsolateral penile shaft, without internal septations, calcifications, or echogenic debris. Color Doppler confirmed a complete absence of internal vascularity and no communication between the cyst and the urethral lumen or corpora cavernosa, effectively excluding urethral diverticulum and paraurethral cyst (Fig. 2).
Elective surgical excision was performed under general anesthesia. Following standard sterile preparation and draping, a fusiform incision was made over the longitudinal axis of the mass. Careful dissection in the subcutaneous plane immediately superficial to Buck's fascia allowed complete en-bloc excision without intraoperative rupture of the cyst wall, preventing spillage of keratinaceous contents and reducing the risk of implantation recurrence. The excision site was closed in layers using absorbable sutures. Hemostasis was secured throughout (Fig. 3).
Gross macroscopic examination confirmed a white-tan-brown soft tissue specimen measuring 20 mm. Microscopic evaluation with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining demonstrated a cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a prominent granular cell layer, its lumen filled with concentric laminated layers of anucleate keratinaceous material. No hair follicles, sebaceous glands, or eccrine sweat glands were identified within the cyst wall, confirming classification as an epidermal inclusion cyst rather than a dermoid cyst. Sections were negative for dysplasia, atypia, and malignancy. The pathological diagnosis was: Benign Epidermoid Cyst, Penis — Excision (Fig. 4)
The patient was discharged on the same day without complications. At the six-month postoperative follow-up, the surgical site was well-healed with a satisfactory cosmetic result. There was no clinical evidence of local recurrence, residual cystic lesion, or distortion of penile architecture, and urinary function remained entirely normal throughout the follow-up period (Fig. 5).

Patient 1 was a 62-year-old female with a history of class 1 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 34.0 kg m−2) and hypertension and no prior history of depression or mood disorders. The patient had lost 26% of her weight while being treated with subcutaneous tirzepatide over the course of 19 months, up to a dose of 15 mg·week−1. The patient joined our online clinic to help optimize her body composition and overall health. Our clinicians introduced her to strength training and recommended dietary changes.
Patient 2 was a 36-year-old female with a history of class 1 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 33.9 kg m−2) along with depression and anxiety. The patient had lost 23% of her weight while being treated with 15 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide over the previous 24 months. She had previously used bupropion but had not taken it for several years. The patient joined our online clinic after seeing an online discussion of potential anhedonia precipitated by tirzepatide use.
Patient 3 was a 64-year-old female with a history of class 3 obesity (pre-treatment BMI 49.9 kg m−2) and no history of depression or mood disorders. The patient had lost 57% of her weight while being treated with 15 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide. The patient was not aware of subjective mood disturbances at this point.
Patient 1 described feeling a lack of motivation to exercise and loss of interest in her other hobbies.
Patient 2 described feeling “flat” and unmotivated despite her weight loss success. She noted that these feelings differed from her feelings when previously diagnosed with depression. The patient also described being aware that she should exercise but being unable to “get herself to do it.”
Patient 3 briefly stopped tirzepatide due to a medical procedure.
The timeline for each patient is displayed in Fig. 2.
Patient 1 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, and current lack of motivation and loss of interest in hobbies. Patient 2 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, history of depression, past bupropion use, and current feelings of “flatness.” Patient 3 was interviewed concerning past and current tirzepatide treatment, weight loss, and changes in medication use surrounding her medical procedure. In all cases, the presence of anhedonia was assessed through patient screening and clinical history taking. Anhedonia was established based on the loss of pleasure in previously rewarding experiences after ruling out organic or biological causes (e.g., hormonal, anemia, nutritional deficiencies, and sleep disturbances) and signs of depression other than anhedonia.
Patient 1 was prescribed a reduced dose of 10 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide for four months, during which the patient's desire to exercise and continue past hobbies improved markedly.
Patient 2 was prescribed a reduced dose of 10 mg·week−1 of subcutaneous tirzepatide for four weeks, during which she noticed significant improvements in her “flat” feelings but did not experience full resolution. At that point, 150 mg·day−1 bupropion XL was prescribed, which further improved her feelings within several weeks.
Patient 3 was required to temporarily stop her medication due to a procedure and resumed tirzepatide at a dose of 7.5 mg·week−1.
Following the initial resolution of anhedonia, Patient 1 chose to self-administer a 12.5 mg·week−1 dose of subcutaneous tirzepatide for two months, followed by a 15 mg·week−1 dose for an additional two months, due to frustration with stalled weight loss. During this time, the patient's lack of motivation quickly returned, and no further weight loss was achieved. At this point, the patient was transitioned back to 10 mg·week−1 tirzepatide for four months, which resulted in improved motivation but some continued “flatness.” As such, the dose was further reduced to 5 mg·week−1 tirzepatide for four additional months. At this dose, the patient maintained previous weight loss while the lack of motivation and prior loss of interest in hobbies and daily activities completely resolved.
Patient 2 lost another 15 pounds (7% of original weight) during 4 months of treatment with 10 mg·week−1 tirzepatide and 150 mg bupropion. The patient reported feeling more motivated to participate in the activities she had stopped performing when being treated with 15 mg·week−1 tirzepatide without bupropion but desired further improvement. Bupropion was subsequently increased to 300 mg·day−1 while tirzepatide was decreased to 7.5 mg·week−1. During the subsequent four months, the patient lost an additional 15 pounds and reported feeling “her best.”
Within two weeks of reducing the dose of tirzepatide, Patient 3 experienced a notable improvement in her desire to complete daily activities she previously did not realize had been affected (i.e., retrospective recognition of reduced drive and motivation). Over the course of three months, she maintained the 7.5 mg·week−1 dose of tirzepatide. This resulted in weight maintenance but substantially improved motivation and desire to perform daily activities.

The patient, a 1-year 9-months-old boy, recently diagnosed with down’s syndrome and bronchial asthma, developed a yellowish to brownish plaque on his left arm.
The patient presented with a 6 months history of localized plaque on the extensor aspect of the left arm. The lesion gradually increased in size but remained asymptomatic, with no associated itching, pain, or preceding trauma. There was no history of similar lesions elsewhere or known triggering factors such as friction, rubbing, or heat exposure.
There were no associated constitutional symptoms such as fever, malaise, or weight loss. The patient had no history of recurrent infections, prolonged cough, gastrointestinal disturbances, or changes in appetite. No ocular, oral, or genital lesions were noted.
The antenatal period was uneventful, with no reported maternal illnesses or complications. The patient was born at term, normal vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 3.2 kg. There were no perinatal complications.
Chromosomal analysis was performed shortly after birth and confirmed the diagnosis of Down syndrome, demonstrating a karyotype of 47,XY,+21, consistent with complete (non-mosaic) trisomy 21.
The patient is the third child of healthy parents, with 2 older siblings reported to be well. The parents are distant cousins. The mother was 30 years old during the pregnancy. On the maternal side, 1 cousin has a child with down syndrome, and another cousin from the paternal side of the mother’s family also has a child with down syndrome.
On examination, the patient appeared well, active, and in no apparent distress. Growth parameters were within the expected range for his age and Down syndrome. No pallor, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy was noted. There were no hepatosplenomegaly or other systemic abnormalities on general physical examination.
A single well-defined, oval-shaped firm, brownish plaque measuring approximately 2-3 cm in diameter is noted on the extensor aspect of the left arm. The surface appears slightly thickened with a rough texture and mildly wrinkled with an irregular border. No overlying scale, crusting, or ulceration was observed. Surrounding skin appears normal [Fig 1].
Dermoscopy revealed hypopigmented center with brownish pigmentation at the periphery. Fine linear vessels were noted. Darier sign was negative.
Routine laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and lipid profile were within normal limits.
A skin biopsy from the left elbow 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.6 cm was obtained. The specimen was bisected and processed in 1 cassette. Lesion revealed a dense, well-circumscribed dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of mast cells with round to oval nuclei and abundant granular cytoplasm. The overlying epidermis showed mild acanthosis and basal hyperpigmentation. The mast cells demonstrated metachromatic granules on toluidine blue staining and were positive for CD117 on immunohistochemistry, confirming the diagnosis of cutaneous Mastocytoma [Fig 2].
Given the patients age and underlying condition, the family preferred a conservative approach and declined surgery. Therefore, patient was managed with topical tacrolimus 0.03% and close observation.

A 54-year-old male was admitted to the hospital due to chest pain persisting for over 13 hours. The patient experienced sudden, unexplained epigastric colicky pain approximately 13 hours prior to admission. The pain was persistent, progressive, and associated with chest tightness, radiation to the left shoulder and left maxillary area, cold sweats, and palpitations. He subsequently presented to our emergency department. Arrival at ER and performed ECG, ECG results indicated: 1. Sinus rhythm, 2. ST-segment depression in leads aVL and V4-V6, 3. T-wave inversion. Troponin T(Point-of-Care Testing) measured was <0.010 μg/L. Hs-cTnI was elevated at 144 ng/L. Based on assessment of Cardiology, a diagnosis of acute NSTEMI was considered.
