A female infant was delivered weighing 2,600g (35th percentile) with Apgar scores of 9, 10, and 10 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes respectively, requiring no resuscitation.
Gross examination of the placenta confirmed the diagnosis of bipartite placenta with velamentous cord insertion (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6). The fetal surface demonstrated the characteristic branching pattern of chorionic vessels, while examination of the cord insertion site revealed the velamentous configuration with vessels traversing the membranes before reaching the placental tissue. The maternal surface showed 2 distinct placental lobes. Both mother and infant had an uncomplicated postoperative course Fig. 4, Fig. 5.

A 29-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive headaches and multiple generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
During the first months, seizures were managed symptomatically in a primary care setting, where they were initially considered idiopathic epilepsy due to the absence of focal neurological deficits. Neuroimaging was performed once neurological symptoms progressed and visual disturbances appeared, prompting referral for specialized neurological assessment.
Neurological examination revealed papilledema, decreased visual acuity, and signs of intracranial hypertension, which prompted urgent brain computed tomography (CT) scan, which demonstrated a left frontoparietal space-occupying lesion, partially calcified and appearing extra-axial, associated with significant mass effect and surrounding vasogenic edema.
However, subsequent Magnetic resonance imaging MRI analysis demonstrated predominantly intra-axial characteristics left frontal lesion involving both cortical and subcortical regions measuring 57 × 70 mm with an anteroposterior extent of 76 mm. The lesion demonstrated mild hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences and marked diffusion restriction within the solid tumor component with low ADC values compared with normal white matter, reflecting high tumor cellularity. Heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement was observed with areas of necrosis and calcifications. Marked peritumoral edema caused compression of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, midline shift, and early signs of subfalcine herniation. The tumor infiltrated the midline with partial extension into the contralateral frontal lobe while sparing the skull base inferiorly and demonstrating associated meningeal involvement laterally without evidence of calvarial bone destruction (Fig. 1). Overall, the lesion can be summarized radiologically as a large predominantly intra-axial frontal mass with heterogeneous signal intensity, marked diffusion restriction, necrotic components, heterogeneous contrast enhancement, extensive vasogenic edema, and significant mass effect with midline crossing.
A staging cervico-thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT scan showed no evidence of extracranial lesions. The patient declined surgical resection; therefore, a stereotactic biopsy was performed.
Histopathological examination revealed a poorly differentiated small round cell tumor composed of densely packed malignant cells. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong membranous expression of CD99 and negative staining for GFAP, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, desmin, S100, and CD45. The Ki-67 proliferative index was approximately 50%. These findings supported the diagnosis of an intracranial Ewing-like sarcoma.
The multidisciplinary tumor board recommended radiotherapy targeting the cerebral lesion followed by systemic chemotherapy using the VDC/IE protocol.
The patient subsequently underwent radiotherapy. The gross tumor volume (GTV) was defined based on the planning CT scan fused with brain MRI. A 1-cm margin was added to generate the clinical target volume (CTV), followed by an additional 3-mm margin to obtain the planning target volume (PTV). A total dose of 58 Gy in 29 fractions was delivered while respecting organs at risk, particularly the brainstem (Fig. 2).
A follow-up cervico-thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT scan was performed after radiotherapy to reassess systemic staging and exclude interval metastatic spread, given the aggressive nature of the tumor and the high metastatic potential of Ewing sarcoma family tumors and demonstrated a slight reduction in tumor size to 48 × 69 × 65 mm compared with the initial 57 × 70 × 76 mm, consistent with a partial tumor response and without evidence of metastatic disease (Fig. 3).
Systemic chemotherapy using the VDC/IE regimen (vincristine, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide and etoposide) was subsequently initiated. After six cycles, follow-up brain MRI showed further tumor reduction to 42 × 62 × 59 mm with decreased perilesional edema, consistent with a partial response (Fig. 4). The patient is currently continuing treatment.
Regarding visual outcome, no visual improvement was observed during follow-up. The patient remained limited to light and shadow perception, consistent with persistent severe visual impairment.
In a retrospective study including 240 children with brain tumors, it is reported that severe irreversible visual loss occurred in approximately 5% of patients and was most often related to optic nerve compression or papilledema secondary to increased intracranial pressure. Importantly, many patients already had significant visual impairment at the time of diagnosis, emphasizing the importance of early detection and treatment to prevent permanent optic nerve damage.
Similarly, a cohort of 18 patients in whom visual disturbances were the primary manifestation of intracranial tumors, including visual loss, visual field defects, and transient visual obscurations. In that series, the mean delay between the onset of visual symptoms and tumor diagnosis was nearly ten months, illustrating how visual complaints may represent the first clinical manifestation of intracranial neoplasms and should prompt early neuroimaging evaluation.
In our patient, rapidly progressive visual loss leading to bilateral blindness was one of the major presenting symptoms.
In our case, imaging did not demonstrate direct optic nerve compression. Visual loss was therefore most likely related to severe intracranial hypertension and papilledema secondary to the large tumor and associated mass effect. Despite tumor response to treatment, no visual recovery occurred, and the patient remained limited to light and shadow perception, highlighting the risk of irreversible optic pathway damage when diagnosis is delayed.
In the present case, imaging demonstrated a large aggressive predominantly intra-axial frontal mass with heterogeneous enhancement, necrotic components, and extensive vasogenic edema producing marked mass effect and midline shift. The tumor also showed meningeal involvement without evidence of calvarial bone destruction.
Historically, intracranial Ewing sarcoma has most commonly been described as an extra-axial or dural-based lesion mimicking meningioma. However, more recent reports increasingly recognize true intra-axial intraparenchymal presentations that may closely resemble high-grade gliomas. Our case fits within this less common intra-axial phenotype and additionally demonstrates midline crossing, an imaging feature that remains particularly unusual.
Calvarial involvement in intracranial Ewing sarcoma appears to be variable. While some cases demonstrate skull destruction with extracranial extension, others—such as the present case—show aggressive intracranial disease without bone erosion. This observation is clinically important, as the absence of bone involvement should not exclude the diagnosis.
Because of its nonspecific radiologic appearance, intracranial Ewing sarcoma is frequently misdiagnosed. The principal differential diagnoses include high-grade glioma, primary CNS lymphoma, aggressive meningioma, metastasis and intracranial small round cell tumors. Features such as marked diffusion restriction reflecting high cellularity, heterogeneous enhancement, necrosis, and extensive edema contribute to this diagnostic overlap. Consequently, imaging alone remains insufficient for definitive diagnosis, and histopathological confirmation is essential.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy, although not available in the present case, may provide additional metabolic information. Small round cell tumors typically demonstrate elevated choline levels, reduced N-acetylaspartate, and occasional lipid peaks reflecting high cellular turnover and necrosis.
A limitation of this report is that whole-spine MRI was not performed. Although staging CT showed no extracranial disease, subclinical cerebrospinal fluid dissemination cannot be completely excluded.
Historically, the vincristine–actinomycin D–cyclophosphamide (VAC) regimen was considered the standard chemotherapy backbone for Ewing sarcoma for several decades. Early cooperative studies, including the Intergroup Ewing's Sarcoma Study, demonstrated that multi-agent chemotherapy combined with local treatment significantly improved outcomes. In particular, a previous study reported that local tumor control in Ewing sarcoma was influenced by radiation dose, treatment volume, and primary tumor site, highlighting the importance of optimized radiotherapy planning in local disease control.
Treatment strategies evolved after the landmark randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine by Grier et al., which demonstrated that the addition of ifosfamide and etoposide to standard chemotherapy significantly improved outcomes in patients with localized Ewing sarcoma. In that study involving 518 patients, the intensified regimen achieved a 5-year event-free survival of 69% compared with 54% with standard therapy.
More recently, the EE2012 phase III trial conducted by Brennan et al. compared two chemotherapy schedules in newly diagnosed Ewing sarcoma. The study showed that the interval-compressed VDC/IE regimen administered every two weeks significantly improved event-free survival compared with the European VIDE regimen. These results support VDC/IE as the preferred induction chemotherapy regimen for Ewing sarcoma.
Ewing-like sarcomas represent a heterogeneous group of undifferentiated round cell sarcomas that share morphological similarities with Ewing sarcoma but harbor distinct molecular alterations, including CIC or BCOR rearrangements. Due to their rarity and the lack of prospective clinical trials, management generally follows therapeutic strategies used for classical Ewing sarcoma and relies on a multimodal approach combining systemic chemotherapy with surgery and/or radiotherapy.
This case also highlights that non-surgical management may achieve meaningful tumor control in selected patients, particularly when surgical resection is not feasible or declined. Our patient achieved a sustained partial response with radiotherapy followed by VDC/IE chemotherapy, supporting the role of multimodal therapy even in the absence of surgery.
Intracranial involvement in Ewing sarcoma is extremely rare. In the retrospective international study, patients with primary intracranial Ewing sarcoma treated with multimodal therapy demonstrated a 3-year overall survival of approximately 70%. In contrast, patients with intracranial metastatic disease had significantly poorer outcomes, reflecting the aggressive nature of disseminated disease.
Another important prognostic factor is the histopathologic response to induction chemotherapy. In a landmark study, it was demonstrated that patients achieving ≥90% tumor necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy had significantly improved survival compared with poor responders. These findings highlight the critical role of systemic therapy and treatment response in determining long-term outcomes in patients with Ewing sarcoma.

A 67-year-old woman with a history of chronic neck pain and right shoulder pain presented with a 15-year history of a progressively enlarging mass over the left occipital region. She reported coexisting cervical spinal stenosis and had previously undergone anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) from C3 to C7 in 2003, which preceded the development of the occipital lesion. The patient first noticed the occipital mass several years after her cervical spine surgery, and no prior imaging or evaluation of the lesion had been performed at the time of the ACDF. The patient had been aware of the occipital mass for 15 years but had declined surgical intervention due to concerns about paralysis related to her cervical stenosis. She described a sensation of pressure over the left side of her face and head. Physical examination revealed an approximately 7-cm, firm, nontender, immobile mass over the left occipital region. There were no overlying skin changes, erythema, or warmth. The mass limited leftward head rotation more than right. Neurologic examination was normal, with intact cranial nerves, full (5/5) strength in all extremities, normal sensation, and no focal deficits (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
Computed tomography (CT) images redemonstrate a large protuberant lesion abutting/arising from the left occipital bone, with multiple dense calcified foci, measuring up to 7 cm. There is no associated destructive change of the occipital bone or cervical spine. On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), the lesion is markedly hypointense on both T1 and T2 weighted images. Imaging also demonstrates postsurgical changes consistent with prior ACDF from C3 to C7 without hardware complication, as well as adjacent segment degenerative disc disease at C6-C7 without evidence of instability.
Based on imaging characteristics, the leading consideration was a benign fibro-osseous lesion. The differential diagnosis included ossifying fibroma, osteoma, and low-grade surface osteosarcoma. The absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, or soft tissue invasion favored a benign etiology. Additionally, the marked hypointensity on both T1- and T2-weighted MRI sequences supported a densely mineralized lesion. Given these features, a protuberant fibro-osseous lesion was favored preoperatively.
Given the patient’s history of ACDF and residual cervical stenosis, the patient had previously been advised that resection of the occipital lesion may carry risk of complications, which contributed to her reluctance to pursue surgery with progressive enlargement of the mass over 15 years. Upon further evaluation, a neurosurgeon determined that surgical resection could be performed safely without significant risk of neurologic compromise. This assessment was corroborated by a second neurosurgical opinion. After thorough discussion of the risks, including the potential need for drilling of the outer table of the skull to achieve complete resection, the patient elected to proceed with surgery.
Intraoperatively, the lesion was found to be adherent to the skull, necessitating a partial craniectomy. Gross total resection was achieved without any complications.
Microscopic examination of hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)–stained sections demonstrated distinct rounded to geographic, somewhat bosselated nodules composed of chondro-osseous matrix with zones of well-formed lamellar bone. These nodules were embedded within a dense, paucicellular fibrous stroma containing thin, curvilinear vascular channels. Foci of direct continuity were identified between the osseous components and the surrounding fibrous stroma. Notably, there was no robust osteoblastic rimming. Cytologic atypia and mitotic activity were absent.
Immunohistochemical analysis showed CD117 positivity highlighting scattered mast cells. Beta-catenin staining revealed no diagnostically abnormal nuclear accumulation. The Ki-67 proliferative index was low to absent within stromal nuclei, supporting a benign process.
Overall, histologic findings were concordant with a benign fibro-osseous lesion known as a protuberant fibro-osseous lesion. Given the bland cytologic features and lack of progression over many years, low-grade parosteal osteosarcoma was considered unlikely. Nonetheless, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) testing for MDM2 amplification was ordered to definitively exclude this possibility, and it confirmed the absence of parosteal osteosarcoma.

An 11-year-old girl was referred to our Department of Otorhinolaryngology for evaluation of a progressive left-sided facial swelling associated with orbital involvement evolving over the previous 7 days (Fig. 1). The swelling initially appeared in the left jugal region and progressively increased in size, accompanied by left-sided orbital proptosis. There was a recent history of an upper respiratory tract infection. There was no history of insect bite, facial trauma, or recent dental extraction, nor any underlying systemic disease such as diabetes mellitus.
The patient had initially been evaluated by a general practitioner, where a diagnosis of orbital cellulitis was suspected. She received empirical treatment with intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid at a dose of 80 mg/kg/day for 5 days. However, due to persistence of symptoms without significant clinical improvement, the patient was referred to our tertiary care center for further evaluation.
On admission, the patient was conscious, afebrile, and hemodynamically stable. Otorhinolaryngological examination revealed a left jugal swelling with overlying erythema, warmth, and tenderness on palpation. The lesion had a soft consistency and poorly defined margins. Examination of the oral cavity was unremarkable. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated inflammatory changes of the nasal mucosa associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy, while the middle and inferior meatuses remained patent. Cervical examination did not reveal palpable lymphadenopathy.
Ophthalmologic examination showed unilateral left-sided proptosis associated with conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis. Ocular motility was restricted in the affected eye. Best-corrected visual acuity was reduced to 7/10 on the left side. Fundoscopic examination revealed vascular tortuosity of the retinal vessels without signs of papilledema. Examination of the contralateral eye was normal. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
Laboratory investigations revealed mild leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 11 × 10³/mm³ (reference range: 3.0-10.0 × 10³/mm³), a hemoglobin level of 15.7 g/dL, and a platelet count of 279 × 10³/mm³. The C-reactive protein level was elevated at 41 mg/L (Normal: 7 mg/L).
An emergency contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head and neck demonstrated marked infiltration of the left jugal soft tissues extending toward the orbital apex and intraconal fat, associated with reactive laterocervical lymphadenopathy, the largest measuring 22 mm in short-axis diameter, with no evidence of abscess formation, suggesting either orbital cellulitis or an inflammatory pseudotumor (Fig. 2).
For further characterization of the orbital lesion, orbital MRI was subsequently performed. MRI revealed a multiloculated lesion consistent with a vascular malformation with predominant lymphatic components. The lesion demonstrated hyperintense signal on T1-weighted sequences, suggestive of intralesional hemorrhagic changes, and marked hyperintensity on T2-weighted sequences. Multiple thin internal septations were identified, showing enhancement after contrast administration. The lesion measured approximately 32 × 56 mm with a craniocaudal extension of about 30 mm. It involved both the intraconal and extraconal compartments, with encasement of the optic nerve and extension toward the intracavernous segment of the internal carotid artery, resulting in grade III proptosis (Fig. 3).
Following multidisciplinary discussion, the diagnosis of orbital lymphangioma was established. The patient continued treatment with intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid (80 mg/kg/day) for 7 days until normalization of inflammatory markers.
Definitive management of the lymphatic malformation consisted of bleomycin-based sclerotherapy. A total of 3 treatment sessions were administered at 1-month intervals. The procedure was well tolerated, with no reported complications or adverse effects.
The patient underwent regular monthly follow-up with comprehensive otorhinolaryngological and ophthalmological examinations. Following the third sclerotherapy session, a significant reduction in proptosis and conjunctival chemosis was observed. Follow-up evaluation included ophthalmologic examination, fundoscopic assessment, complete ENT examination, and orbital MRI.
Progressive clinical improvement was observed during follow-up. Complete resolution of pain, proptosis, and conjunctival chemosis was achieved 5 months after the final sclerotherapy session. At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic, with no evidence of recurrence (Fig. 4).

This study investigated a 74-year-old man who presented to our department a few days after sustaining a minor head injury. The patient underwent computed tomography (CT) scan as part of routine evaluation after minor head trauma, despite the absence of neurological symptoms. A CT scan performed as part of the acute evaluation revealed an incidental dural-based extra-axial mass in the right middle cranial fossa (Fig. 1A). A subsequent contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a 3-cm, well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing lesion consistent with a meningioma (Figs.1B–D). The mass showed iso-intensity on T1-weighted imaging, faint high intensity on T2-weighted imaging, and strong homogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted imaging. Notably, a significant T2-hyperintense peritumoral edema involving the adjacent right temporal lobe was observed. Despite extensive edema, the patient showed no neurological symptoms, including seizures, aphasia, or cognitive decline, and the findings of his physical and neurocognitive examinations were entirely normal. Although venous outflow disturbance has been reported as an important contributor to PTBE, definitive evidence of tumor-related venous compression was not demonstrated in this case. The observed focal narrowing was located away from the tumor, and therefore its contribution remains uncertain. Although focal narrowing was observed, it was not located adjacent to the tumor but rather in a more distal convexity segment.
Since the tumor had been discovered incidentally during his head injury workup and the patient remained entirely asymptomatic, an active surveillance strategy was initiated. An MRI follow-up was performed every 6-12 months over the next 3 years. Importantly, the patient was not administered corticosteroids or any other anti-edema therapy during this period.
Throughout the 3-year observation period, the patient remained neurologically stable and asymptomatic. The serial MRI scans indicated minimal changes in tumor size but showed a gradual, significant reduction in peritumoral edema, which had markedly regressed by the third year, with only a trace residual hyperintensity remaining (Figs. 2A–D). A small cystic lesion with a punctate isointense focus was observed within the edematous region (Fig. 3A–D), the significance of which remains unclear but may represent a focal fluid collection or degenerative change. As the edema resolved, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cleft sign (initially obscured) became more clearly visible around the tumor margin, although the definitive assessment of widening was limited by slice variability. Moreover, the lesion itself remained approximately 3 cm in diameter, with no new enhancement or evidence of hemorrhage or necrosis. Serial measurements confirmed that the tumor size remained stable throughout the follow-up period. This spontaneous resolution of PTBE, occurring without any therapeutic intervention during the 3-year follow-up period, was considered the defining radiologic feature of this case.

A 59-year-old female presented to our orthopedic clinic with chronic medial left ankle pain and progressive antalgic gait (lameness), occurring approximately 7 weeks (53 days) post-traumatic laceration to the medial aspect of her left ankle from broken glass during a household accident. The initial injury was managed at an urgent care facility with basic saline irrigation (volume unspecified) and primary closure using interrupted sutures, without the use of imaging, tetanus prophylaxis, or assessment for underlying tendinous, neurovascular, or osseous damage. Over the subsequent 4-6 weeks, her condition progressed insidiously, characterized by dynamic medial instability, impaired stair negotiation, and intolerance to standing for more than 10-15 minutes. Her past medical history was significant only for controlled essential hypertension and hypothyroidism.
Physical exam revealed 3-4 cm laceration scar along the medial ankle, posterior to the medial malleolus, without erythema, induration, or discharge. Palpation demonstrated focal tenderness over the tibialis posterior tendon sheath; the flexor digitorum longus sheath showed mild tenderness as well. The patient was unable to perform a single-leg heel rise on the left side, with compensatory subtalar eversion and mild flexible planovalgus foot alignment observed during weight-bearing stance. Active and passive range of motion at the ankle and subtalar joint eversion was preserved and symmetric bilaterally. Other neurovascular examination was normal in sensation. In vessels examination, Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis arteries puses were detectible with normal capilliary filling in toes. No signs of infection, wound dehiscence, or deep vein thrombosis were found.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left ankle revealed complete laceration of both the tibialis posterior tendon and the flexor digitorum longus tendon, with retraction of the tendon ends to proximal side. Soft-tissue edema was obvious as well, but no bony injury, fracture, or additional tendon damage was observed (Fig. 1).
Given the delayed presentation and functional deterioration, surgical exploration and repair were recommended. Intraoperatively, both tendons were found to be sharply transected, with moderate retraction, but with preserved tissue quality. Because the tendon ends were visible without extreme gap, primary end-to-end repair of both the tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus tendons was performed using nonabsorbable core sutures reinforced with epitendinous stitches (Fig. 2).
Postoperatively, the ankle was immobilized by short leg casting in plantarflexion and inversion positin for six weeks, with non-weight-bearing instructions. Left ankle physiotherapy, emphasizing restoration of ankle mobility with muscle strengthening was initiated for patient after six weeks. At the three-month follow-up visit, the patient demonstrated significant improvement, with remarkable reduction in medial ankle pain and gait normalization. Additionally, she was able to initiate a partial single-heel raise, indicating favorable tendon function recovery. It is worthy to note, no complications were observed.

A 41-year-old Moroccan woman with a history of intellectual disability and no known medical or surgical comorbidities was referred to our Department of Otorhinolaryngology for evaluation of persistent headaches evolving over a 7-month period. The headaches were predominantly right-sided and retro-orbital, with progressive worsening during the last 2 months prior to presentation. In addition, the patient reported right-sided hearing loss that had developed 3 months earlier.
She had been treated with step III analgesics for approximately 3 months without clinical improvement, prompting neurological evaluation during the seventh month of symptom progression, followed by referral to our otorhinolaryngology department for further assessment.
The patient denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or any previous history of tuberculosis. There were no known immunosuppressive conditions, and she was not receiving any long-term medications.
On general examination, the patient was conscious and clinically stable, with normal respiratory and hemodynamic parameters. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy demonstrated normal-appearing nasal mucosa without turbinate hypertrophy or choanal obstruction. A right-sided exophytic, non-bleeding mass arising from the lateral wall of the nasopharynx was identified, with no bleeding on contact (Fig. 1). Otoscopic examination revealed a normal external auditory canal and an intact tympanic membrane, associated with right-sided serous otitis media. No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy was detected.
Pure-tone audiometry demonstrated a right-sided conductive hearing loss, with an average air–bone gap corresponding to a mean hearing loss of 39 dB.
Laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 15.3 g/dL and an elevated white blood cell count of 12,700/mm³. Inflammatory markers were increased, with a C-reactive protein level of 29 mg/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h. Liver and renal function tests, serum electrolyte levels, coagulation parameters, and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c: 5.3%) were within normal limits. Serological testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative.
Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging was performed on a 1.5-T system. The imaging protocol included axial and coronal T1-weighted sequences (slice thickness: 4 mm), axial and coronal T2-weighted sequences, fat-suppressed T2-weighted images, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with b-values of 0 and 1000 s/mm², with corresponding apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, and post-contrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted sequences following intravenous administration of a gadolinium-based contrast agent (0.1 mmol/kg). The imaging field of view included the nasopharynx and the cervical region.
MRI demonstrated a large infiltrative mass involving the right posterolateral wall of the nasopharynx. The lesion exhibited irregular and poorly defined margins, was isointense on T1-weighted images and showed intermediate signal intensity on T2-weighted images, without evidence of central necrosis, with marked hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 1000 s/mm²), consistent with diffusion restriction. However, quantitative ADC values were not available in this case. The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement following gadolinium administration. The mass measured approximately 45 × 35 mm and extended into the right parapharyngeal fat and infratemporal fossa, with encasement of the right carotid–jugular vascular bundle. Although the lesion extended superiorly toward the skull base, no clival marrow signal abnormality, skull base foraminal involvement, perineural spread, or dural enhancement was identified, and there was no evidence of intracranial extension. No cervical or retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy was identified on imaging, and no necrotic lymph nodes were detected (Fig. 2). Chest radiography revealed no abnormalities.
A biopsy of the nasopharyngeal lesion was performed using a rigid 30-degree endoscope. Histopathological examination demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation composed of epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, associated with central caseous necrosis (Fig. 3). Nested TB-PCR testing was positive, confirming the diagnosis of nasopharyngeal tuberculosis.
The patient was started on standard antituberculous therapy consisting of a 2-month intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by a 4-month continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid (2RHZE/4RH). In parallel, a transtympanic ventilation tube (T-tube) was inserted in the right ear for management of the serous otitis media.
Treatment was well tolerated, with no reported adverse effects. Monthly follow-up included a comprehensive otorhinolaryngological examination with flexible nasopharyngoscopy, cervical assessment, chest radiography, and monitoring of liver function tests. A computed tomography scan performed at 5 months demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the nasopharyngeal mass (Fig. 4).
Clinical evolution was favorable. At 9 months of follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic, with no clinical or endoscopic evidence of disease recurrence.

A 4-months-old male child presented with a progressive right arm swelling noticed by his parents at 2 months of age. There was no fever, and the child was fully immunized with normal developmental milestones. General and systemic examinations was unremarkable. Local examination revealed a well-defined, firm, non-pulsatile mass measuring 4*3 cm along the long axis (Fig. 1).
The X-ray showed no bony abnormalities. Ultrasound demonstrated well circumscribed heterogenous soft tissue mass measuring 3,5*2,5 cm without Doppler hypervascularity (Fig. 2). MRI confirmed an oval extra-aponeurotic mass subcutaneous mass measures 5 cm * 3,5 cm with irregular contours, intense contrast enhancement, central necrotic, and close contact with deltoid and biceps aponeurosis - suggesting possible invasion - but separated from the humeral bone by the muscular and neurovascular structures (Fig. 3). So, a sarcomatous origin was suspected. All imaging examinations were performed within a short time frame, minimizing the likelihood of true lesion size variation, and this minor variations may be explained by differences in imaging techniques and acquisition planes.
A biopsy of the tumor revealed small round tumor cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, scant basophilic cytoplasm, focal melanin pigment within thickened trabeculae of a fibrous stroma. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for CK, synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD99 and THMB45; Negative for of PHOX2B (excluding neuroblastic tumor), melan A, CD45, desmin, myogenin, PLAP or S100. FISH ruled out Ewing sarcoma. The diagnosis was melanotic neuro ectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI).
The infant received neoadjuvant chemotherapy per SMOP-NBL1 protocol (2 cycles: CADO/CARBO - VP16), reducing tumor volume by 45% on follow-up local examination and MRI (Fig. 4). Surgical exploration revealed a mass adherent to brachialisand biceps brachii muscles, pectoralis major tendon, triceps muscle and musculocutaneous nerve, but sparing the radial nerve (Fig. 5). Complete resection included portions of involved muscles and adjacent periosteum, followed by pectoralis major reinsertion, tension-relieving incisions, and layered closure. 6-month follow-up showed complete wound healing, full range of motion and without recurrence.

A middle-aged man living in a riverine endemic region presented with chronic lower urinary tract symptoms, including dysuria, urinary frequency, and intermittent hematuria spanning several years. The patient reported repeated freshwater exposure since childhood. There was no history of previous urological surgery, known tuberculosis, or prior antiparasitic treatment.
Laboratory investigations revealed microscopic hematuria on urinalysis. Renal function was mildly impaired (serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL). Urine cytology was negative for malignant cells. Parasitological confirmation by urine filtration for Schistosoma haematobium ova was not available at presentation. Chest radiography was unremarkable, with no features to suggest pulmonary tuberculosis.
Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis was performed to evaluate the urinary tract. The examination demonstrated circumferential calcification of the bladder wall consistent with a porcelain bladder (Fig. 1). Calcifications of the seminal vesicles were also observed. Sagittal reconstructions revealed bilateral ureteral mural calcifications extending proximally (Figs. 2A and B). Associated right-sided ureteropyelocaliceal dilatation was present (Fig. 2A). No renal parenchymal calcifications, cortical scarring, or calyceal deformities were identified (Fig. 3).
The combination of extensive bladder wall calcification, ascending ureteral involvement, and preserved renal morphology suggested advanced chronic urogenital schistosomiasis.

A 69-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of intermittent severe headache (Visual Analogue Scale 7/10) and markedly elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein 189 mg/L). The patient had no co-morbidities and no medical treatment in her medical history. She reported neither visual disturbances nor jaw claudication. There were no focal neurological deficits and no signs of infection on physical examination. Initial noncontrast CT of the head and CT angiography of the head and neck revealed no significant findings. Subsequent brain MRI and ultrasound of the temporal arteries did not show signs of vasculitis. Analgesic therapy led to symptomatic improvement and consequently the patient was discharged.
Four days later, the patient returned with persistent systemic inflammation and ongoing clinical symptoms. To search for a potential infectious focus, PCCT (NAEOTOM Alpha, Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Germany) of the chest and abdomen in venous phase was performed. The scan protocol included intravenous administration of 80 mL of iodinated contrast material (Iopamidol 370 mg I/mL) followed by a saline chaser of 30 mL, both at an injection rate of 4.0 mL/s.
Thoracic imaging was acquired with a pitch of 3.2 and a gantry rotation time of 0.25 s at 120 kV and 35 effective mAs, resulting in a volume CT dose index (CTDIvol) of 2.8 mGy. Abdominal imaging was performed using a pitch of 0.8 at 140 kV and 30 effective mAs, with a CTDIvol of 3.44 mGy. The thoracic images were reconstructed as virtual monoenergetic images at 65 keV and were obtained in ultra-high-resolution (UHR) mode. The abdominal images were reconstructed as virtual monoenergetic images at 70 keV.
The examination incidentally demonstrated concentric wall thickening of the thoracic and abdominal aorta as well as the supra-aortic branches. Exploiting the intrinsic spectral capabilities of PCCT, iodine maps were retrospectively reconstructed (syngo.via, Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Germany). Iodine uptake of the aortic wall was measured by placing regions of interest (ROIs) within the thickened aortic wall while avoiding the vessel lumen. Measurements were performed along short vessel segments and averaged across multiple ROIs. Quantitative analysis revealed an increased iodine uptake within the aortic wall of up to 2.7 mg I/mL, favoring active vascular inflammation over noninflammatory atherosclerotic wall thickening (Fig. 1).
Subsequent contrast-enhanced MRI confirmed circumferential mural thickening and enhancement of the aorta and its major branches. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated corresponding increased tracer uptake, consistent with active aortitis. Repeat ultrasound of the temporal arteries revealed wall thickening of the parietal and frontal branches, supporting the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis.
Corticosteroid therapy was initiated immediately after CT-based suspicion of large-vessel vasculitis, 4 days after the initial presentation, starting with Prednisolone 50 mg/d. Despite initial treatment, inflammatory markers remained elevated, with CRP decreasing from 189 mg/L at presentation to 36 mg/L, prompting temporary dose escalation followed by gradual tapering. Approximately 6 weeks later, additional immunosuppressive therapy with Tocilizumab (162 mg/wk) was initiated, allowing further reduction of corticosteroid dosage (Fig. 2).
Over a follow-up period of 2 months, the patient showed complete clinical remission with normalization of inflammatory markers. At the most recent follow-up, corticosteroid dosage had been successfully reduced to 5 mg/d under Tocilizumab therapy, with no recurrence of symptoms. Follow-up imaging has not yet been performed but is planned as part of routine disease monitoring.

The patient was a 54-year-old right-handed woman with a medical history of transient ventricular tachycardia during pregnancy at the age of 40 years and a known nickel allergy. She had a 34-year smoking history of 10 cigarettes per day and no history of alcohol consumption. She was found collapsed at home and was transported to our hospital approximately 18 hours after the last known well time. Neurological examination revealed left-sided incomplete hemiparesis, dysarthria, motor aphasia, and sensory disturbances of the left upper and lower extremities, with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score of 20. Electrocardiography showed no abnormalities. Blood pressure was 128/68 mmHg, and heart rate was 74 beats per minute with a regular rhythm. Based on a height of 158 cm and body weight of 56.6 kg, her body mass index was 22.67 kg/m². Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 6,740/µL, hemoglobin level of 12.4 g/dL, platelet count of 323 × 10⁴/µL, C-reactive protein level of 0.09 mg/dL, brain natriuretic peptide level of 55.4 pg/mL, total cholesterol level of 225 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol level of 67 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level of 148 mg/dL, triglyceride level of 73 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c level of 5.9%, activated partial thromboplastin time of 26.3 seconds, prothrombin time–international normalized ratio of 0.97, and D-dimer level of 3.8 µg/mL. Noncontrast head CT showed no early ischemic changes (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score of 10), whereas a hyperdense sign was observed in the distal M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery (Fig. 1A). Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated occlusion of the distal M1 segment without evidence of an embolic source in the aortic arch or venous thrombosis within the scanned range; most of the pulmonary arteries were outside the field of view (Fig. 1B–D). Because approximately 18 hours had elapsed since the last known well time, intravenous thrombolysis was not performed, and mechanical thrombectomy was undertaken.
The procedure was initiated 54 minutes after hospital arrival. Cerebral angiography via a guiding catheter placed in the right internal carotid artery confirmed distal right M1 occlusion (Fig. 2A).
A macroscopically red thrombus was retrieved using a combined technique involving an aspiration catheter and a stent retriever (Fig. 2B), and successful recanalization (modified Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction grade 2c) was achieved 18 minutes after procedure initiation (Fig. 2C). Right common carotid angiography revealed no abnormalities suggestive of an embolic source in the cervical internal carotid artery (Fig. 2D). The patient’s neurological deficits improved rapidly after the procedure, and postprocedural head CT showed no intracranial hemorrhage.
On day 2, diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a new cerebral infarction in the right lenticular nucleus (Fig. 3A and B). Magnetic resonance angiography showed sustained patency of the right M1 segment without restenosis or reocclusion (Fig. 3C). At this stage, the embolic source remained undetermined; therefore, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 100 mg/day was initiated. A comprehensive evaluation for an embolic source was performed. Transthoracic echocardiography conducted by a cardiologist on day 2 showed no abnormalities, and lower-extremity venous ultrasonography revealed no thrombi in the bilateral femoral or popliteal veins. On day 3, repeat transthoracic echocardiography performed by a clinical laboratory technologist was also unremarkable, and venous ultrasonography demonstrated no thrombi from the inferior vena cava to the calf veins. The patient had no history of oral contraceptive use or hormone replacement therapy. Additional laboratory testing, including evaluations for coagulation disorders, thrombophilia, and autoimmune diseases, revealed no abnormalities. Continuous in-hospital cardiac monitoring and 24-hour Holter electrocardiography showed no arrhythmias.
Histopathological examination of the retrieved thrombus demonstrated a mixed thrombus predominantly composed of fibrin and platelets, with red blood cells accounting for approximately 40% of the thrombus volume (Fig. 3D and E). There was no evidence of endothelial cells, atherosclerotic plaque components, or infection.
On day 8, transesophageal echocardiography with a microbubble test demonstrated a grade 2 right-to-left shunt at rest, which increased to grade 4 during an adequate Valsalva maneuver (Fig. 4A). The patent foramen ovale had a tunnel length of 10.4 mm, an opening diameter of 2.1 mm, and a width of 13.4 mm, with demonstrable shunt flow on color Doppler imaging (Fig. 4B). The atrial septal excursion was 17 mm, consistent with an atrial septal aneurysm (Fig. 4C). No embolic sources were identified in the left atrial appendage, left atrium, or cardiac valves. On day 14, carotid MRI showed no high-intensity plaque on T1-weighted images in the right cervical internal carotid artery. On day 16, aortic MRI revealed no high-intensity plaques in the aortic arch on T1-weighted images; however, a high-intensity lesion suggestive of thrombus was observed in the right pulmonary artery (Fig. 5A and B). On the same day, contrast-enhanced CT of the trunk, including the lower extremities, demonstrated no evidence of deep vein thrombosis but revealed a contrast defect suggestive of thrombus in the right pulmonary artery (Fig. 5C and D). No findings suggestive of malignancy or infection were identified. Based on these findings, paradoxical cerebral embolism was considered highly probable. Aspirin was discontinued on day 17, and anticoagulation therapy with edoxaban 30 mg/day was initiated. The patient remained neurologically intact and was discharged home on day 23 with a modified Rankin Scale score of 0. Follow-up contrast-enhanced CT on day 37 confirmed complete resolution of the pulmonary artery thrombus, with no evidence of venous thrombosis (Fig. 5E). Because of her nickel allergy, percutaneous closure of the patent foramen ovale was not performed. Anticoagulation therapy has been continued, and no recurrent thromboembolic events have been observed during 6 months of follow-up.

A 39-year-old male presented with progressive left-sided lower limb pain for over 3 months. The pain radiated from the lower back to the anterior thigh and medial leg, corresponding predominantly to the L3–L4 dermatomal distribution. It was sharp, severe in intensity, aggravated by movement, and refractory to analgesics and physiotherapy.
There was no history of trauma, prior spinal surgery, fever, weight loss, or known hereditary skeletal disorders such as multiple hereditary exostoses. Family history was non-contributory.
On physical examination, there was localized tenderness over the lumbar spine. Neurological examination revealed reduced motor strength (4/5) in left hip flexion and knee extension, with diminished patellar reflex. Sensory examination showed decreased sensation in the L3–L4 dermatomes on the left side. No bowel or bladder dysfunction was noted.
Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine demonstrated a well-defined bony lesion arising from the inferior articular process of the L3 vertebra, projecting into the spinal canal. The lesion caused severe canal stenosis with compression of the cauda equina nerve roots and associated T2 hyperintensity suggestive of nerve root edema (Fig. 1A and 1B).
Subsequent computed tomography (CT) confirmed a pedunculated osseous lesion with cortical and medullary continuity with the parent vertebra, consistent with osteochondroma (Figure 2A and 2B), which is considered pathognomonic.
The patient underwent posterior decompression and complete surgical excision of the lesion. Intraoperatively, a bony mass compressing the Dural sac and nerve roots was identified and excised.
Histopathological examination confirmed osteochondroma, demonstrating a cartilage cap overlying mature trabecular bone.
Postoperatively, the patient experienced significant improvement in radicular pain and gradual recovery of motor function during follow-up.

A 5-year-old girl presented with several months of progressive bilateral proptosis and eyelid swelling. There was no history of trauma or systemic illness. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/32 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. Examination revealed bilateral eyelid erythema, chemosis, and 5 mm of proptosis on Hertel exophthalmometry, with moderate restriction of ocular motility in all gazes. Pupillary reactions were normal in both eyes, and fundus examinations were unremarkable.
Orbital computed tomography (CT) scan without contrast revealed bilateral infiltrative orbital soft tissue masses involving both lacrimal glands, with involvement of all extraocular muscles and their tendons, as well as enlargement of the left infraorbital nerve. The lesions demonstrated posterior extension toward the orbital apex with molding of the globes. No calcification or bone destruction was noted. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated bilateral homogeneously enhancing superolateral orbital lesions with irregular margins.
The patient underwent a left superolateral orbitotomy with tumor biopsy. Histopathologic analysis showed dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with cluster of differentiation 138 (CD138) positivity and approximately 25 IgG4-positive plasma cells per HPF, confirming IgG4-related disease. Serum IgG4 level was within normal limits. Systemic review and multidisciplinary evaluation revealed no evidence of extraorbital IgG4-related disease or other systemic involvement.
The patient received systemic corticosteroids and multiple immunosuppressive agents, including methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine, and mycophenolate mofetil, but her disease remained refractory. Due to progressive proptosis and exposure keratopathy in her left eye, lateral and medial tarsorrhaphy were performed for corneal protection. Rituximab therapy was then initiated, resulting in marked bilateral reduction of proptosis, chemosis, and eyelid swelling, with resolution of left eye exposure keratopathy within three months. The patient was followed for 1 year, with sustained clinical improvement and no evidence of recurrence (Fig. 1).
An 11-year-old girl presented with a one-month history of progressive right eye proptosis without pain or diplopia. There was no positive history of trauma or systemic disease. BCVA was 20/20 in both eyes. On examination, mild right upper eyelid ptosis and 2 mm of right-sided proptosis were noted on Hertel exophthalmometry. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was absent. There was no chemosis, eyelid swelling, or limitation of eye movements, and fundus examination was normal bilaterally.
Orbital CT scan without contrast showed bilateral lacrimal gland enlargement, more prominent on the right side, with associated involvement of the right superior rectus muscle, levator palpebrae superioris complex, and their tendons, together with a superior infiltrative orbital mass. There was no bone invasion or intraconal extension. The patient underwent right superior orbitotomy with lacrimal gland biopsy. Histopathology confirmed IgG4-related disease, with CD138 positivity and >25 IgG4-positive plasma cells per HPF. Serum IgG4 level was elevated at 156.24 mg/dL (reference range 6.2–112.7 mg/dL). Further systemic assessment and specialty consultations showed no signs of multisystem IgG4-related disease. She received systemic corticosteroids and azathioprine. At three months, the patient demonstrated significant improvement in right eye proptosis. At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable with no evidence of recurrence (Fig. 2).
A 16-year-old girl presented with proptosis and globe displacement in the left eye. She had no history of systemic disease or trauma. BCVA was 20/20 in both eyes. Examination revealed left eye proptosis with inferior displacement of the globe. Hertel exophthalmometry measured 5 mm of left-sided proptosis. Ocular motility of the left eye was restricted in abduction and adduction. Pupillary responses were normal, and fundus examinations were unremarkable bilaterally.
A prior incisional biopsy performed at another center had been reported as angiolymphoid hyperplasia, without immunohistochemical (IHC) staining. Orbital CT scan without contrast revealed a diffuse infiltrative mass in the superomedial compartment of the left orbit, extending around the globe and causing globe indentation, with involvement of the anterior optic nerve, superior rectus muscle, levator palpebrae superioris complex, medial rectus muscle, lateral rectus muscle, superior oblique muscle, and lacrimal gland.
The patient underwent deep left lateral orbitotomy with excisional biopsy. IHC staining supported the diagnosis of IgG4-related disease, showing CD138 positivity and >40% IgG4-positive plasma cells. Serum IgG4 level was within normal limits. Comprehensive systemic evaluation demonstrated no associated systemic manifestations of IgG4-related disease. She was treated with systemic corticosteroids and mycophenolate mofetil. The patient was followed for 1 year, with gradual regression of proptosis and no evidence of recurrence (Fig. 3).

A 56-year-old man with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, previously treated with systemic therapy (osimertinib), was referred to our department for right eye symptoms, including decreased vision and elevated IOP.
Upon initial examination, the best-corrected visual acuity was 0.3 in the right eye and 1.2 in the left eye. Although the right pupil was fixed and the view was limited by corneal edema, relative afferent pupillary defect was assessed by reverse testing (observing the left pupillary response) and was not detected. The right eye exhibited a markedly elevated IOP of 48 mmHg (vs. 15 mmHg in the left), fixed mydriasis, corneal edema, and anterior chamber inflammation with 2+ cells and 2+ flare, as well as multiple elevated white nodules on the iris surface (Fig. 1A). The fundus details were partially obscured in the right eye due to corneal edema, but there were no apparent signs of retinal or choroidal involvement in both eyes. The fixed dilated pupil in the right eye was thought to result from tumor infiltration or iris sphincter dysfunction.
IOP was initially managed with topical antiglaucoma medications (including a prostaglandin analog, beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, alpha-2 agonist, and Rho-kinase inhibitor) and oral acetazolamide. Five days after initial presentation, the patient underwent combined phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation and microhook trabeculotomy, resulting in transient IOP control (range, 6-10 mmHg). However, the IOP gradually increased to 50 mmHg despite maximal topical antiglaucoma therapy (five classes: a prostaglandin analog, beta-blocker, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, alpha-2 agonist, and Rho-kinase inhibitor) and oral acetazolamide, prompting three sessions of transscleral cyclophotocoagulation (TS-CPC). TS-CPC was performed in three sessions for recurrent IOP elevation at days 50, 104, and 144 after initial presentation. At each session, laser treatment was applied from 4 to 8 o'clock inferiorly and from 10 to 2 o'clock superiorly (total 8 clock hours), sparing the 3 and 9 o'clock meridians, at 2500 mW, with 80 s delivered to each arc (total 160 s per session). During follow-up, rubeosis iridis developed in the right eye; therefore, two intravitreal injections of aflibercept (2.0 mg each) were administered to treat iris neovascularization in the right eye. The second injection was given 35 days after the first because neovascularization persisted. The longitudinal IOP trend and timing of interventions are shown in Fig. 2.
Cytological analysis of the aqueous humor sample, obtained by anterior chamber paracentesis immediately before the second intravitreal aflibercept injection, revealed many cohesive clusters and isolated atypical glandular epithelial cells, characterized by marked nuclear pleomorphism, prominent nucleoli, and evidence of glandular differentiation (Class V) (Fig. 3). These cytomorphological features are notable indicators of metastatic adenocarcinoma. Considering the patient's clinical history of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and the absence of other clinically evident progressive visceral metastases at that time, the diagnosis of iris metastasis was established based on aqueous humor cytology alone. Following the cytologic findings, systemic restaging was performed, including contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen and brain magnetic resonance imaging, which demonstrated multiple bone metastases in the spine, sacrum, pelvis, bilateral humeri, bilateral femora, bilateral scapulae, and sternum. Notably, this case demonstrates that anterior chamber paracentesis can yield diagnostically sufficient cytological material even without an iris biopsy, offering a minimally invasive alternative in selected cases.
Subsequent management was focused on preserving vision and ocular comfort. As the iris tumors demonstrated slow progression and the patient's visual acuity and symptoms remained stable, enucleation was not required.
However, approximately 8 months after the initial visit, similar iris lesions with multiple white nodules developed on the surface of the temporal iris in the left eye (Fig. 1B). This finding was consistent with bilateral metastatic involvement of the iris. Ultimately, 9 months after the initial visit, despite ongoing therapy, the patient died from systemic progression of lung cancer.

A 32-year-old man presented with a slowly enlarging, protuberant mass on his left upper thigh/groin region. The lesion had been present for several months, causing mild irritation, especially during physical activity. The patient reported a history of a similar lesion in the same location, which excised 2 years prior, though no records or pathology report were available. Physical examination revealed a 3-cm firm, nodular mass with slight ulceration overlying the femoral vasculature. A preliminary clinical impression by the referring primary care physician suggested a keloid.
Excision was performed, and histopathological examination revealed a dermal-based, moderately cellular proliferation of bipolar and unipolar spindle and stellate cells with minimal nuclear atypia and scant eosinophilic cytoplasm. The stroma was predominantly myxoid, with prominent arborizing thin-walled vessels and scattered inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and eosinophils (Figure 1A-C). Small areas exhibited prominent storiform fascicles composed of uniform spindle cells with elongated thin nuclei, even chromatin, minimal cytoplasm, and indistinct cell borders, with transition to hypocellular myxoid areas containing multinucleated giant cells (Figure 1C). Adjacent areas demonstrated infiltration of subcutaneous adipose tissue in a honeycomb pattern, consistent with DFSP (Figure 1D). Additional areas showed multinucleated giant cells lining focal pseudovascular clefts within fibrous and myxoid stroma, supporting giant cell fibroblastoma features (Figure 1E). Rare mitotic figures were observed without evidence of necrosis, and no histologic features of fibrosarcomatous transformation were seen. Immunohistochemical staining showed diffuse positivity for CD34 (Figure 1F), while the tumor cells were negative for SMA, desmin, S100, SOX10, EMA, MUC4, and GLUT1 (SLC2A1). Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis revealed a PDGFB rearrangement (Figure 2), confirming the diagnosis of myxoid DFSP with giant cell fibroblastoma features.
Due to tumor involvement at inked specimen margins, the patient subsequently underwent a wide re-excision, achieving negative peripheral margins. However, the deep margin remained involved by the hypocellular component of the tumor, leading to sarcoma tumor board discussion. Imaging and an orthopedic oncology consultation were recommended to evaluate the possibility of a second re-resection. Given the low metastatic potential of DFSP, routine surveillance was advised. The patient remains under clinical surveillance, with no evidence of recurrence at 11 months following wide re-excision.

We present the case report of a 56-year-old male currently undergoing treatment for metastatic HNSCC, having recently completed radiotherapy treatment for recurrent lung metastases. At this time his disease status was considered stable and he was entering a program of disease surveillance.
Following complaints of slowly worsening persistent right hip and mid-thigh pain, a radiograph was initially obtained. The patient had previously undergone an uncomplicated right total hip arthroplasty. The femur radiograph [Fig. 1A, B] demonstrates an intramedullary lesion in the distal femoral shaft measuring 92 mm craniocaudal with characteristics of a typical chondroid lesion with an additional aggressive lytic component posteriorly with deep endosteal scalloping, periosteal reaction and focal cortical breach. A working diagnosis of dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma arising from the underlying enchondroma was suspected.
Further investigation with unenhanced CT [Fig. 2A–C] better characterised the chondroid matrix mineralisation typical of a benign intramedullary enchondroma, whereas the localised destructive lytic component eroding the cortex with focal full-thickness breach and periosteal reaction supported the concerns for in situ malignant transformation of the underlying enchondroma. Given the concurrent metastatic head and neck malignancy, a nuclear medicine bone scan SPECT was ordered for both complimentary assessment and exclusion of additional lesions or metastatic bone disease. Only the solitary femoral lesion demonstrated abnormal tracer uptake [Fig. 2D].
MRI showed the biphasic imaging characteristics and enhancement pattern of the mass [Fig. 3] with the low-signal chondroid mineralisation was visualised in the larger cartilage lesion with mild peripheral enhancement. The aggressive posterior component demonstrates a homogeneous solid T1 intermediate signal with uniform enhancement, endosteal erosion and irregular circumferential enhancing periosteal oedema, corresponding to the solid lytic destructive component on CT [Fig. 3D-–F].
Multimodality imaging characteristics and biphasic morphology were altogether supportive of the working diagnosis of dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma arising from an underlying enchondroma. Following discussion at the State Sarcoma Service Multidisciplinary Meeting, the consensus decision was for en bloc oncological resection of the mass with surgical reconstruction of the distal femur with hinged arthroplastic endoprosthesis.
En bloc surgical resection identified the malignant squamous cell carcinoma tumour-to-tumour metastasis to the benign intramedullary enchondroma. On cut section [Fig. 4], there was the larger pale glistening appearance of the benign cartilage lesion (*) with the smaller peripheral solid areas of expanding creamy/pale yellow tissue (arrows) associated with the endosteal erosion and cortical thinning indicating the areas of metastatic SCC.
Radiopathological correlation demonstrating the different components of the mass across multiple different modalities [Figs. 1, 2, 3, and 4].
Macroscopic appearances were substantiated on microscopy H&E assessment [Fig. 5] with multiple nodules of hyaline cartilage were seen abutting host bone, surrounded by a halo of reactive new bone (benign bone encasement growth pattern). There was no destructive or permeative growth with lack of trabecular entrapment by the enchondroma. Within the chondroid matrix was a mildly cellular population of bland chondrocytes in lacunar spaces, without significant myxoid change, atypia or mitotic activity [Fig. 5B]. Juxtaposed were irregular islands of keratin-forming and mitotically active pleomorphic squamous cells representing metastatic SCC [Fig. 5A]. There was also an area of infiltration along the endosteal interface with focal partial thickness erosion through the cortex by the SCC [Fig. 5C].

A 55-year-old woman presented with clinical features of bowel obstruction which were demonstrated on cross-sectional imaging along with multiple hepatic metastases (Figure 1A, B). She had a history of endometriosis, for which she underwent exploratory laparotomy more than 30 years earlier and a right salpingo-oophorectomy 15 years earlier. She presented at a community hospital with complaints of pain and rectal bleeding. She underwent a colonoscopy with terminal ileal biopsy. One week later, she was hospitalized due to a small bowel obstruction and underwent a right hemicolectomy and liver biopsy. Pathologic examination revealed stage IV adenocarcinoma involving the colon and small bowel with metastases to the liver and 7 of 22 lymph nodes.
The tumor cells were interpreted as positive for epithelial markers, keratin 7, PAX8, and TTF-1 (NKX2-1), focally positive for thyroglobulin, and negative for keratin 20, CDX2, podoplanin (D2-40), GATA3, and WT1. Molecular analysis demonstrated a microsatellite stable (MSS) tumor with a low tumor mutational burden (TMB: 6.3 mut/Mb) and multiple genetic alterations, including KRAS p.G12V (activating) and ATM p.S1092 mutations. No alterations were detected in BRAF, MET, or RET genes. Tumor tissue was also submitted for CancerTYPE ID molecular analysis (Biotheranostics), which revealed a 90% probability of renal cell carcinoma, though thyroid and endometrial origins could not be excluded (reported as 6% and <5% probability, respectively). The patient was started on carboplatin and paclitaxel chemotherapy for carcinoma of unknown primary.
The patient was referred to a cancer center for further evaluation where a diagnosis of carcinoma involving small bowel, appendix, lymph nodes, and adipose tissue, most compatible with metastatic thyroid primary, was rendered. However, extensive workup including various imaging studies failed to identify a definitive primary site. Neck ultrasound revealed a normal thyroid gland without nodules or lymphadenopathy. Transvaginal ultrasound showed no adnexal or uterine masses, although adenomyosis was noted.
The patient sought a second opinion at our institution. Review of the right hemicolectomy and liver biopsy slides revealed tumor transmurally infiltrating the colonic and small intestinal walls with involvement of the appendix. Seven lymph nodes contained metastatic deposits, and a concurrent liver biopsy was positive for metastatic carcinoma. Small foci of endometriosis, highlighted by ER and PR, were identified within the appendix and colonic peritoneum.
The tumor cells were arranged in a variety of architectural patterns, including papillary, cribriform, glandular, ductal, glomeruloid, and retiform. Scattered psammomatous calcifications were present. The tumor cells were cuboidal to low columnar, with mild to moderate nuclear atypia, and vesicular chromatin (Figure 2A-F). Mitotic figures were increased. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were diffusely positive for keratin AE1/AE3, EPCAM, keratin 7, PAX8, and TTF-1; patchy positive for CD10 (luminal) and p16 (INK4a/CDKN2A); focally positive for GATA3 and very focally for thyroglobulin; and negative for keratin 20, CDX2, WT1, D2-40, and BRAF (Figure 3A-F). p53 demonstrated a wild-type expression pattern. ER and PR were essentially negative (focal weak ER staining was observed in <5% of cells).
Based on the combination of the morphological features, immunophenotype, molecular profile, and the presence of endometriosis, a final diagnosis of endometriosis-associated MLA was rendered.

A 15-year-old male patient presented to the hospital with complaints of swelling in the eyelids, hands, and feet, as well as pain in the ankle. His medical history revealed a sore throat lasting a few days approximately 15 days prior to admission, followed by the onset of swelling in the hands, feet, and eyelids over the past four days. On physical examination at presentation, his general condition was good, he was conscious, his blood pressure was 135/75 mmHg, his body temperature was 36.9 °C, his pulse rate was 110/min, and his respiratory rate was 24/min. Two or more pitting edema and bifissure edema were detected in the pretibial region. Breath sounds were normal, and there were no abdominal ascites or scrotal edema. Cardiac examination revealed a pansystolic murmur to the apical 3/6 left axilla and a diastolic murmur in the left third intercostal space.
Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin of 12.7 g/dL, leukocyte count of 8,440/mm3, platelet count of 251,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 42 mm/hour, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 1.9 mg/dL, and ASO level of 555 IU/mL. Kidney function tests showed BUN of 42 mg/dL, creatinine of 1.04 mg/dL, total protein of 5.7 g/dL, albumin of 3.6 g/dL, pro-BNP of 2216 pg/mL, and a decreased serum C3 level (0.14 g/L). Urinalysis revealed + 4 proteinuria, + 3 hematuria, and microscopic examination of the urine identified 468 dysmorphic erythrocytes per field. Urine, throat and blood cultures were obtained and all were negative. Anti-DNA, antinuclear antibodies, anti neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), double-stranded DNA antibody, anti-glomerular basement membrane and rheumatoid factor were negative. The patient was hospitalized with a preliminary diagnosis of nephritic syndrome, and furosemide therapy was initiated. Electrocardiography showed a PR interval of 0.20 s, and chest radiography revealed cardiomegaly and bilateral pleural effusion. Echocardiography revealed moderate aortic regurgitation, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, mild mitral regurgitation, and moderate to severe acute rheumatic carditis (Fig. 1). The patient was diagnosed with both APSGN and (ARF, and treatment was initiated with benzathine penicillin (1,200,000 U, IM) and prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day, oral) for a duration of eight weeks. By the third day of hospitalization, a decrease in pro-BNP levels was observed, and by the seventh day, the pro-BNP value had returned to the normal range. However, since the patient's arterial blood pressure remained elevated, antihypertensive therapy with amlodipine was initiated. On the 9th day of hospitalization, laboratory evaluation showed a rising trend in C3 levels. Concurrently, regression of pretibial edema was observed, leading to a reduction in the furosemide dose to 0.5 mg/kg. On the 15th day of hospitalization, the patient had no edema, and the serum C3 level was measured at 0.71 g/L. He was discharged with ongoing treatment including prednisolone, amlodipine, and furosemide.
At the first follow-up, regression of edema was observed, microscopic hematuria persisted, but proteinuria was not detected. The serum C3 level was found to have reached the normal range (1.03 g/L). Based on these findings, a gradual tapering of the prednisolone dose was planned. Echocardiography revealed significant improvement in cardiac findings, yet mild valvular regurgitation persisted. At the first month follow-up, no pathological findings were noted other than mild aortic regurgitation. Prednisolone treatment was terminated after a total of 8 weeks. The patient continued amlodipine and furosemide therapy along with benzathine penicillin prophylaxis administered every 21 days. At the three month follow-up, the patient's arterial blood pressure values remained stable, and amlodipine and furosemide treatments were discontinued. Microscopic hematuria and mild aortic regurgitation on echocardiography persisted.
At the six month follow-up, physical examination findings and all biochemical parameters, including complete urinalysis, were normal (Fig. 2), and mild aortic regurgitation persisted in echocardiography. Informed consent was obtained from the patient's parents.

A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, whose only medications were lisinopril for many years and tirzepatide for 1 year, developed a diffuse pruritic eruption with erythematous, scaly papules on the trunk and extremities (Fig 1). The first biopsy favored an eczematous process with follicular involvement, and topical triamcinolone was started. One month later, the eruption worsened; a second biopsy demonstrated superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered dermal eosinophils. The patient continued topical triamcinolone for 6 weeks without improvement and was referred to a tertiary dermatology center for further evaluation.
A third biopsy demonstrated similar findings, prompting initiation of oral doxycycline for 1 month to target a possible follicular component, along with alternating topical triamcinolone and tacrolimus. When no improvement was observed, a 4-week prednisone taper was added; however, the eruption persisted. Given that lymphomatoid papulosis was also considered based on the clinical morphology (despite the absence of epidermotropism on histopathology), methotrexate was trialed for 6 weeks without benefit. A fourth and final biopsy revealed eosinophil-rich spongiotic dermatitis. At that time, direct immunofluorescence was performed as the differential diagnosis had broadened to include urticarial-phase bullous pemphigoid. The direct immunofluorescence study was negative, making bullous pemphigoid less likely. No vesicles or bullae developed during the clinical course.
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, metabolic panel, and liver function tests, remained within normal limits throughout the course, and no peripheral eosinophilia was observed. Given the severity and persistence of disease, as well as the eosinophil-rich spongiotic dermatitis seen on histopathology and the eczematous clinical morphology, dupilumab was initiated. However, 3 weeks after starting dupilumab, the patient noticed a flare of the eruption following his routine tirzepatide injection, and based on the temporal correlation between drug administration and symptom exacerbation, tirzepatide was discontinued.
Following cessation of tirzepatide, the patient experienced complete resolution of the morbilliform eruption with a brief 1-week prednisone taper and continuation of topical triamcinolone. The dramatic improvement upon drug withdrawal, combined with the temporal relationship and characteristic histopathological findings, suggested a tirzepatide-induced morbilliform drug eruption. The eosinophil-rich infiltrate observed in our patient's final biopsy (Fig 2) is consistent with a type IVb hypersensitivity mechanism, supporting the diagnosis of a drug-induced morbilliform eruption.

A 24-year-old male arrived at the outpatient clinic with symptoms of diffuse brown hyperpigmentation, notable scalp hair thinning, and discoloration along with fragile fingernails and toenails. The hyperpigmentation was first observed at birth, initially confined to the trunk, but progressively spread over the next 3 years to include the proximal limbs, palms, soles, head, neck, and tongue within that period. The thinning of the scalp hair and nail issues began with the onset of puberty. Along with the skin and nail changes, he also exhibited a lack of dermatoglyphics, excessive sweating, and an intolerance to heat. The patient reported no prior injuries to the fingers or exposure to chemicals.
During the clinical examination, the patient displayed widespread reticulate hyperpigmentation on the trunk, face, neck, upper limbs, palms and soles (Fig 1). The areolae also showed increased pigmentation (Fig 2). Examination of the scalp showed diffuse, nonscarring hair loss in the frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital areas (Fig 3). The hair-pull test yielded negative results. All fingernails exhibited onychodystrophy, with some toenails also being affected (Fig 4). Dermatoglyphics were absent (Fig 5). The oral examination revealed mucosal lesions and diffuse hyperpigmentation on the dorsum of the tongue (Fig 6), normal teeth and no signs of pallor. Physical and mental examinations were both normal.
Routine laboratory tests, such as a complete blood count, liver and kidney function assessments, and tumour markers, were all within expected parameters. Punch biopsy showed compact hyperkeratosis, irregular bulbous acanthosis and increased basal layer pigmentation. Upper dermis showed dilated congested capillaries with mild lymphocytic infiltrate; deep dermis was normal (Fig 7).
On extended history taking, it was noted that, the 28 y old sister of case 1, born of a non-consanguineous marriage, also presented to the outpatient dermatology department with similar symptoms including reticulate hyperpigmentation all over the body and nail dystrophy since birth, along with hypohidrosis and heat intolerance that worsens during summer. The patient reported no fading or reduction of pigmentation since its onset in early childhood, and no childhood photographs were available for retrospective comparison. Notably, there were no other affected first- or second-degree relatives. On general physical examination, the patient appeared thin with xerotic skin, while systemic, scalp and mental examinations were unremarkable. Baseline investigations were within normal limits.
On dermatological examination, the patient had reticulate pigmentation over the entire body, including the palms and soles (Fig 8). On oral examination, mucosal lesions were present on the tongue as well as abnormal dentition with yellow discoloration and enamel defects (Fig 9). The skin on the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet appeared to be xerotic and shiny, whereas the finger- and toenails were severely dystrophic (Fig 10), with an absence of dermatoglyphics. Biopsy from a hyper pigmented macule showed hyperkeratosis with focal pigment in the keratin layer, increased melanin in basal keratinocytes, increased melanocytes, scattered dermal melanophages and minimal pericapillary inflammation (Fig 11). Molecular analysis involving a dysplasia gene panel and Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB) genepanel was also used to rule out overlap with EB.This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE (Case Report) guidelines.

A 66-year-old man with interstitial lung disease presented with itchy violaceous papules and plaques on the neck and dorsal aspect of the bilateral hands, and psoriasiform lesions on the back for 3 months (Figure 1). He had been diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years earlier and completed a 6-month course of antitubercular therapy. Subsequently, he developed interstitial lung disease and was initially treated with inhaled formoterol fumarate and budesonide, with minimal clinical benefit. Four months prior to presentation, oral nintedanib monotherapy at a dose of 150 mg twice daily was initiated. One month after starting nintedanib, he developed the cutaneous lesions, for which topical steroids were prescribed, resulting in minimal improvement. Examination of the mucosae did not reveal any lesions.
Routine blood investigations were within normal limits. Skin biopsy showed parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer, lymphocytic infiltrate at the interface, melanin incontinence and rare eosinophils in the upper dermis (Figure 2). The Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale value was calculated to be 9, which indicates a definitive adverse drug reaction to nintedanib. Based on the clinical and histological findings, a diagnosis of lichenoid drug eruption secondary to nintedanib was made.
Nintedanib was stopped after discussion with the treating physician, and the patient was started on oral prednisolone 40 mg daily (approximately 0.5 mg kg−1 daily).
