Venous blood gas analysis showed a glucose level of 50 mmol/L, ketones 3.0 mmol/L, pH 7.48, and bicarbonate 31.3 mmol/L. HbA1c on admission was 76. Routine laboratory investigations are summarised in Table 1, including mild hyponatraemia (129 mmol/L) and elevated FT4 (26.5 pmol/L), whereas diabetes-specific investigations, including pancreatic autoantibodies and C-peptide measurements, are presented in Table 2.
As shown in Table 2, autoimmune diabetes markers (GAD, IA-2, and ZnT8 antibodies) were negative. The UCPCR of 0.53 nmol/mmol indicated intermediate endogenous insulin secretion, while the blood C-peptide concentration of 266 pmol/L was below the normal reference range, consistent with reduced but preserved β-cell function. Taken together with the abrupt onset of severe hyperglycaemia following ICI therapy, these findings support a diagnosis of checkpoint inhibitor-associated diabetes mellitus, characterised by significant insulin deficiency with residual endogenous insulin production rather than complete β-cell failure.
The patient was initially managed with a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRII). Following review by the diabetes specialist nurse (DSN) team, the patient was transitioned to subcutaneous biphasic insulin therapy with Humulin M3, prescribed as 22 units in the morning and 14 units in the evening. The patient received education regarding glucose monitoring and insulin dose adjustment and was advised to increase the preceding insulin doses by increments of 2 units according to glucose readings.
Following discharge, the insulin regimen was modified in the community by the DSN team to a basal-bolus regimen consisting of Abasaglar (insulin glargine) 22 units in the evening and NovoRapid (insulin aspart) 8 units with each meal.
At follow-up, the patient remained on a basal-bolus insulin regimen comprising Abasaglar and NovoRapid. She continues to be reviewed regularly by the DSN, with ongoing insulin dose optimisation according to glycaemic control. Pembrolizumab therapy has been completed, and she remains under oncology follow-up every three months. A repeat HbA1c measurement was not available at the time of writing.
In addition, the patient developed diarrhoea, which began during the hospital admission and fluctuated following discharge. A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) was positive, and the patient is currently awaiting colonoscopy. The gastrointestinal symptoms raised concern for possible immune-related gastrointestinal toxicity associated with ICI therapy, although alternative gastrointestinal pathology remains under investigation.

A 75-year-old female patient presented with a four-week history of altered mental status, poor memory, fatigue, thirst, and generalized weakness. Symptoms developed approximately one month after the initiation of tirzepatide 2.5 mg subcutaneously weekly. She denied any abdominal pain, constipation, or polyuria. Her medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and hypocalcemia secondary to hypoparathyroidism. Hypothyroidism and hypoparathyroidism occurred after a total thyroidectomy and parathyroidectomy for a large multinodular goiter and primary hyperparathyroidism, respectively, two years prior to presentation. Her medication list included calcium carbonate 1.25 g daily, alfacalcidol 1 mcg daily, bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg daily, tirzepatide 2.5 mg subcutaneously once weekly, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and amitriptyline 10 mg daily. She denied any over-the-counter herbal remedies, dietary supplements, or alternative therapies. She also denied the use of tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs. She was independent with all activities of daily living. She had no significant family history.
On examination, she was confused and lethargic but able to obey simple commands. She had a respiratory rate of 17 breaths per minute, blood oxygen saturation levels of 96% on room air, blood pressure of 136/79 mmHg, heart rate of 74 beats per minute, and a temperature of 36.7 degrees Celsius. Chest, abdominal, and neurological examination did not reveal any abnormal findings. She weighed 78 kg (body mass index: 35.2 kg/m2).
Initial blood results demonstrated severe hypercalcemia, low vitamin D levels, mild hypokalemia, mild hypomagnesemia, suppressed PTH levels in keeping with underlying hypoparathyroidism, and stage 2 acute kidney injury (Table 1). Further investigations (full blood count, liver enzymes, serum protein electrophoresis, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme [ACE], C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) were normal. An electrocardiograph demonstrated sinus rhythm and left ventricular hypertrophy. Historical results indicated that her baseline calcium levels ranged from 1.91 to 2.26 mmol/L from after her parathyroid surgery two years prior up until two months before tirzepatide was initiated. Her baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 30-40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Bendroflumethiazide, calcium carbonate, and tirzepatide were all stopped during her admission. She was administered intravenous fluids for rehydration, along with oral magnesium and potassium replacement therapy.
Serum calcium levels normalized, and her eGFR improved to 25 mL/min/1.73 m2 by day 8 of admission. Following discharge, bendroflumethiazide and calcium carbonate were not restarted. Tirzepatide was restarted at a dose of 2.5 mg once weekly, alfacalcidol 1 mcg daily was continued, and cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) 800 units daily was added. At her one-month and two-month follow-ups, serum calcium levels remained in the acceptable range of 2.1-2.3 mmol/L, and kidney function returned to baseline (30-40 mL/min/1.73 m2). The patient reported complete resolution of symptoms and returned to her baseline functional status.

A 3-year-old Merino ewe originating from teaching farm of the University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine of Cluj-Napoca (USAMV Cluj-Napoca), located in Cojocna, Transylvania (Romania), was referred to the University Ruminant Clinic of the same institution for clinical evaluation due to respiratory issues. The flock, established from animals purchased from Romanian farms, comprises approximately 300 sheep and 120 cattle raised under extensive production system, with the two species managed separately. Sheep are housed in a concrete building from December to March and are maintained on pasture during the grazing season. The sheep flock is subjected to regular health monitoring, including routine parasitological examinations and systematic vaccination against clostridial diseases and anthrax. According to the farm records and the animal caretakers, the ewe had exhibited gradually worsening respiratory signs over the previous few days, characterized by persistent bilateral seromucous nasal discharge and progressively pronounced stertorous breathing. No other animals in the flock showed comparable respiratory signs at the time of presentation, although occasional coughing had been observed in a few sheep. The ewe had not received any specific treatment for the respiratory condition prior to referral.
During the clinical examination, the ewe was alert and in good body condition (body condition score 3/5). Respiratory rate was increased, whereas rectal temperature, heart rate, and other physiological parameters were within normal limits. Respiratory distress was predominantly inspiratory. Intranasal examination revealed proliferative masses within both nasal cavities, resulting in complete obstruction of the right nasal passage (Fig. 1A) and partial obstruction of the left one (Fig. 1B). Thoracic auscultation did not reveal abnormal lung sounds, and no clinical evidence of lower respiratory tract involvement was detected. A subsequent farm visit was conducted to evaluate the overall health status of the flock and to identify additional clinical cases. No other animals presenting comparable upper respiratory abnormalities were observed.
Based on the clinical presentation and the intranasal proliferative changes observed during examination, a neoplastic process was initially suspected. Coprological analysis included flotation, sedimentation, and the Baermann technique was performed. No lungworm capable of explaining the respiratory signs were identified. Strongyle-type eggs were detected, with an estimated burden of approximately 200 eggs per gram of feces. Hematological analysis was performed using an automated hematology analyzer (Element HT5+, Antech Diagnostics/Heska, Loveland, CO, USA) and revealed no significant abnormalities.
Swabs collected from both nasal cavities were submitted for bacterioscopic and bacteriological examination, including antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Bacterioscopic examination was performed on Gram-stained smears prepared directly from the nasal swabs.
Samples were cultured on selective media, including Xylose Lysine Deoxycholate (XLD) agar and MacConkey agar, and incubated at 37 °C for 48 h. Colonies morphologically consistent with Salmonella spp. were subsequently sent to the Institute for Diagnosis and Animal Health (IDSA, Bucharest, Romania) where serotyping was performed by slide agglutination using specific antisera according to the ISO/TR 6579-3:2014 guidelines. In parallel, the isolate was submitted to a reference laboratory in Spain (Exopol, Zaragoza) for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) based molecular confirmation. Both laboratories confirmed the presence of SED.
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed using the disk diffusion method (Kirby–Bauer) on Mueller–Hinton agar, following standard laboratory procedures. The isolate was tested against lincomycin, erythromycin, oxytetracycline, sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim, colistin, tylosin, neomycin, and marbofloxacin.
The highest susceptibility was observed for marbofloxacin, followed by sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim and tylosin. The isolate demonstrated resistance to the remaining tested antimicrobials.
Infrared thermography was used as a complementary diagnostic tool, given its reported utility in the assessment of upper respiratory tract inflammatory processes (Ferrer-López et al.). Thermal imaging was performed using a FLIR E6-XT thermal imaging camera (FLIR Systems Inc., Wilsonville, OR, USA), revealing bilateral hyperthermia of the nasal region, with marked right-sided predominance (Fig. 2), supporting the presence of an active inflammatory process. Based on the thermographic findings in conjunction with the clinical presentation, CPR was included among the differential diagnoses.
Helical CT of the head was performed using a 16-slice Siemens Somatom Scope scanner. The ewe was positioned in dorsal recumbency under general anesthesia, following premedication with midazolam (0.2 mg/kg IV) and butorphanol (0.1 mg/kg IV), induction with ketamine (2 mg/kg IV) and propofol (2 mg/kg IV to effect). Axial images were acquired using a 512 × 512 matrix, 3 mm slice thickness, and a pitch of 1.5. Images were obtained during the late phase following contrast administration. Multiplanar reconstructions were generated in both soft tissue and bone algorithms at a slice thickness of 1 mm.
CT examination revealed diffuse thickening of the nasal mucosa, with accumulation of fluid-attenuating material within the nasal meatus. The nasal turbinates showed mild atrophy and focal lysis, more pronounced in the middle and ventral areas (Fig. 3). The maxillary sinuses and maxillary recesses contained soft-tissue and fluid-attenuating material, with moderate contrast enhancement of the sinus mucosa. Moderate to severe obstruction of the nasal meatus was observed, particularly in the middle and ventral passages. No significant lysis of the nasal bones was detected (Fig. 4). These findings were consistent with chronic rhinosinusitis characterized by a secretory component and mild turbinate atrophy. The overall imaging pattern was compatible with an inflammatory or infectious process.
Five days after CT examination and initiation of antimicrobial therapy, under the same general anesthesia protocol described above, rhinoscopy was performed using a 2.7 mm Karl Storz rigid telescope (Karl Storz SE & Co. KG, Tuttlingen, Germany) with a 30o viewing angle and an operative sheath providing a working channel of 3.5 mm outer diameter. Endoscopic examination revealed abundant mucous secretion within both nasal passages, more pronounced on the right side. The mucosa appeared markedly thickened, hyperemic, and irregular with severe luminal obstruction (Fig. 5). During the procedure, tissue specimens were collected from the proliferative lesions within both nasal cavities for pathological investigation. The ewe developed cardiorespiratory arrest after the procedure and died.
Following skin reflection, the skull was sectioned sagittally along the nasal septum to expose the turbinates, nasal meatuses, and ethmoid region for examination. The nasal mucosa was bilaterally and irregularly thickened, forming multiple firm, gray-pink, coalescing nodular projections that resulted in marked narrowing of the nasal passages. The lesions were more pronounced on the right ventral turbinate (Fig. 6C and D). Small amounts of gray seromucous exudate was present within the nasal meatuses.
Tissue samples were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin. After paraffin embedding, sections of 2 μm were obtained and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E), Masson Trichrome (MT) and Alcian Blue Periodic Acid-Schiff (ABPAS). Selected paraffin blocks were submitted to the Pathology service of the University of Zaragoza for IHC detection of Salmonella enterica subsp. diarizonae, while for IHC of cellular markers, the tissue sections were processed within the Department of Anatomic Pathology at USAMV Cluj-Napoca. All reagents and antibodies used for IHC are listed in Table 1.
Immunohistochemical staining for vimentin, CD3 and PAX5 was performed using an automated immunostainer (Leica Bond-Max system), with all the reagents being dispensed automatically. For ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), manual processing was conducted with serial dilutions applied after deparaffinization and rehydration. The procedure was performed using a Dako EnVision Flex + kit (mouse, high pH) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and antigen retrieval was achieved through heat-induced epitope retrieval using Novocastra™ Epitope Retrieval Solution (1:10 dilution) for 30 min. The primary antibody was incubated overnight at 4 °C.
Immunohistochemistry for detection of Salmonella spp. was performed using a mouse anti-Salmonella antibody (BioRad MCA 2832) and a polymer-based detection system (VECTOR ImmPRESS), following full antigen retrieval and overnight incubation. Following deparaffinization, sections underwent heat-induced antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0), endogenous peroxidase blocking and overnight incubation with the primary antibody at 4 °C. Immunoreactivity was visualized using ImmPACT DAB (Vector Laboratories), and sections were counterstained with hematoxylin. Negative controls were obtained by replacing the primary antibody with normal mouse serum.
The slides were examined with the optical microscope Olympus BX51, and photomicrographs were captured using an Olympus SP350 digital camera and Stream Basic imaging software, version 1.5.1 (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan).
Microscopical examination showed that the nasal mucosa was diffusely thickened, due to proliferative changes, forming polypoid to finger-like projections (Fig. 7A). The lamina propria was markedly expanded by large numbers of inflammatory cells (Fig. 7B), interspersed with abundant Vimentin positive fibrovascular tissue containing thick and irregular collagen fibers, confirmed by MT stain (Fig. 7C). The overlying epithelium was hyperplastic composed of multiple layers of MCK + epithelial cells, with an increased number of ABPAS+ Goblet cells (Fig. 7D). The nasal glands were also hyperplastic, slightly dilated with mucus and lined by well-differentiated epithelial cells. The inflammatory infiltrates were composed predominantly of CD3 + T and PAX5 + B lymphocytes (Fig. 8A and B), and plasma cells, with moderate numbers of IBA1 + macrophages and rare neutrophils (Fig. 8C). Additionally, immunohistochemistry revealed aggregates of Salmonella within hyperplastic epithelial cells, mucoid exudate and macrophages (Fig. 8D).
Although the proliferative nature of the lesions was not typical for nasal oestrosis, an empirical treatment with ivermectin (Evomec 10 mg/ml, Pasteur) was administered subcutaneously at a dosage of 0.2 mg/kg (1 mL/50 kg). No clinical improvement was observed. Anti-inflammatory treatment with dexamethasone was administered for three consecutive days to reduce mucosal swelling and improve airflow. Based on the antimicrobial susceptibility testing results and in agreement with the available literature for the treatment of CPR (Rubira et al.), antimicrobial therapy with marbofloxacin was initiated at 100 mg/kg once daily for a planned duration of 14 days. On day 5 of treatment, the ewe died developed cardiorespiratory arrest during the rhinoscopy and died.

A 28-year-old woman presented with acute bilateral visual deterioration lasting one day. She had previously maintained good uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) and did not require corrective lenses. For the past three weeks, she had been taking HCTZ and betadine for Meniere's disease, an inner ear disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of disabling vertigo, nausea, fluctuating hearing loss, and tinnitus.
On examination, uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA) was worse than 20/400 in both eyes (oculus dexter [OD] and oculus sinister [OS]). Cycloplegic refraction revealed bilateral myopia, with spherical equivalents of -4.0D in each eye (Table 1). After refractive correction, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) improved to 20/20 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure (IOP) measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry was 14mmHg in the right eye (OD) and 13 mmHg in the left eye (OS). The anterior segment examination was unremarkable, with no conjunctival chemosis or evidence of anterior chamber shallowing. Foundusexamination revealed bilateral radiating retinal folds in the macula (Figure 1).
A diagnosis of drug-induced myopia was made, and HCTZ was discontinued. Five days later, the patient reported complete resolution of visual symptoms and ocular findings (Figure 1). At follow-up, UCVA was 20/25 (OD) and 20/20 (OS) with best-correct visual acuity (BCVA) 20/20 in both eyes. Refractive testing confirmed a return to the baseline spherical equivalent of -0.75D in both eyes (OU).
The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Santa Casa de Misericórdia de São Paulo, CAAE: 94152125.8.0000.5479; # 8.043.580.

A 35-year-old multigravid woman at 24 weeks of gestation was referred to the Fetal Medicine Department of Instituto de Medicina Integral Prof. Fernando Figueira (Pernambuco, Brazil) in May 2023 due to MMC identified on an obstetric ultrasound performed at an outside institution in another state.
The patient underwent a second-trimester morphological ultrasound, which revealed discontinuity of the lumbosacral spine, confirming the diagnosis of MMC or open spina bifida. The defect originated at the L5 vertebral level and measured approximately 2.6x2.4cm. Additional ultrasound findings associated with this fetal malformation were also observed, including the lemon sign (altered shape of the skull), banana sign (abnormal cerebellar configuration secondary to herniation into the posterior fossa), a posterior ventricular diameter of 12mm, and medial deviation of the right foot.
The patient and her companion received counseling regarding the fetal abnormalities, and the available surgical options, including intrauterine and postnatal repair, were discussed. After explanation of the maternal and fetal risks and benefits, and confirmation that the case met the eligibility criteria proposed by the Management of Myelomeningocele Study (MOMS) - (2011) and endorsed by the Brazilian Federation of Associations of Gynecologists and Obstetricians (FEBRASGO) for intrauterine repair, the couple opted for fetal surgery.
During surgery, the fetal medicine team performed the standard surgical steps according to the modified mini-hysterotomy technique described by Callou et al. These steps included ultrasound-guided identification of the incision site, uterine opening (hysterotomy) measuring approximately 4.5cm to expose the fetus at the site of the MMC, opening of the amniotic membrane with drainage of clear amniotic fluid, and fixation of the amniotic membrane to the uterine wall. Before the uterine incision, intraoperative ultrasound was performed to identify the optimal site for hysterotomy and confirmed the absence of the fetal umbilical cord at the level of the defect.
At this stage, under direct visualization, instead of identifying the fetal region affected by MMC, the umbilical cord was observed crossing the hysterotomy site (Figure 1). Careful external manipulation was required to reduce and lateralize the umbilical cord, allowing exposure only of the fetal dorsal region, corresponding to the MMC site. To achieve this, the assistant surgeon inserted the fifth finger between the uterine wall and the fetal back, on the side opposite to the umbilical cord presentation, in order to decompress the cord and facilitate careful manipulation by the primary surgeon. This maneuver was performed without complications. Fetal heart rate (FHR) was monitored throughout the procedure using intraoperative ultrasonography, together with inspection of the umbilical cord. The patient was subsequently transferred to the obstetric intensive care unit (ICU) for postoperative surveillance and was discharged on the fifth postoperative day. During hospitalization after the intervention, fetal follow-up included FHR assessment and cardiotocography. No episodes of fetal bradycardia were observed.
At 30 weeks of gestation, the patient developed signs of chorioamnionitis, and delivery by cesarean section was indicated. The male newborn weighed 1,665g, and had Apgar scores of 8 and 7 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. After birth, he was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (ICU), where he remained hospitalized for 10 days, followed by an additional 22 days in the ward before hospital discharge. As of February 2025, the child was 1 year and 7 months old demonstrated good motor development, and had not required any postnatal surgical interventions.

A 5-year-old male Rottweiler was referred with multiple skin nodules and progressive weight loss of less than 2 months’ duration. Physical examination revealed vital parameters within the normal range for the species, and no abnormalities were detected on palpation of the lymph nodes. The nodules were predominantly located in the dorsal region, presenting as plaque-like lesions with increased volume. They were adherent, nonulcerated, soft to firm in consistency, and ranged from 3.0 to 6.0 cm in their largest dimension (Figure 1).
At the initial consultation, cytological examination was performed but yielded inconclusive results. A complete blood count and serum biochemical profile (creatinine, urea, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, albumin, and total protein) were performed, along with abdominal ultrasonography, thoracic radiography, and echocardiography, all of which revealed no abnormalities. For diagnostic purposes, an incisional biopsy was performed, and three skin fragments were collected from different lesions, focusing on the largest lesions. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses were subsequently performed.
Histopathological examination revealed a neoplastic proliferation of round cells infiltrating the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. The neoplastic cells had indistinct cell borders, eosinophilic and slightly vacuolated cytoplasm, elliptical nuclei with condensed to finely granular chromatin, and one or more prominent nucleoli. Thirty mitotic figures were observed in 10 high-power fields (40× objective; Figure 2A). Immunohistochemical analysis showed no immunostaining for CD3, CD79a, MUM1, E-cadherin, c-Kit, or Melanoma Cocktail antigens. In contrast, diffuse membranous to cytoplasmic immunostaining for CD18 (Figure 2B) and cytoplasmic immunostaining for granzyme in approximately 60% of the neoplastic cells (Figure 2C) were observed. The immunohistochemical profile, together with the morphological features, supported a diagnosis of non-B, non-T LGL lymphoma of NK-cell origin.
The patient returned 10 days later to begin treatment, showing worsening of its general clinical condition and progression of the skin lesions, with multiple nodules disseminated throughout the trunk. The nodules were adherent, some were ulcerated, and all had a firm consistency. The largest lesion measured 15.0 × 12.0 cm. Chemotherapy with lomustine was initiated at an oral dose of 70 mg/m2 every 21 days. The dog underwent the first three chemotherapy sessions, maintaining stable disease, and the dose was progressively increased. Before the fourth session, the dog’s condition worsened markedly, with hyporexia, weight loss, anemia, and a considerable increase in lesion size. Euthanasia was performed, resulting in a survival time of 93 days from the initial consultation.
Necropsy revealed moderate enlargement of the subscapular, retropharyngeal, and submandibular lymph nodes, as well as marked enlargement of the mesenteric lymph nodes. Cardiac examination revealed a white, raised, firm mass measuring 4.0 × 2.0 cm beneath the epicardial surface of the left ventricle (Figure 3A), extending into the underlying myocardium. The serosal surface of the gastric antrum also contained an irregular, white, raised, firm mass measuring 4.0 × 3.0 cm (Figure 3B). The liver was markedly enlarged and contained multiple small yellowish foci on the surface of all hepatic lobes. Microscopic examination of these tissues revealed a cellular proliferation similar to that observed in the skin biopsy specimens. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings were consistent with those of the cutaneous lesions, confirming the diagnosis of LGL lymphoma with involvement of the skin, heart, stomach, liver, and lymph nodes.

A 38-year-old woman with known Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, manifested by recurrent pneumothorax and fibrofolliculomas of the face, was referred for baseline renal surveillance with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) because of the increased risk of renal neoplasia associated with the syndrome.
Renal MRI was performed on a 3-T MAGNETOM Vida system (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) and included the following sequences: (a) multi-breath-hold axial and coronal T2-weighted HASTE (Half-Fourier Acquisition Single-shot Turbo Spin-Echo) sequences with and without fat-saturation (slice thickness: 4 mm; interslice gap: 0 mm); (b) axial T1-weighted 3D gradient-echo Dixon sequences (slice thickness: 2.5 mm) before and after intravenous administration of a gadolinium-based extracellular contrast agent (gadobutrol; Gadovist®, Bayer, Germany), administered at a rate of 2 mL/s, followed by a bolus of 20 mL saline flush, during the arterial, venous and delayed phases (3-, 5- and 10 min delayed acquisitions); (c) coronal T1-weighted 3D gradient-echo Dixon sequences (slice thickness: 2 mm), acquired before and after contrast administration (10 min delay) and (d) free-breathing axial diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with b-values of 50 and 800 s/mm2 (slice thickness: 4.5 mm; interslice gap: 0 mm).
MRI demonstrated a 7-mm stricture of the main pancreatic duct at the junction of the pancreatic corpus and cauda, with focal upstream dilatation up to 3 mm (Fig. 1a). Distal to the dilated duct, an approximately 9-mm enhancing lesion was identified in the delayed phase (Fig. 1b). No abnormal signal intensity was detected on diffusion-weighted imaging (Fig. 1c). Since this was the baseline MRI examination, no prior MRI studies were available for comparison. Retrospective review of a prior abdominal computed tomography (CT) examination performed 8 years earlier for acute appendicitis did not reveal any abnormalities at the corresponding location (images not shown). Based on these findings, a small fibrotic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor was considered in the differential diagnosis, and dedicated pancreatic CT was recommended for further evaluation.
Pancreatic CT, performed 10 days after the initial MRI, revealed an approximately 2-cm poorly defined lesion in the corpus–cauda transition with slightly progressive contrast enhancement, mild upstream duct dilatation, and distal parenchymal atrophy (Fig. 1d–f), raising suspicion of PDAC. The multidisciplinary team considered that even a negative endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) would not reliably exclude malignancy. Therefore, no preoperative EUS or EUS-guided tissue sampling (EUS-FNA/FNB) was pursued, and distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy was performed.
Gross examination showed a distal pancreatectomy specimen measuring 10 cm with attached spleen and omentum. In the corpus–cauda transition, a poorly defined light-brown lesion measuring 0.8 cm was identified within the pancreatic parenchyma. The lesion appeared confined to the pancreas. The closest resection margin was posterior, at a distance of 0.7 cm. Mild upstream duct dilatation was present. The spleen and omentum were unremarkable.
Histologic examination revealed a poorly circumscribed infiltrative tumor measuring 12 mm in greatest dimension, composed of sheets and nests of polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm and small uniform nuclei without prominent nucleoli (Fig. 3a). No necrosis, increased mitotic activity or nuclear pleomorphism was seen. The tumor extended along interlobular septa and encased small pancreatic ducts (Fig. 2a, b) and also surrounded small peripheral nerves without definite intraneural invasion (Fig. 4). Periodic acid–Schiff with diastase (PAS-D) stain demonstrated diffuse intracytoplasmic diastase-resistant granules (Fig. 3b).
Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were diffusely positive for S100, SOX10, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), CD68, inhibin-α and were negative for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1, ISLET1, desmin and HMB45 (Figs. 2b and 4). The Ki-67 index was below 1%. These findings were consistent with a granular cell tumor.
Twenty-two regional lymph nodes showed no metastases. The postoperative course was uneventful.

A 49-year-old woman was diagnosed with NPC (T4N1M0) in November 2021. Then, she underwent a concurrent chemoradiotherapy. Following treatment, she complained of mild headache, which gradually worsened despite symptomatic management. On April 11, 2023, the patient experienced spontaneous nasal bleeding (100 mL). Three days later, she had a recurrent episode of bleeding (400 mL) and was referred to our hospital. Upon presentation, she developed massive nasal bleeding (800 mL) and lost consciousness. Emergency angiography showed a dilated left vertebral artery and well-developed right cerebral arteries via the posterior communicating artery (Fig. 1A). Pseudoaneurysm was identified in the C3 segment of the right ICA (Fig. 1B). Coil embolization was performed urgently, resulting in resolution of the aneurysm (Fig. 1C) and complete cessation of bleeding. She was subsequently transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), where she received norepinephrine and metaraminol for hemodynamic support alongside other symptomatic and supportive interventions.
Twenty-four hours later, the patient regained consciousness and was successfully extubated. However, computed tomography angiography revealed cerebral infarction in the right parietal lobe and left frontoparietal lobes (Fig. 2A), as well as bilateral ICA occlusion starting from the C1 segment (Fig. 2B).
Following multidisciplinary consultation, supportive treatment was initiated. Thirteen days later, the patient abruptly developed unconsciousness and hyperthermia (41 °C) without any inducements. After a comprehensive discussion of the patient’s prognosis and available treatment options, her family opted to withdraw treatment and pursue discharge. The patient succumbed to her condition 8 -hs later.

This case report describes a 56-year-old man who was previously independent in activities of daily living. His medical history included smoking (20 pack-years) and daily alcohol consumption (3–6 beers/day). He lived alone and his sister was identified as the primary caregiver.
The patient was admitted to hospital on December 9, 2025, following progressive neurological symptoms that began approximately eight days earlier, including decreased strength in the left upper limb, speech impairment, gait imbalance, and falls. Brain CT angiography revealed ischemic lesions in the territory of the right middle cerebral artery. Doppler ultrasonography identified carotid stenosis of 90% on the left and 50% on the right. A diagnosis of multifocal ischemic stroke involving the right and left middle cerebral arteries was established.
During hospitalization, the patient experienced a fall resulting in transient neurological worsening, with expressive aphasia and confusion. On December 17, 2025, he underwent right carotid endarterectomy with bovine pericardial patch angioplasty under cerebral protection.
At admission to the RN program, the patient was conscious, oriented, and motivated for rehabilitation. Mild dysarthria was present, although communication and comprehension were preserved. Functional assessment demonstrated moderate dependence in activities of daily living and impaired mobility, balance, and gait.
Motor assessment using the MRC revealed marked weakness predominantly affecting the left upper limb, particularly wrist and hand function, accompanied by reduced sensory and proprioceptive function. Static and dynamic balance were moderately impaired, and the patient presented a high risk of falls. Cognitive function was preserved.
Based on the RN assessment, the intervention plan focused on muscle movement, balance, gait training, self-care, and preparation for continuity of care. The RN program combined conventional therapeutic exercises with sensorimotor stimulation using a viscoelastic product applied during upper limb exercises (Table 1).
The RN program consisted of eight sessions conducted over 21 days, with progressive adjustment of exercise complexity according to the patient’s functional evolution.
Functional improvement was observed throughout the intervention period. The Barthel Index score increased from 75 to 95 points, reflecting progression from moderate to mild dependence in activities of daily living (Table 2).
Muscle strength improved in both the left upper and lower limbs, with more pronounced gains in shoulder, wrist, and hand function (Table 3).
Dynamic balance improved progressively throughout the rehabilitation program. At the initial assessment, the patient demonstrated impaired dynamic seated balance, while static balance was preserved. By the fourth session, improvements in postural control and trunk stability were observed, with preservation of both static and dynamic balance maintained until the end of the program.
Regarding gait performance, the patient initially presented imbalance during walking, particularly during directional changes and the swing phase of the left lower limb, requiring assistance for safe ambulation. Progressive improvements in gait pattern, stability, and functional mobility were observed throughout the intervention, resulting in independent walking by the final assessment.

A 79-year-old woman underwent revision of an Oxford medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) to TKA because of progression of osteoarthritis in the lateral compartment (Figure 1). Her medical history included polymyalgia rheumatica, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. Of significance, the patient received several short courses of oral dexamethasone to manage her pain before her decision to have revision surgery. Having passed all routine preoperative investigations, the patient received medical clearance for surgery. Under spinal anesthesia, we included the previous surgical scar in our standard midline skin incision. Using a medial parapatellar arthrotomy to access the joint, the implants were noted to be stable with no evidence of infection. We carefully explanted the prosthesis using oscillating saws and osteotomes to minimize bone loss and meticulously removed any residual cement (Figure 2).
The femoral and tibial surfaces were well preserved, and we proceeded to prepare the knee using our standard surgical technique. After adequate balance was achieved with the trial implants, the final prosthesis was cemented in place ensuring good alignment and stability. We did not resurface the patella but instead chose patelloplasty, with removal of large osteophytes and denervation of the peripatellar synovium with electrocautery. Having tolerated the procedure well and commenced routine rehabilitation the day after surgery, the patient was discharged at 48 hours under the supervision of a registered physical therapist.
Six weeks after her operation, the patient reported mild knee pain with an excellent range of motion (0° −110°), and radiographs confirmed that the prosthesis was stable and well aligned (Figure 3, A and B). Notably, at this visit, the patient mentioned that she had begun to experience ipsilateral ankle pain. Clinical examination revealed normal ankle movement, with tenderness along the lateral aspect, particularly over the peroneal tendons. Our working diagnosis was peroneal tendinitis, and we prescribed topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication and advised her to continue with physiotherapy.
Over the next 8 weeks, the patient presented twice with worsening ankle pain, then severe while standing or walking. On examination, we again found lateral ankle tenderness, but ankle movement remained preserved and relatively pain free when unloaded. Plain radiographs were considered normal but given the persistence and escalation of symptoms, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan was requested. The T2-weighted images revealed a high signal area within the talus, with a linear hypointense band crossing the full thickness of the talar neck—findings consistent with an undisplaced insufficiency fracture (Figure 4). No abnormalities were seen in the peroneus longus or brevis tendons.
The patient was diagnosed with an insufficiency fracture of the neck of the talus. Our treatment included immobilization in an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) for three months, partial weight bearing with a walking stick, and continued physiotherapy focused on the knee. The patient was followed up with serial ankle radiographs every 6 weeks until the AFO was removed. At the 1-year follow-up, the patient had resumed full activity without pain in either her knee or ankle. Clinical examination was normal, and radiographs of the ankle revealed complete healing of the fracture with no signs of osteonecrosis or nonunion of the talus (Figure 5).

A 5-year-old boy underwent esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for evaluation of suspected CeD. Routine testing on the day of the procedure revealed severe anemia with hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL (mean corpuscular volume 81 fL); repeat testing confirmed hemoglobin 4.0 g/dL. EGD demonstrated duodenal scalloping (Figure 1).
Seven weeks prior, he was evaluated for fatigue and poor weight gain by his pediatrician. Testing then showed markedly elevated tissue transglutaminase IgA (>250 mg/dL) with normal total IgA (172 mg/dL). Mild normocytic anemia was present (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume [MCV] 82 fL). Over the subsequent 4–6 weeks, he developed worsening fatigue and a “slapped cheek” facial rash.
Following EGD, he was admitted for packed red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. On examination, he appeared pale and tachycardic but normotensive. There was no evidence of gastrointestinal bleeding and no family history of hematologic disease.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrated normocytic anemia with ferritin 30 ng/mL, serum iron 37 µg/dL, total iron-binding capacity 290 µg/dL, and iron saturation 13%. Reticulocyte count was elevated at 182,000/µL (9.0%). Haptoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, folate, vitamin B12, thyroid function tests, hemoglobin electrophoresis, eosin-5-maleimide testing, and flow cytometry were unremarkable. Peripheral blood smear showed mostly normocytic, normochromic RBCs with a small proportion of RBCs that were hypochromic, microcytic. A next-generation sequencing panel for congenital anemias identified no pathogenic variants. Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus polymerase chain reaction were negative. PB19 polymerase chain reaction was positive (2.4 IU/mL).
He received packed RBC (10 mL/kg) and intravenous ferric gluconate (1.5 mg/kg), with improvement in hemoglobin and energy (Figure 2). Duodenal biopsies demonstrated Marsh 3 histology, confirming CD (Figure 1). He was discharged on oral iron supplementation and a strict gluten-free diet. At follow-up, we concluded that his severe anemia was most likely attributable to prolonged PB19-infection leading to PRCA superimposed on preexisting anemia of chronic disease from CD.

In February 2025, a 50-year-old female presented to her primary care physician (PCP) with a one-week history of bilateral upper extremity numbness and paresthesias involving both arms and hands. She denied any history of trauma but reported a remote history of intermittent neck pain without prior intervention. She had no relevant medical comorbidities. One week after her initial presentation, she was referred to our office. At the spine clinic, she presented with worsening axial neck pain and chronic low back pain. Her neck pain was rated 8/10 on the visual analog scale (VAS) and described as sharp and stabbing. She also reported shooting pain down the right arm, soreness in the left forearm, and bilateral hand numbness. She reported worsening hand dexterity, difficulty with overhead activity, dropping objects, weak grip strength, and difficulty performing activities of daily living. She required a walker for ambulation. She also reported chronic low back pain with posterior thigh radiation and right foot dragging for two months before her presentation.
Neurologic examination demonstrated an ataxic and unsteady gait. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk at 3/4 in the brachioradialis, biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Hoffmann sign was positive on the right and negative on the left. Disequilibrium was noted with rapid hand movements, and clonus was absent. Sensation to light touch and pinprick was diminished bilaterally from C4 through T2. Motor strength was graded using the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale and demonstrated 4-/5 strength in the deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist flexors, and wrist extensors, while grip strength was graded at 3/5 bilaterally. Lower extremity strength was 4/5 throughout except for right ankle dorsiflexion, which was 2/5. Mild thenar eminence atrophy was noted. Based on the progressive bilateral sensorimotor symptoms, gait dysfunction, hyperreflexia, and right Hoffmann sign, the initial differential diagnosis included compressive cervical myelopathy, inflammatory or demyelinating spinal cord disease, and other neurologic or autoimmune etiologies.
Cervical and lumbar MRI studies were ordered to evaluate the progressive cervical symptoms and assess for lumbar pathology that might explain the lower extremity findings. No cervical CT was obtained because the clinical presentation raised concern for spinal cord or neurologic pathology rather than isolated osseous disease; MRI was selected to evaluate spinal cord compression, intramedullary signal abnormalities, and possible demyelinating disease. The patient was placed in a rigid Aspen collar. Laboratory evaluation showed C-reactive protein (CRP) 0.5 mg/L (reference range: < 8.0 mg/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 1 mm/hr (reference range: 0-18 mm/hr), negative rheumatoid factor (RF), and positive antinuclear antibody (ANA).
Initial cervical MRI without contrast demonstrated multilevel spondylosis with moderate C4-C5 and severe C5-C6 canal stenosis, as well as abnormal intramedullary T2 hyperintensity extending from C3-T1 with cord expansion at C5-C6 and the C6 level (Figures 1A-1B). Lumbar MRI demonstrated mild degenerative changes without high-grade canal stenosis or compressive pathology to explain her lower extremity symptoms (Figure 2). Because the signal abnormality extended beyond the level of maximal compression, additional diagnostic evaluation was pursued.
Brain MRI showed no intracranial demyelinating disease, mass, or pathologic enhancement. Repeat cervical MRI with and without contrast demonstrated a slightly expansile central cord T2 hyperintensity from C4-C7 with mild patchy enhancement (Figures 3A-3D). The primary radiographic differential favored TM, with an intramedullary neoplasm considered less likely. Lumbar puncture was performed to exclude malignancy, multiple sclerosis, and infection. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was colorless and clear, with a normal nucleated cell count, mildly elevated protein, elevated glucose, negative cytology, absent oligoclonal bands, and negative infectious testing (Table 1).
The patient was referred to neurology for further evaluation. Neurology diagnosed TM preoperatively and recommended high-dose corticosteroid therapy to decrease spinal cord inflammation, treat suspected demyelination, and minimize the risk of intraoperative secondary injury. The patient completed intravenous Solu-Medrol 1,000 mg daily for five days. Following completion of corticosteroid therapy and a negative workup for malignancy, multiple sclerosis, and infectious etiologies, she underwent C4-C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). At her final preoperative evaluation after completing corticosteroid therapy, objective examination demonstrated no change compared with her most recent preoperative clinic assessment. However, the patient reported subjective improvement in neurologic symptoms involving both upper extremities. Pre-positioning neuromonitoring was utilized because of the severe cervical stenosis and concomitant inflammatory spinal cord pathology. A standard left-sided anterior approach was performed without intraoperative complications or neuromonitoring changes.
At the first documented postoperative clinic visit, neck pain was 3/10 and described as a dull posterior neck ache consistent with expected surgical pain. Shooting pain down the right arm improved by 100%, left arm soreness improved by 50%, and burning dysesthesias in the hands and feet improved by 100%. Hand numbness continued to improve. Balance improved, although she still veered to the side while walking. She progressed from using a preoperative walker to primarily using a cane, while continuing to use a walker at home. A two-month postoperative cervical MRI with and without contrast showed improved canal patency on T2-weighted sequences and mild intramedullary enhancement consistent with persistent but slightly improved inflammatory myelitis on T1-weighted post-contrast images (Figures 4A-4D).
At the three-month follow-up, the patient reported approximately 85% overall improvement, although she continued to use a walker and reported residual arm and leg weakness with bilateral hand numbness and tingling. Her modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score improved from 10 preoperatively to 13 at three months and 16 at one-year follow-up, representing a transition from severe to mild myelopathy based on established mJOA severity criteria. At later follow-up, upper extremity sensation was documented as normal from C5-T1, and upper extremity strength was 5/5 in major muscle groups, although hyperreflexia and the right Hoffmann sign persisted. One-year postoperative MRI demonstrated mild signal abnormality on T2-weighted sequences and mild enhancement on T1-weighted post-contrast sequences, representing substantial improvement in both inflammatory and compressive findings compared with the prior imaging studies (Figures 5A-5D).

A 74-year-old female presented with hematemesis and abdominal pain for 2 days. She had a history of ischemic heart disease (IHD) and was on a beta-blocker and clopidogrel oral medications. Surgical history included cholecystectomy and hysterectomy.
The patient was alert, oriented, and hemodynamically stable.
Laboratory investigations showed mild leukocytes 11.7 × 109/L (normal range: 3.4–9.6 × 109/L) and C-reactive protein 13.3 mg/L (normal range: below 3.0 mg/L), indicating an underlying inflammation (Table 1). Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) showed blood in the esophagus and stomach with a tear in the cardia, while full assessment was limited by patient irritability (Fig. 1). Abdominal US (ultrasonography) demonstrated multiple dilated fluid-filled bowel loops with sluggish peristalsis and free fluid. Subsequently, a computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast demonstrated multiple dilated small bowel loops with a distal ileal transition point in the pelvis, mild terminal ileal wall thickening, and mild ascites, without definite evidence of bowel ischemia, suggestive of adhesive SBO (Fig. 2).
The patient was admitted, and high-dose esomeprazole was initiated. Blood preparation and repeat EGD within 24–48 h were recommended. She had gastrointestinal bleeding, considered secondary to the SBO rather than solely the cardia tear. A midline laparotomy was performed. The peritoneal cavity contained ~400 mL of free reactive fluid, with no pus or blood. Intraoperatively, the small bowel was dilated due to terminal ileal obstruction from a compressing adhesive band arising from a previous hysterectomy. The affected small bowel segment was ischemic with multiple patches of gangrene, but without perforation. Segmental resection with enterostomy was performed. The patient remained in the intensive care unit for the first 3 days due to hypotension requiring noradrenaline support. Oral intake was started after 3 days.
The patient improved clinically. She was discharged 7 days after surgery on her cardiac medications.

We present the case of a 58-year-old female who had her first seizure at the age of 11 years, triggered by physical aggression from her father (an event with loss of consciousness without other details known or remembered by the patient or family).
Since then, she has been using antiseizure medication, and she has never had a significant seizure-free period. She was unable to work for the past 5 years due to epileptic seizures and accidents associated with the events, so she was completely dependent on one of her daughters.
The current semiology of seizures before the surgical procedure was of focal seizure with impaired consciousness. At the beginning of the seizures, she experienced an occasional sensation of tightness in the throat, followed by behavioral arrest, staring, dystonic posture in the upper limbs (with no side preference), and inability to speak, lasting approximately 2 min. She then experienced postictal aggressiveness and drowsiness. All the seizures presented the same semiology, with rare evolution to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures. The current frequency was two to three times per week with the use of adequate doses of topiramate, carbamazepine, and clobazam.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed left temporal sclerosis ( Fig. 1 ). The video-electroencephalogram documented five electroclinical seizures beginning in the left anterior and middle temporal region, with two of the five progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
Based on the findings, it was decided to perform a left ATL under neurophysiologic monitoring.
The patient was placed supine, with a roll under her left side, head turned to the right, and secured in a three-pin cranial fixation device. A question mark-shaped incision and musculocutaneous flap were made, beginning just above the zygomatic arch, curving superior and posterior to the ear, and extending to the anterior hairline along the superior temporal line ( Fig. 2 ). A temporal craniotomy was performed, and the dura mater was opened in a double-Y fashion. Resection of the neocortex and mesial temporal structures was performed through a completely subpial technique. Dynamic retraction using a brain spatula was employed during resection of the mesial temporal structures. The amygdala was resected using bipolar coagulation and suction, followed by en bloc hippocampectomy, with the inferior choroidal point serving as the posterior limit of resection. Bipolar coagulation was routinely used during dissection and hemostasis at a setting of 7, with continuous irrigation using normal saline provided by the assistant during coagulation. During the final inspection using a brain spatula near the inferior choroidal point, a transient decrease in motor-evoked potentials from the ipsilateral hand and foot was observed, which partially recovered before completion of the procedure.
There was no significant bleeding during the procedure. The procedure was closed routinely, and a subgaleal drain was left in place for 48 h. The patient was extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit and then to the regular ward. Muscle strength was grade 5/5 in all four extremities, and no facial paralysis was initially evident. Immediate postoperative brain computed tomography showed a good extent of resection of temporal lobe neocortex and mesial structures without hematomas in the surgical bed ( Fig. 3 ).
The patient was discharged 72 h later and returned for a follow-up visit a week later. A House–Brackmann grade 4 peripheral facial paralysis on the left side was noted, which the family member reported noticing the day after arriving home ( Fig. 4 ). The patient reported ear pain and hyperacusis on the left side. Muscle strength in all four extremities remained 5/5, with no evidence of blisters or crusting in the external auditory canal. Postoperative brain computed tomography (CT) scan shows no evidence of intracranial hematomas or bony defects on the petrous bone. Oral corticosteroids were started with progressive tapering over the next 10 days. Two weeks after starting corticosteroids, the patient showed evident improvement in the left peripheral facial paralysis ( Fig. 4 ).

A four-month-old puppy was diagnosed with severe ectopic dioctophymosis during ultrasonographic screening conducted in a temporary animal shelter in Pelotas, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, established after the severe flooding events that affected southern Brazil in 2024. Ultrasonographic assessment revealed tubular structures with hyperechoic margins and a hypoechoic center, encircling the entire right kidney (Fig. 1A - D), without evidence of intrarenal involvement in either kidney. Notably, the dam of the puppy was also diagnosed with renal dioctophymosis. The patient, weighing 4 kg, presented with abdominal distension, pain on palpation, lethargy, and mild dehydration. Hematological analysis indicated mild anemia (Hct 31.7% - reference range 34–40%; Hb 10.5 g/dL – reference range 11–15.5 g/dL) and eosinophilia (1815/mm³ - reference range 100–1250 / mm³).
The patient was referred for surgical management to remove the worms from the abdominal cavity using gasless laparoscopy. Premedication consisted of methadone (0.3 mg/kg, IM). Anesthesia was induced with propofol administered to effect until orotracheal intubation was achieved. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane vaporized in 100% oxygen. Intraoperative analgesia was provided by a continuous rate infusion of fentanyl (3 µg/kg/h).
After clipping of the entire abdominal region and anesthetic stabilization, the animal was positioned in dorsal recumbency. A multidirectional traction platform (VET 90000; Bhio Supply®, RS, Brazil) was placed transversely to the patient. The system consisted of a base fixed to the surgical table, to which a central vertical rod and a horizontal rod were attached. The horizontal rod supported hemostatic forceps used to secure the sutures for elevation of the abdominal wall musculature.
The procedure began with placement of a 6-mm umbilical port using the Hasson technique, followed by abdominal inspection with a 5-mm 30° rigid endoscope. Subsequently, immediately cranial to the first surgical access, a 2 − 0 nylon suture incorporating the muscular fascia was placed to elevate the abdominal wall. This suture was tensioned and secured to the VET 90000 platform. Two additional traction sutures were placed craniolaterally, to the right and left of the initial access. A second 6-mm port was positioned in the right paramedian region, caudal to the first. Both ports were used without gas control valves, as the gasless technique employs normobaric pneumoperitoneum (Fig. 2A).
Inspection of the abdominal cavity revealed a marked inflammatory reaction and a moderate amount of reddish free fluid, predominantly located near the right kidney. Tissue manipulation was performed using straight atraumatic fenestrated grasping forceps. Nematodes were found encircling the entire right kidney, interspersed within the omentum in cranial, medial, and caudal regions. Cranial positioning of the ports limited inspection of the caudolateral region, which was resolved by lateralization of the patient. The serosanguineous fluid was aspirated and submitted for analysis.
The 5-mm endoscope initially used did not provide sufficient illumination. Therefore, the paramedian port was replaced with a larger one (11 mm), and a 10-mm rigid endoscope with a 30° viewing angle was employed. A total of nine worms were grasped and directly removed through the 6-mm port (Fig. 2B). The entire abdominal cavity was thoroughly inspected. After completion of the search for worms, the cavity was irrigated with 250 mL of warmed saline solution. Abdominal closure was performed in three layers. The muscular layer was closed using a simple cruciate suture pattern, and the subcutaneous tissue with an interrupted horizontal mattress pattern, both using 3 − 0 polydioxanone. The skin was sutured using an interrupted horizontal mattress pattern with 4 − 0 nylon, resulting in two skin sutures (Fig. 2C). Total surgical time was 105 min. Postoperative medications included tramadol (4 mg/kg, SC), dipyrone (25 mg/kg, IV), and meloxicam (0.1 mg/kg, PO) administered for three days.
Four females measuring 41, 35, 22, and 22 cm, and five males measuring 18, 16, 11, 10, and 10 cm were removed from the abdominal cavity (Fig. 2D). Analysis of the abdominal fluid revealed a cytological sample composed of inflammatory cells, a moderate number of erythrocytes, and D. renale eggs. The patient exhibited good appetite and activity. A follow-up abdominal ultrasonographic examination ruled out the presence of free worms. Telephone follow-up with the owner revealed that the patient remained clinically stable 180 days after gasless laparoscopy.

Reproductive failure occurred in a herd of 50 Holstein × Gir crossbred dairy cows belonging to the School Farm of the Federal University of Mato Grosso (UFMT), located in the municipality of Santo Antônio de Leverger, Mato Grosso, Brazil. Animals were maintained on improved pastures (Brachiaria brizantha and Brachiaria humidicola) with free access to mineral supplementation and water. During the dry season, cows received corn silage twice daily after milking. The herd was routinely vaccinated against Brucella abortus, bovine herpesvirus type 1 (BoHV-1) and bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV). Artificial insemination (AI) was used as the standard reproductive method, and pregnancy was diagnosed by ultrasonography 30 days after AI.
A 5/8 Girolando bovine fetus at approximately eight months of gestation was submitted to the Veterinary Pathology Laboratory at UFMT for postmortem examination. The period leading up to the abortion was marked by unstable weather and atypical rainfall. The dam was a seven-year-old cow with no additional clinical signs at the time of abortion; however, this was the second abortion recorded for this animal.
At necropsy, the fetus measured 74 cm crown-to-rump, compatible with approximately eight months of gestation. Gross findings included mild jaundice of the mucous membranes and carcass, moderate accumulation of light-yellow fluid within the thoracic cavity, and pulmonary collapse. The liver was markedly enlarged with diffuse moderate yellow-to-orange discoloration (Fig. 1A). Moderate splenomegaly was observed (Fig. 1B), and the kidneys showed diffuse moderate dark-red discoloration (Fig. 1C). Hepatic and perirenal lymph nodes were enlarged, with firm to smooth consistency and blackish-brown coloration (Fig. 1D). Multifocal hemorrhages were present on the parietal surface of the thymus. Blood smears were prepared during necropsy and stained with Panótico Rápido® (Laborclin, Brazil) for Cytological evaluation. Tissue samples from the brain, skeletal muscle, eyelid, and major thoracic and abdominal organs were collected, fixed in 10% buffered formalin, routinely processed, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin for histological examination under light microscopy.
Genomic DNA was extracted from the spleen and from a pool of liver, spleen and lymph node samples using a commercial kit (PureLink Genomic DNA Mini Kit, Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions, and stored at − 20 °C until analysis. DNA quantity and purity were assessed using a NanoDrop™ spectrophotometer (260/280 nm). PCR assays were performed according to the protocols described in Table 1. The pooled sample was subjected to PCR assays targeting Leptospira spp., Piroplasms, and Anaplasma spp., whereas the spleen sample was subjected to two distinct protocols: one specific for B. bovis and the other for B. bigemina. Amplified products were separated by electrophoresis on 1.5% agarose gels and visualized under UV transillumination. Amplicons of expected size were purified (PureLink kit, Invitrogen®) and sequenced using an automated Sanger sequencer. Generated sequences were compared with those available in GenBank using BLAST analysis. Additional blood, liver, spleen and lymph node samples were stored at − 20 °C for PCR testing for Leptospira spp., as previously described (Henker et al.). Samples of fetal lung was sectioned at 3 μm, mounted on silanized slides (immunoslide/Easypath diagnostic slide Erviegas) and subjected to an IHC panel. Data on the antibodies used, dilution, antigen recovery and clone/brand used are found in Table 2.
Cytological evaluation of blood smears revealed intraerythrocytic basophilic peripheral pinpoint structures measuring approximately 1 μm in diameter, consistent with A. marginale (Fig. 1E), as well as intraerythrocytic structures morphologically compatible with Babesia-like merozoites (Fig. 1F).
Microscopic lesions were most pronounced in the liver, kidneys, spleen, lymph nodes and lungs. The liver showed abundant golden-yellow pigment within bile ducts, hepatic sinusoids and hepatocytes (Fig. 2A). Renal lesions consisted of brownish pigment interpreted as hemoglobin casts within proximal tubular epithelial cells and tubular lumina (Fig. 2B). The spleen exhibited diffuse marked erythrophagocytosis associated with hemosiderosis. In the lungs there are macrophages with moderately abundant, occasionally vacuolated cytoplasm and are distributed within the sinuses and interstitium. Moderate amounts of brownish intra-alveolar material interspersed with amorphous eosinophilic structures morphologically compatible with meconium and keratin were observed. Leukocytostasis was present within vessels of the lungs (Fig. 2C), liver, kidneys, spleen, and lymph nodes. The lymph nodes there is marked vascular and sinusoidal congestion, with multiple distended vascular spaces filled with erythrocytes. There is expansion of the lymphatic sinuses by an abundant predominantly mononuclear cellular infiltrate composed of macrophages (Fig. 2D) and lymphocytes, associated with a moderate diffuse increase in parenchymal cellularity. Multifocal areas of hemorrhage and erythrocyte extravasation are noted, along with mild disruption of the normal cortical and medullary architecture.
PCR testing for Leptospira spp. was negative. The pool sample tested positive for Piroplasms and Anaplasma spp. in the PCR. The spleen sample tested positive for B. bovis in the first-round cPCR using species-specific primers. Conversely, B. bigemina was only detected in a second-round PCR species-specific, utilizing the initial amplicons as a template alongside its species-specific primers (Table 1). The product of the PCR from the pool positive for Anaplasma spp. demonstrated 100% similarity with uncultured Anaplasma spp. sequences deposited in GenBank MG910977.1 from cattle. The sequence of this study was deposited under number: PZ437093.
Immunohistochemistry demonstrated increase of macrophages (MAC387) (Fig. 3A), lymphocytes T (CD3) (Fig. 3B) and few lymphocytes B (CD20) (Fig. 3C) within vascular lumina of lungs, indicating intravascular accumulation of leukocytes.
Lung sections immunolabeled for MAC387 and CD3 were quantitatively evaluated and compared with control tissues from two bovine fetuses (five and nine months of gestation) obtained from a slaughterhouse, both lacking pulmonary lesions. For quantification, five images per immunolabel were captured using a 40× objective. Images underwent color deconvolution, and semi-automated counting of immunolabeled cells in alveolar walls was performed using regions of interest (ROI) in QuPath software (version 0.5.0).
In the fetus that tested positive via molecular and microscopic examination for Anaplasma spp (probably (A) marginale). and (B) bovis and B. bigemina, mean counts 36.8 MAC387-positive macrophages per field, and 27.6 CD3-positive per field (Table 3). No immunolabeling for MAC387 (Fig. 3D), CD3 (Fig. 3E) and CD20 (Fig. 3F) was detected in control animals.
This study was approved by the Animal Ethics Committee (Comissão de Ética no Uso de Animais – CEUA) of the Federal University of Mato Grosso (Protocol no. 23108.103506/2021-18).

A 4-month-old female presented with turribrachycephaly, moderate frontal bossing, and supraorbital retrusion. Cephalic index was 0.99, with 3 mm of axial cranial vault asymmetry. CT imaging demonstrated bicoronal and partial left squamosal craniosynostosis, without evidence of elevated ICP. Preoperative ophthalmologic exam was negative for papilledema. Physical exam and rapid craniosynostosis panel were negative for syndromic diagnoses. PV En-DO was performed at 6-months-old. Operative time was 128 min, with 50 mL EBL and no blood transfusion. She was discharged on POD2 after distractor activation began. Activation lasted for 37 days and showed 35 mm radiographic advancement (Figs. 2 and 3).

A 42-year-old male was diagnosed with HIV in August 2024 and initiated on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF). Initial CD4 count was 897 cells/mm3 nd HIV-1 RNA was 14 000 copies/mL. Baseline genotype demonstrated wild-type virus without resistance-associated mutations (RAMs).
TB interferon gamma release assay was ordered as initial screening and resulted positive (TB1 Ag 9.78 IU/mL, TB2 Ag Response 9.78 IU/mL, reference range <0.35 IU/mL). Chest radiography was unremarkable, and the patient had no signs or symptoms of active TB infection, thus he was diagnosed with LTBI.
The patient was counseled regarding the importance of LTBI treatment. After discussion of all available treatment options and through shared clinical decision-making, he and his care team opted for a rifamycin-based treatment regimen. In mid-September 2024, he was prescribed a 3-month course of isoniazid 300 mg daily plus rifampin 600 mg daily plus pyridoxine 50 mg daily (3HR). Of note, rifampin was utilized in lieu of rifapentine as insurance did not approve rifapentine, so it was cost-prohibitive. Due to rifampin-associated interactions with both TAF (via P-gp induction) and BIC (via CYP3A, UGT1A1, and P-gp induction), his ART was adjusted to daily tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus twice-daily dolutegravir (TDF/FTC + BID DTG). HIV-1 RNA prior to LTBI treatment, after ∼6 weeks of BIC/FTC/TAF, had appropriately decreased to 33 copies/mL.
He filled a 1-month supply of both his LTBI and antiretrovirals in mid-September 2024 but was unable to fill his prescriptions in mid-October due to insurance issues, resulting in a 1-month interruption of both therapies; however, he restarted BIC/FTC/TAF in the interim. In mid-November, LTBI treatment was restarted with a new 3-month course; HIV-1 RNA at that time was <20 copies/mL.
He traveled to Guatemala in February 2025 and reported completing his LTBI treatment shortly after returning home. During this period, he reported running out of his ART for 2 days and taking 2 doses of a friend's medication, which he identified on pill chart as either elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine or elvitegravir/cobicistat/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (EVG/COBI/TAF/FTC or EVG/COBI/TDF/FTC). He also acknowledged missing “some” evening doses of his twice-daily DTG during his LTBI treatment course.
Following completion of LTBI therapy, he continued TDF/FTC+ BID DTG for 1 additional month to allow for more than sufficient time for rifampin washout and reversal of enzyme induction prior to transitioning back to once daily BIC/FTC/TAF in April 2025. HIV-1 RNA after completing LTBI treatment was 161 copies/mL. LTBI and ART regimens are outlined in Figure 1.
The patient later expressed interest in transitioning to LAI CAB/RPV and his case was reviewed for medical eligibility, consistent with our clinic's standard practice.
At the time of review, he was noted to have persistent low-level viremia (HIV-1 RNA ranging from 47 to 161 copies/mL), a recent history of rifamycin-based therapy for LTBI, and reported adherence gaps with twice-daily dosing of DTG. Given these findings, a proviral DNA archive genotype was obtained as part of the eligibility evaluation for LAI CAB/RPV prior to proceeding with any ART modification.
The proviral DNA archive genotype identified a Q148H RAM, which confers high-level resistance to raltegravir (RAL), EVG, and CAB, as well as low-to-intermediate reductions in susceptibility to DTG and BIC. The patient was informed that, due to the presence of the Q148H mutation, he would not be eligible for LAI CAB/RPV.
Given the Q148H integrase pathway mutation along with the persistent low-level viremia, he was transitioned to darunavir/cobicistat/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (DRV/COBI/TAF/FTC) and he achieved complete virologic suppression with an HIV-1 RNA of <20 copies/mL on this regimen. A regimen containing twice-daily DTG was not pursued due to prior adherence challenges with twice-daily dosing.

A 30-year-old, gravidity five, parity four, ethnic Karen woman presented after travelling for more than 5 h to reach a clinic in conflict-affected Myanmar. Supported by her husband they reported a 1-year history of increasing muscle cramps, then a gradual onset of a progressive bilateral tremor in the upper and lower limbs. At the time of presentation, the tremor was so severe that she was not able to walk, stand or sit by herself. She was carried to the bathroom, and food and water were provided by her mother, husband or children. She had a very quiet voice, appeared withdrawn, and had experienced weight loss during the current pregnancy (gestation confirmed by a late ultrasound). Her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and she had delivered each of them at home. She did not consume alcohol. On further questioning her sister had developed a similar progressive tremor, and died at 20 years through a chest infection. Her family had already sought care at two other hospitals but were told nothing could be done.
On examination she had marked positional and intention tremor, (Supplementary Material 1: Video 1) which was bilateral but asymmetric (worse on the left). Her power was preserved throughout, there was no wasting, reflexes and sensation were normal, and coordination was limited largely by tremor. On examination of her eyes, Kayser–Fleischer rings were present bilaterally (Fig. 1). She had poverty of facial expression and hypophonia but no slurring of speech. Her eyesight was grossly normal, and while there was no nystagmus, she followed objects with delay. She had mild bilateral palmar erythema which may have related to her pregnancy. The cardio-respiratory examination was normal and there was no palpable hepatomegaly or signs of chronic liver disease.
Off-site investigations showed a mild anaemia, haemoglobin 9.7 g/dL (12–16), and slight increase of liver enzymes, Alanine Transferase 21 U/L (< 35), Aspartate Aminotransferase 37 U/L (< 35), Alkaline Phosphatase 137 U/L (30–120), Total Bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL (0.3–1.2), Direct Bilirubin 0.1 mg/dL (< 0.2), and Gamma-glutamyl Transferase 69 U/L (< 38). Other biochemistry values were normal. She was HIV, Hepatitis B and C, negative. The cluster of Kayser–Fleisher rings, bilateral and progressive tremor, and suspicious family history pointed to Wilson’s disease: serum ceruloplasmin was low at 0.091 g/L (normal range 0.2–0.6) and the 24-h urine copper was high at 2325 μG/day (normal < 35). Genetic testing, 6 months after first presentation, via a sample sent to Siriraj Hospital, Mahidol University, Bangkok Thailand, showed a homozygous pathogenic ATP7B variant (c.2692C > T(p.Gln898*) and the diagnosis of Wilson’s disease was confirmed.
The patient was initially treated with a low copper diet and oral zinc sulphate 30 mg orally, three times daily. Liver function tests repeated after 1 month, indicated rising Alkaline Phosphatase [240 U/L (30–120)] which may occur with increasing gestational age but also in zinc deficiency, and it was continued as the pregnancy was near term. D-penicillamine capsules [Samarth Life Sciences PVT (India)] 250 mg once daily, and Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 20 mg twice daily, were commenced. Skilled birth attendants at Shoklo Malaria Research Unit clinic supported a vaginal breech birth, without complications or oxytocic drugs at 39 + 1-week gestation, 2 weeks after commencement of the D-penicillamine. The female baby of 3010 g, had Apgar scores of 9 and 10 (at 5 and 10 min) and a normal newborn surface examination, including cardio-respiratory auscultation, and absence of Kayser–Fleischer rings. The mother wanted to breastfeed and required support as she could not physically hold the child. She agreed to a 5-year implant as a post-partum contraceptive. At 2-month post-partum her symptoms were improved and she was able to walk without support. (Supplementary Material 2: Video 2) Currently, after 1 year and 5 months, the symptoms have significantly improved on daily D-penicillamine (adjusted over time; maximum daily dose 875 mg), pyridoxine and zinc, and her baby remains healthy. (Supplementary Material 3: Video 3). All the live children (n = 4; her second born child was an early neonatal death) have undergone testing for serum ceruloplasmin and 24-h urine copper excretion, which indicate they are unlikely to have Wilson’s disease; however, they remain under follow-up.
The biggest barrier to this patient receiving appropriate care was reaching a clinic within conflict-affected Myanmar that did a complete neurological examination. In person follow-up has been adapted to be less frequent than recommended for D-penicillamine with periods of up to 6 months between visits; due to difficulty of travel within a conflict zone, and exceptional travel costs.

A 39-year-old woman who worked as an office clerk presented with a three-week history of bilateral ocular redness, itching, foreign-body sensation, and blurred vision. She was otherwise healthy, denied any systemic complaints, and reported no history of immunodeficiency, surgery, or trauma. She had kept a pet parrot at home for two years and had daily close contact with it. Her husband and son lived in the same household but did not have frequent direct contact with the bird. Both were examined in our clinic. Neither reported ocular redness, foreign-body sensation, or other ocular discomfort, and slit-lamp examinations showed no conjunctival congestion or corneal epithelial lesions. Before referral, the patient had been diagnosed with dry eye disease at another hospital and had received fluorometholone, sodium hyaluronate, and levofloxacin eye drops without clinical improvement.
Uncorrected visual acuity (UCVA), measured using a standard logarithmic visual acuity chart at 5 m, was 0.8 decimal (0.10 logMAR) in both eyes. Pinhole testing did not improve visual acuity. Intraocular pressure, measured using a non-contact air-puff tonometer, was within the normal range bilaterally. Anterior segment examination showed bilateral mixed conjunctival and ciliary injection, with papillae and follicles on the lower palpebral conjunctiva (Figure 1a). There was no ocular discharge, membrane or pseudomembrane formation, and chemosis or preauricular lymphadenopathy. Corneal examination showed bilateral superficial punctate infiltrates, mainly in the central cornea (Figure 1b). Fluorescein staining revealed diffuse punctate epithelial staining in both eyes (Figure 1c). The anterior chamber, iris, and lens were unremarkable.
The initial working diagnosis was keratoconjunctivitis of undetermined cause.
Adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis, particularly epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC), was first considered because the patient had bilateral conjunctival inflammation and corneal epithelial lesions. However, she had no known contact with patients with keratoconjunctivitis. She also had no watery discharge, subconjunctival hemorrhage, membrane or pseudomembrane formation, or preauricular lymphadenopathy. The corneal infiltrates were already present at the initial examination, rather than appearing after resolution of epithelial disease, which was less consistent with EKC.
Thygeson's superficial punctate keratitis (TSPK) was also considered because of the bilateral superficial punctate corneal lesions. However, the prominent conjunctival congestion, papillae, and follicles were atypical for TSPK. The disease had not followed a chronic relapsing course, and the patient had not improved after topical fluorometholone. These findings made TSPK less likely.
Dry eye disease was less likely because the prominent follicular-papillary conjunctival reaction was atypical, and the symptoms had not improved with sodium hyaluronate. Drug-induced toxic keratopathy could not explain the onset because the symptoms preceded the prescribed topical medications. In treatment-refractory keratoconjunctivitis, the combination of pet-parrot exposure and superficial punctate epithelial infiltrates should raise suspicion for MKC and prompt corneal scraping for microbiological examination.
Accordingly, a corneal scraping was obtained from the left eye for microbiological assessment. Only one eye was sampled to avoid bilateral epithelial injury. Giemsa staining showed scattered bluish-purple, oval, spore-like structures adjacent to epithelial cells (Figure 2a). Bacterial and fungal cultures were negative.
The corneal scraping sample was then submitted for mNGS.
