Finally, other causes of hyperglycemia were excluded, like infectious diseases, medications (e.g. corticosteroid, atypical antipsychotics), other endocrinopathies (e.g. Cushing), and pancreatic pathologies. Therefore, the clinical diagnosis was attributed to ICI-DM. HbA1c values at presentation were unfortunately unavailable, limiting further characterization of the chronicity of hyperglycemia. Gradually, a basal-bolus insulin regimen was initiated with a progressive glycemic control, according to an insulin optimization. After 5 days of hospitalization the patient was discharged in good clinical conditions. A multidisciplinary discussion with medical oncologists and endocrinologists was conducted to define a potential pembrolizumab restart. However, considering advanced age, comorbidities, high risk of glycemic decompensation and time since last administration of pembrolizumab, clinicians agreed on its discontinuation.
During follow-up, the patient remained permanently insulin-dependent, with no recovery of endogenous insulin secretion. After discontinuation of pembrolizumab, diabetes remained under control, with no further episodes of glycemic decompensation. Long-term oncological surveillance demonstrated a disease control until December 2025, when thoracic–abdominal CT showed no evidence of systemic progression, while brain MRI revealed intracranial disease progression, with the appearance of a new lesion in the left postcentral gyrus, for which he subsequently underwent SBRT, 21 Gy in 1 fraction. Blood glucose values ​​persisted within the normal range despite the initiation of brain metastases prophylactic therapy with dexamethasone. The patient remains clinically stable under oncological and endocrinological follow-up (Figure 2).

The first patient was a 46-year-old male who presented to our hospital with a chief complaint of penile head enlargement lasting one month. The patient denies any chronic diseases and personal/family history of melanoma or other skin diseases. Upon specialized physical examination, the patient was found to have phimosis and a mass measuring approximately 2.0 × 2.0 cm located on the penile glans. No foul odor or ulceration is present. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes are palpable in both inguinal regions, without tenderness. No suspicious lesions were found on the remaining skin and mucous membranes.
Subsequently, the patient underwent a series of examinations at our hospital. Inguinal and penile ultrasound showed a moderately echogenic mass visible anteriorly and to the left of the penis, measuring approximately 3.54 × 2.42 × 2.05cm with a poorly defined border and abundant blood flow. Multiple lymph node echoes are visible in both inguinal regions, with the largest measuring approximately 0.72 × 0.35cm in the right and 2.89 × 2.72cm in the left. They appear round with relatively low echogenicity and show linear blood flow. To further clarify the nature, an abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a soft tissue mass with ill-defined borders in the glans penis. In the non-contrast phase, it demonstrates a CT value of approximately 46 HU. Following contrast administration, it exhibits heterogeneous enhancement with a CT value of approximately 86 HU. Multiple enlarged superficial lymph nodes are visible bilaterally in the inguinal regions with partial fusion, among which the largest is located in the left inguinal region, measuring approximately 3.2 x 2.7cm. It demonstrates heterogeneous enhancement on contrast-enhanced imaging, with areas of non-enhancing necrosis visible within some lymph nodes, and no involvement of pelvic lymph nodes was observed. A diagnosis of penile malignant tumor with probable lymph node metastasis was made (Supplementary Figure 1).
We performed a partial penile resection on the patient following discussion, and bilateral inguinal lymph node dissection was preliminarily planned to be conducted one month later. The surgery aims to achieve complete tumor resection while ensuring negative margins to preserve the quality of life. The glans penis presented with a phimosis-like appearance. After positioning supine, a 2 cm incision was made along the dorsal foreskin, revealing extensive black cauliflower-like growths centered around the urethral meatus, which were suggested to be malignant melanoma by intraoperative pathology (Figure 1). A circular incision was made at least 3cm above the diseased tissue, and a ligation of the deep dorsal penile artery was performed. The corpus cavernosum was incised down to the surface of the tunica albuginea of the corpus spongiosum. Approximately 1cm of urethra was dissected free toward the external urethral orifice, transected, and the diseased portion of the penis was removed. The corpus cavernosum, fascial layer, subcutaneous tissue, and skin were sutured sequentially. The urethra was everted to reconstruct the external urethral orifice, and a urinary catheter was finally placed. The patient was discharged on the fifth day postoperatively.
The postoperative histopathological diagnosis was confirmed as malignant melanoma, and the immunohistochemical findings supported this diagnosis: CK(±), Vimentin(+), HMB-45(+), Melan A(+), S-100(+), SOX-10(+), Ki-67(>30%) (Figure 2). Given the rarity of the disease, genetic testing is performed: KRAS(-), NRAS(-), PIK3CA(-), BRAF(-). The patient declined further bilateral inguinal lymph node biopsy and dissection and underwent intravenous chemotherapy with Albumin-bound paclitaxel and Carboplatin. Following four treatment cycles, he refused further intravenous chemotherapy and follow-up due to treatment intolerance after another two cycles. In subsequent ultrasound and CT records, the patient’s inguinal lymph nodes were found to have enlarged before chemotherapy. After chemotherapy, it decreased by 1.2 cm compared to before chemotherapy (Table 1, Figure 3).
Six months later, the patient experienced dizziness and headaches. A follow-up enhanced cranial CT scan presented a nodular lesion at the left frontal-temporal junction with well-defined borders, ring-like enhancement, and a fluid-filled area, measuring approximately 2.1 × 1.9cm (Supplementary Figure 2). Because of the considered brain metastasis, the previous intravenous chemotherapy regimen was continued, supplemented with stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) subsequently. However, this treatment series did not prevent the progression of metastasis, and the patient died 18 months after diagnosis of brain metastases.
The second patient was a 67-year-old male who presented with a penile mass with ulceration for five years. Biopsy from the dermatology department yielded a diagnosis of penile melanoma. Detailed physical examination also found a movable, firm mass in the left inguinal region, approximately the size of a soybean. No suspicious lesions were found on the remaining skin and mucous membranes. Inguinal ultrasound showed multiple bilateral enlarged lymph nodes. The largest node on the right measures approximately 0.69 × 0.34cm and shows no blood flow, while the largest on the left measures approximately 0.71 × 0.41cm and shows punctate blood flow. Given the possibility of distant metastasis, PET-CT was performed, which showed increased density in the anterior abdominal wall of the left inguinal region and within the pelvic cavity, with unevenly increased FDG uptake.
Following the discussion, a partial penile resection was performed under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia. The other detailed surgical process is similar to that of case 1. During postoperative pathology examination, spindle-shaped tumorous cells were distributed diffusely under the microscope, with large nuclei and oval nucleoli. Mitotic figures are frequently observed, and extensive melanin deposits are visible within the cytoplasm. The final diagnosis of primary penile melanoma was in line with the former report (Supplementary Figure 3). The patient left the hospital 7 days after surgery and was advised to undergo adjuvant treatment in our Department of Oncology. Following up by telephone, the patient refused adjuvant treatment. He underwent total gastrectomy for primary gastric cancer 68 months after the initial surgery and died half a year later.
The third patient was a 64-year-old male who presented with a 1-year history of ulceration on the inner foreskin, which had enlarged over the past 3 months. The patient underwent penile mass excision at our hospital six years ago for penile carcinoma (Postoperative pathology indicated squamous cell carcinoma), and no adjuvant therapy was administered subsequently. We conducted a physical examination on his admission this time. The patient presented with a redundant prepuce and retractable foreskin. A single, approximately 1cm in diameter, roundish mass is observed on the dorsal aspect of the glans near the corona. An ulcerated area measuring approximately 3.0 × 3.0cm with red spots is visible on the ventral inner foreskin without foul odor, which bleeds readily on palpation. No suspicious lesions were found on the remaining skin and mucous membranes. Considering his medical history and physical examination results, a pelvic enhanced CT examination was suggested, during which an oval shadow measuring approximately 4.7 × 3.2cm is visible inferior to the left iliac artery and vein within the left pelvic wall.
Following discussion and communication with the patient, a surgical plan was made, including glans excision, circumcision, and pelvic mass resection. Following successful anesthesia and supine positioning, exploration revealed scar-like changes on the right surface of the glans penis, extending deep and firm. The lesion was excised with 0.5cm of surrounding normal tissue intact. Intraoperative pathology of the excised lesion indicated granulomatous inflammation. Then circumcision was subsequently performed, and a urinary catheter was placed. Before the third procedure of pelvic mass resection, we elevated the left lower abdomen and reapplied the routine antiseptic. An oblique incision was made in the left lower abdomen, sequentially cutting through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the muscle layer until reaching the extraperitoneal space, aiming to expose the left iliac vessels. A left pelvic mass was then revealed, measuring approximately 4.0 × 5.0cm, closely adherent to the left pelvic wall, iliac vessels, obturator vessels, and obturator nerve. The mass was dissected along its margins and completely excised.
Postoperative histopathological examination revealed atypical cell proliferation diffusely distributed throughout the tissue. Immunohistochemical staining of the penile mass showed CK(–), Vimentin(+), S-100(+), HMB-45(+), Melan A(+), Ki-67 (approximately 50%+)(Supplementary Figure 4), while that of pelvic mass presented CK (-), Vimentin (+), P63 (-), Synaptophysin (-), CD56 (-), GATA-3 (-), CK7 (-), S-100 (-), HMB-45 (+), Melan A (+), Ki-67 (approximately 50%+). These findings indicated a diagnosis of penile melanoma with pelvic metastasis. The patient left the hospital 10 days after surgery and was recommended for adjuvant treatment. After telephone follow-up, the patient refused reexamination and adjuvant treatment and died 13 months later.
The three patients with penile melanoma reported herein all denied a prior history of melanoma, and no suspicious cutaneous or mucosal lesions were detected on physical examination. After multidisciplinary discussion, all patients underwent surgical treatment, and postoperative pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of primary penile melanoma. The clinical data are summarized as follows (Supplementary Table 1).

The proband was a 7-year-8-month-old boy who was referred for evaluation of short stature. Growth retardation and mild global developmental delay had been noted since infancy and had persisted for more than 7 years. There was no history of seizures, fractures, or other major chronic medical conditions. Birth weight and birth length were unavailable. The parents were non-consanguineous. The mid-parental target height was approximately 162 cm.
At presentation, his height was 117 cm (−2.09 SDS), weight was 18 kg (−2.56 SDS), and body mass index (BMI) was 13.15 kg/m² (−1.87 SDS). Blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg.Head circumference was 51 cm, with no evidence of microcephaly or macrocephaly. Additional anthropometric assessment showed an upper segment of 61 cm and a lower segment of 56 cm, giving an upper-to-lower segment ratio of 1.09. The upper-to-lower segment ratio was within the expected range for age. His arm span was 115 cm, and arm span minus height was -2 cm. Physical examination showed short stature, small hands and feet, and brachydactyly involving both the hands and feet. Craniofacial features included a depressed nasal bridge, short philtrum, and short neck (Figures 1A, C, D–F). Dental crowding and caries were also noted. No scoliosis, chest wall deformity, or genital abnormality was observed.
Developmental assessment using the Gesell Developmental Schedules demonstrated mild global developmental delay, with developmental quotients of 62 in adaptive behavior, 66 in gross motor function, 72 in fine motor function, 56 in language, and 64 in personal-social function. Before this evaluation, he had not received systematic rehabilitation, physical therapy, or speech therapy. He attended a regular first-grade primary school. According to the family, his teacher reported poor academic performance.
Biochemical and endocrine evaluation showed no major abnormalities.IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 were within age- and sex-specific reference ranges; no biochemical evidence of thyroid dysfunction, calcium-phosphate metabolism disorder, or hormone resistance was observed.
Radiographs showed generalized shortening of metacarpals I–V and the corresponding phalanges, rather than predominant involvement of the fourth and fifth rays (Figures 2A–C). Premature epiphyseal fusion and metaphyseal widening were observed in the metacarpals. Foot radiographs showed diffuse shortening of the metatarsals and phalanges. Chest, pelvic, and spinal radiographs were unremarkable. Bone age, assessed by the Greulich–Pyle method, was 7 years at a chronological age of 7 years and 8 months.
Family history revealed similar skeletal findings in the patient’s mother. She had short stature, with an adult height of 140 cm (-3.81 SDS), and brachydactyly affecting both hands and feet. Digital shortening was more pronounced in the third to fifth digits (Figures 1G, H). Her weight was 60 kg (+1.12 SDS), and BMI was 30.61 kg/m², consistent with obesity. Additional anthropometric assessment showed an upper segment of 72 cm and a lower segment of 68 cm, corresponding to an upper-to-lower segment ratio of 1.05. Her arm span was 138.5 cm, and arm span minus height was -1.5 cm.
She also showed craniofacial features similar to those of the proband (Figure 1B). Radiographs of the mother showed marked shortening of metacarpals III-V with cone-shaped epiphyses (Figure 2D). Foot radiographs also demonstrated shortening of the metatarsals and phalanges(Figure 2E).On physical examination, the mother had no obvious dental anomalies, mammary abnormalities, or thyroid enlargement. Further laboratory evaluation for thyroid function, glucose and lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance was recommended but declined by the family.
According to the family’s report, the maternal grandparents had no apparent short stature or hand/foot abnormalities, but both had died before this study and were unavailable for clinical examination or genetic testing. The mother had no siblings; therefore, further segregation analysis in maternal relatives could not be performed. The father’s height was 171 cm (−0.21 SDS), and no comparable skeletal abnormalities were identified in him.
Trio whole-exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous nonsense variant in PTHLH, NM_198965.2:c.82G>T, p.(Glu28Ter), corresponding to chr12:27969413C>A in GRCh38.This variant is located in exon 4 of PTHLH. Sanger sequencing confirmed the presence of the variant in both the proband and his affected mother, whereas the unaffected father did not carry the variant (Figure 3). This segregation pattern supported autosomal dominant inheritance.
The variant was classified as pathogenic according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines based on PVS1, PM2_Supporting, and PP4. PVS1 was applied because PTHLH is an established haploinsufficient gene and loss of function is a known disease mechanism for PTHLH-associated brachydactyly type E. PM2_Supporting was applied because the variant is absent from gnomAD v4.0. PP4 was applied because the patient’s phenotype, including brachydactyly type E, short stature, characteristic radiographic findings, and normal biochemical evaluation, is highly specific for PTHLH-associated disease. The variant has been submitted to ClinVar as a pathogenic variant under accession number SCV007602660.
A structured literature search was performed in PubMed and Web of Science from database inception to February 2026. Search terms included “PTHLH,” “PTHrP,” “brachydactyly type E,” “BDE2,” “short stature,” “metacarpal shortening,” and “metatarsal shortening.” A total of 74 records were identified through database searching (PubMed, n=34; Web of Science, n=40). After removal of duplicates (n=32), 42 unique records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 21 were excluded. Twenty-one full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 10 were excluded for the following reasons: non-PTHLH etiology (n=6), structural variants including duplications or microdeletions (n=2), non-human study (n=1), and lack of extractable individual-level clinical data (n=1). Ultimately, 11 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis (Table 1; Supplementary Table 1).
Extracted data included nucleotide and protein variants, variant consequence, protein region, number of reported individuals, height data, stature category, BDE skeletal phenotype, and additional clinical features. Because of the small number of reports, familial clustering, and heterogeneous reporting of height data, the analysis was descriptive and exploratory; no inferential genotype–phenotype statistics were performed.
Together with the present family, the pooled dataset included 19 variant- or report-level entries and 47 affected individuals. Stature information was available for 42 individuals. Twenty of 42 individuals (47.6%) had height ≤ −2 SDS and were classified as having short stature. When individuals explicitly described as having short stature in the original reports but without sufficient numerical height data were also included, 31 of 42 individuals (73.8%) were classified as having short stature or reduced stature. These findings indicate that short stature is common but incompletely penetrant in PTHLH-associated brachydactyly type E.
Predicted loss-of-function variants, particularly early truncating variants, frameshift variants, and variants affecting the signal peptide or initiation region, were more often reported with growth impairment. However, because of the small number of cases, familial clustering, and heterogeneous reporting of height data, this pattern was interpreted descriptively rather than statistically. The c.166C>T, p.(Arg56Ter) variant, which has been reported in several unrelated cases or families, showed discordant stature phenotypes, and several familial cases demonstrated marked intrafamilial variability. These findings indicate that variant consequence and protein region may provide useful risk-stratification information but are insufficient for reliable individual-level prediction of short stature.
The family’s main concern at presentation was the proband’s short stature and small hands and feet. Before molecular diagnosis, the family hoped that clarifying the etiology of short stature might guide treatment, including whether recombinant growth hormone therapy was appropriate. After PTHLH-associated brachydactyly type E was diagnosed, the family was counseled that the proband’s short stature was more likely related to altered growth-plate regulation than to a primary GH-IGF-1 axis defect. Given the absence of clear GH deficiency and the lack of evidence supporting GH therapy specifically for PTHLH-associated BDE, recombinant growth hormone was not initiated. The genetic diagnosis helped the family understand the shared mother-son phenotype, clarified recurrence risk, and guided long-term growth monitoring and reproductive counseling.

Case 1: A 41-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital due to right parotid gland mass for 1 week. Physical examination: A palpable mass with 2.5*2.0 cm in size was in the lower pole of right parotid gland, with moderate texture and clear boundary, general mobility and no obvious tenderness. No significantly enlarged lymph nodes were found in bilateral neck and supraclavicular region.(The normal size range of lymph node is 0.2-0.5cm.)Color Doppler imaging: A 3.3*2.4 cm solid nodule in right parotid gland, absence of right thyroid gland, no significant occupying lesion in left thyroid gland, bilateral neck and supraclavicular region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): Oval abnormal signal shadows were observed in right parotid region, ill-defined boundary with 3.0*2.4 cm, slightly high signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), equal signal on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), significant high signal intensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), significant low signal intensity on apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Less homogeneous signal intensity, heterogeneous mild to moderate enhancement after contrast enhancement, clear boundary, several slightly larger lymph node shadows scattered in bilateral neck (Figures 1A, B). No significant abnormality in nasopharynx or oropharynx. FNAC biopsy report: (Solid nodule in right parotid gland) numerous lymphocytes, several small piles of heterocysts, suspected poorly differentiated carcinoma.
Case 2: A 37-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with the chief complaint of “discovering a space-occupying lesion in the left parotid gland for 3 months”. Physical examination: A mass measuring approximately 4.5*3.0 cm was palpable in the left parotid gland, with hard texture, poor mobility, and no obvious tenderness. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were palpable in the left neck with hard texture, while no significantly enlarged lymph nodes were found in the right neck or bilateral supraclavicular regions. Color Doppler imaging: A 4.5*2.6 cm hypoechoic nodule was observed in the lower pole of the left parotid gland, with relatively clear boundaries, irregular shape, and lobulated edges (Figure 1C). Multiple hypoechoic lesions were detected in the left neck, with clear boundaries and plump morphology, and no lymphoid hilum structure was seen. No significant occupying lesions were found in the right parotid gland, bilateral submandibular glands, right neck, or bilateral supraclavicular regions. Computed tomography (CT): A mass in the left parotid gland region with irregular shape and heterogeneous enhancement, accompanied by multiple enhanced lymph nodes in the left neck (some enlarged) (Figure 1D). MRI: A mass in the left parotid gland region and multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the left neck, considering malignant tumor. FNAC biopsy report: (Left parotid gland mass) poorly differentiated carcinoma; parotid lymphoepithelial carcinoma is considered after excluding metastases such as nasopharyngeal non-keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma.
Case 3: A 26-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital due to right cervical lymphadenopathy for 2 months. Physical examination: Several palpable confluent masses were in the right parotid gland, with the largest 4.0*3.0 cm in size, firm and fixed texture, ill-defined boundary, and no obvious tenderness. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in right neck, among which the larger one was in V region with 2.0*2.0 cm in size, firm and fixed texture, ill-defined boundary, and no obvious tenderness. No enlarged lymph nodes in left neck. Color Doppler imaging: Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in Ib, II, III, IV and V regions of right neck, no enlarged lymph nodes in left neck. MRI: Patchy enhancement of the right parotid gland, multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the right neck and parotid region, which tended to metastasize, and multiple slightly larger lymph nodes in the left neck. FNAC biopsy report: (Right cervical lymph node) metastatic lymph node epithelial carcinoma. Laryngoscopy and nasopharyngoscopy revealed no significant abnormalities. Positron emission tomography/CT (PET/CT): Multiple nodules in right parotid gland, ill-defined boundary, with the largest 1.7*1.5 cm in size, increased fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), malignant tumors were considered.
All three patients directly received surgical treatment without pre-operative medications. Case 1 and case 2 underwent right radical parotidectomy + submandibular gland resection at the department of Head and Neck Surgery in Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center, while case 3 at the Xiamen Branch, Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center. Cervical lymph node metastasis may occur at an early stage in patients with salivary gland lymphoepithelial carcinoma. Ipsilateral cervical lymph node metastases are detected in 17%–30% of patients when diagnosed, presenting as hard, fixed cervical masses predominantly involving intraparotid, level II and level Ib lymph nodes. Previous studies have confirmed that occult cervical lymph node metastases are present in 20%–22% of patients. Neither preoperative imaging examination of Case 1 nor Case 2 indicated lymph node metastasis, both patients underwent elective neck dissection (levels I-III).Preoperative imaging revealed multiple cervical lymph node metastases in Case 3, who subsequently received radical neck dissection(levels I-V).
Postoperative pathology of case 1: (Right parotid gland) nests of atypical epithelial cells in highly proliferative lymphoid tissue, could not exclude possibility of LEC, tumor size 2.0*1.5 cm. (Right cervical lymph node) no metastasis in lymph nodes (0/14). Immunohistochemistry: AE1/AE3 (+), CK5/6 (+), P16 (partly +), CK7(-), CK20(-), CD117 (+), calponin (-), Ki-67 (around 70%+), P63 (+), EBV-encoded RNA(EBER) (+).
Postoperative pathology of case 2: (Left parotid gland and left submandibular gland) LEC. Tumor size: 4.0*2.5*2.0 cm. Vascular invasion (+), perineural invasion (+). Cancer metastases were detected in 3 out of 9 surrounding lymph nodes. (Left cervical lymph nodes) Cancer metastases were detected in 6 out of 27 lymph nodes. Immunohistochemistry: AE1/AE3 (+), P63 (+), P40 (+), EBER (+), EGFR (+), Ki-67 (approximately 70%+), CK5/6 (+), P16 (-), Syn (-), S-100 (-), Programmed death-ligand 1(PD-L1) 22C3 (CPS approximately 80%),GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3) (-), trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 1 (TRPS1) (-).
Postoperative pathology of case 3: (Superficial lobe of right parotid gland) LEC, infiltrating the surrounding fibroadipose tissue. Tumor size: 62.52.5 cm. Vascular tumor thrombus (+), no definite perineural invasion. (Deep lobe of right parotid gland) Cancer involvement identified. (Right submandibular gland) No cancer involvement. (Right cervical lymph nodes) Cancer metastases detected in 9 out of 43 lymph nodes. Immunohistochemistry: AE1/AE3 (+), CK5/6 (+), P63 (+), P40 (+), EBER (+), SOX10 (-), D2-40 (vascular +), Ki-67 (90%+), CD20 (-), CD5 (-), P53 (partly +), Bcl-2 (+), CD117 (+) (Figure 2). Additional note: No positive human papillomavirus (HPV) subtypes detected.
All 3 cases received postoperative radiotherapy.

A 49-year-old man was admitted to thoracic surgery on March 17, 2025, after surveillance imaging showed a right lower-lobe pulmonary nodule. He reported mild cough with sputum but denied fever, chills, abdominal pain, diarrhea, appetite change, or weight loss. He had no smoking or alcohol-drinking history, no known autoimmune disease, and no family history of lymphoma, lung cancer, or other malignant tumors. His history included occupational welding exposure, hypertension, prior hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, previous antituberculosis treatment after detection of a pulmonary nodule, and resection of a left thyroid microcarcinoma followed by levothyroxine therapy. The complete clinical timeline is summarized in Table 1.
Physical examination showed no palpable superficial lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Breath sounds were clear, and the abdomen was soft and non-tender. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated moderate obstructive ventilatory impairment: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1), 1.88 L; FEV1 percentage predicted, 65.3%; forced vital capacity, 2.81 L; FEV1/FVC, 66.95%; and maximal voluntary ventilation percentage predicted, 89.7%.
A preoperative chest CT on March 17, 2025, showed a right lower-lobe part-solid/high-density nodule measuring 12 × 9 mm with indistinct margins and no abnormal enhancement. Additional right-lung ground-glass opacities and a stable left upper-lobe solid nodule were also reported. A retrospective review of the available serial CT reports showed that right-lung ground-glass opacities had been present since at least January 2021 and were repeatedly described as unchanged or essentially unchanged through May 2024. In January 2025, two right-lung ground-glass lesions were described as slightly fuller than on the preceding examination, whereas the March 2025 preoperative report again characterized them as essentially unchanged and without abnormal enhancement. Thus, the additional opacities predated surgery by several years and did not represent newly appearing postoperative lesions. The baseline CT appearance of the resected right lower-lobe nodule is shown in Figure 1.
On March 20, 2025, the patient underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic right lower-lobe superior segmentectomy with hilar and mediastinal lymph-node sampling. Intraoperative frozen section suggested a lymphoid proliferative lesion. Gross examination showed a 1.0 × 1.8 × 0.7 cm gray-white lesion in the resected segment. The lesion was approximately 2.8 cm from the stapled margin, 3.5 cm from the bronchial margin, and 0.2 cm from the visceral pleura. The bronchial stump, visceral pleura, and stapled margin were uninvolved. The only separately documented nodal specimen, LN7, showed reactive hyperplasia with anthracotic pigment deposition and no lymphoma (0/1).
Histopathology and immunohistochemistry supported extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. Tumor cells were positive for CD20, CD79a, CD43, BCL2, MNDA, and BCL10; BCL6 showed scattered positivity. The cells were negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, CD23, cyclin D1, SOX11, and IgD. Follicular dendritic-cell meshworks were highlighted by CD21 and CD23. The Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 5%, and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA in situ hybridization was negative. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation did not identify a monoclonal protein. Representative histopathological and immunohistochemical findings are shown in Figure 2.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue using an API2/MALT1 dual-color fusion probe (Anbiping). API2/BIRC3 at 11q22 was labeled red and MALT1 at 18q21 was labeled green. Hybridization was performed with a ThermoBrite system; signals were evaluated by fluorescence microscopy with dual-person technical review and appropriate positive and negative controls. The abnormal 2F1R1G signal pattern was present in 35.0% of analyzed cells, exceeding the laboratory positivity threshold of 5.0%, and was interpreted as BIRC3::MALT1 fusion positive. The original pathology report did not explicitly document lymphoepithelial lesions, bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue distribution, plasmacytic differentiation, light-chain restriction, or immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene rearrangement testing.
Laboratory tests obtained on postoperative day 1 (March 21, 2025) showed lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 408 U/L, fibrinogen 4.91 g/L, D-dimer 1.07 mg/L, and antithrombin III 77.3%. Because these measurements were obtained immediately after thoracic surgery, the LDH and coagulation abnormalities were considered potentially confounded by tissue injury, inflammation, or hemolysis and were not used as evidence of aggressive or disseminated lymphoma. Before anti-CD20 therapy, HBV testing showed HBsAg <0.05 IU/mL, anti-HBs >1000 mIU/mL, HBeAg <0.10 S/CO, anti-HBe 0.14 S/CO, anti-HBc 21.68 S/CO, normal transaminases, and HBV DNA below the detection threshold; prophylactic entecavir was administered.
PET/CT on March 31, 2025, 11 days after surgery, showed metabolically active changes in the operative bed and right chest wall that were interpreted as postoperative inflammation. Multiple right upper-lobe ground-glass opacities had only mild FDG uptake; the largest was approximately 0.7 cm with SUVmax 1.0. In view of their documented presence for several years and overall stability on serial preoperative CT reports, these lesions were classified as longstanding indeterminate pulmonary opacities rather than evidence of multifocal pulmonary MALT lymphoma.
PET/CT also showed circumferential thickening of the horizontal duodenum with SUVmax 4.0. Gastroscopy on April 2, 2025, showed erosive gastritis but no obvious duodenal mucosal abnormality, and neither duodenal biopsy nor endoscopic ultrasound-guided sampling was performed. Bone marrow cytology and biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The minimum confirmed disease extent was therefore a completely resected pulmonary MALT lymphoma without proven nodal or marrow involvement. Under the Ann Arbor/Lugano framework, the pathologically confirmed disease was assigned a working stage IE, while recognizing that nodal assessment was limited to the documented LN7 specimen and that the additional pulmonary and duodenal findings were not pathologically characterized.
The patient recovered from surgery but reported fatigue and night sweats in mid-April 2025, without documented fever or weight loss. At that time, the treating team selected systemic therapy because of the new symptoms, limited pulmonary reserve, and concern that the indeterminate pulmonary and duodenal abnormalities might represent additional disease. This decision was made in the setting of diagnostic uncertainty. Neither mild pulmonary FDG uptake, the duodenal PET/CT finding, postoperative LDH elevation, nor BIRC3::MALT1 positivity independently established dissemination or constituted a standard indication for chemotherapy.
The patient received two cycles of R-CVP on April 15 and May 6, 2025: rituximab 630 mg on day 0, cyclophosphamide 1,200 mg on day 1, vincristine 2 mg on day 1, and prednisone 100 mg on days 1-5. After abdominal magnetic resonance imaging on May 28 described persistent and apparently more extensive duodenal wall abnormality, the regimen was changed at the treating team’s discretion to R-CHOP on May 29 and June 19, 2025: rituximab 640 mg on day 0, cyclophosphamide 1,200 mg on day 1, doxorubicin 70 mg on day 1, vincristine 2 mg on day 1, and prednisone 100 mg on days 1-5. After four cycles, the treating team recorded the overall radiologic assessment as stable disease, and orelabrutinib 150 mg orally once daily was subsequently started. Entecavir prophylaxis was continued. This treatment sequence is reported as the actual clinical course and should not be interpreted as a generalizable strategy for localized or BIRC3::MALT1-positive pulmonary MALT lymphoma.
Follow-up included chest CT and abdominal magnetic resonance imaging on May 26, 2025; chest CT on June 17; chest CT and abdominal magnetic resonance imaging on July 10; PET/CT on September 15; gastroscopy on December 8; and chest CT plus abdominal magnetic resonance imaging on May 1, 2026. The September PET/CT showed no abnormally increased pulmonary FDG uptake and near-complete resolution of the previously described right-lung opacities. Because those opacities had been longstanding, were not biopsied, and had shown only minimal baseline uptake, their subsequent radiologic change cannot retrospectively establish lymphoma involvement or be used as proof of lymphoma response.
In contrast, thickening and FDG uptake in the horizontal duodenum remained essentially unchanged from the March PET/CT. Repeat gastroscopy in December 2025 again did not document biopsy-proven duodenal lymphoma. The absence of a clear treatment-associated response further weakened the attribution of this lesion to MALT lymphoma. At approximately 1 year of follow-up, the patient denied fever, cough, sputum, chest discomfort, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, or diarrhea, and no clinical progression of the pathologically confirmed pulmonary lymphoma was identified. A comparison of the March 31 and September 15 PET/CT findings is shown in Figure 3.

Two biological sisters were included in this report. Both patients presented with gastrointestinal tumor-like lesions, and GIST was considered the leading preoperative differential diagnosis. Other subepithelial lesions, including neuroendocrine tumor, leiomyoma, lipoma, inflammatory lesions, and ectopic pancreas, were also considered in the differential diagnosis according to lesion location, enhancement pattern, clinical presentation, and available endoscopic or imaging features. The final diagnosis was established by postoperative histopathology. A brief clinical timeline of the two patients is summarized in Table 1.
The patient was the younger sister, a 24-year-old woman who underwent a routine health check-up in 2018 despite having no abdominal symptoms. Screening gastroscopy during this check-up showed a submucosal lesion in the gastric body. She had no obvious abdominal pain, abdominal distension, nausea, vomiting, or other discomfort at that time. Further endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) showed a hypoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria. The layers of the gastric wall were clear and intact. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed a markedly enhanced nodule along the lesser curvature of the stomach. Another enhanced nodule was also found in the small intestine. Based on the lesion locations and enhancement patterns, a gastrointestinal subepithelial tumor was suspected, with GIST considered as the leading preoperative diagnosis (Figure 1).
This preoperative impression was mainly based on the gastric lesion arising from the muscularis propria, the marked enhancement of the gastric nodule, and the presence of an additional enhancing small intestinal nodule. A neuroendocrine tumor was considered less likely because there were no specific clinical manifestations or biochemical findings suggesting a functioning neuroendocrine tumor, although a nonfunctioning lesion could not be excluded by imaging alone. Leiomyoma or other mesenchymal tumors were also considered, but the presence of two enhancing lesions at different gastrointestinal sites made definitive preoperative classification difficult. Ectopic pancreas was a possible differential diagnosis, but typical features such as central umbilication, a duct-like structure, or enhancement clearly similar to the orthotopic pancreas were not identified.
Surgery was selected instead of surveillance because GIST could not be excluded, the gastric lesion appeared to arise from the muscularis propria, and an additional enhancing small intestinal lesion was present. Routine endoscopic biopsy was considered unlikely to provide a reliable diagnosis for a muscularis propria-based lesion. Therefore, surgical resection was performed for both diagnostic confirmation and definitive treatment.
On December 20, 2018, the patient underwent laparoscopic and endoscopic resection of the gastric body lesion under general anesthesia. Laparoscopic resection of the small intestinal lesion was performed during the same operation. Postoperative histopathology confirmed ectopic pancreas in both the gastric and small intestinal lesions. Further pathological review showed mature pancreatic parenchymal structures within the lesions. Pancreatic acini, ducts, and islets were all well differentiated. The proportions of these three components were close to those seen in normal pancreatic tissue. These findings were consistent with Heinrich type I and Gaspar-Fuentes type I ectopic pancreas, corresponding to mature-type ectopic pancreas (Figure 2). No histological features suggestive of GIST were identified.
The small intestinal specimen measured approximately 3.0 × 2.5 cm, with negative resection margins. Preoperative CT showed that the enhanced small intestinal nodule was approximately 10 mm, whereas the postoperative specimen was larger on gross examination. This difference may be related to different measurement methods. Imaging mainly reflected the more obviously enhanced part of the lesion, while gross pathological measurement was based on the entire resected specimen. The gastric lesion measured approximately 2.2 × 2.0 × 1.5 cm. One resection margin was close to the lesion, while the other margin was negative.
The patient recovered well after surgery. During 2019–2020, the patient experienced several episodes of incomplete small bowel obstruction, which resolved after conservative treatment. The relationship between these episodes and the previous surgery remained uncertain. No evidence of lesion recurrence was found during subsequent follow-up. At follow-up in April 2026, the patient had no obvious abdominal symptoms. Repeat abdominal CT and gastroscopy showed no obvious abnormalities.
The patient was the elder sister, a 41-year-old woman who presented in January 2026. On January 23, 2026, she developed abdominal pain without an obvious trigger. The pain was mainly located in the right upper abdomen and radiated to the back. She also had low-grade fever, with a maximum temperature of 37.8 °C. During the disease course, she experienced intermittent chest tightness. Electrocardiography and myocardial enzyme tests showed no abnormalities.
Laboratory tests on January 25, 2026, showed a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 24.96 mg/L and a white blood cell count of 9 × 109/L. The patient received intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 2.0 g as anti-infective treatment. After 5 days of treatment, the abdominal pain did not improve significantly. Abdominal CT showed focal thickening of the small intestinal wall with outward protrusion. Inflammatory exudative changes were observed around the lesion.
Because the symptoms persisted, contrast-enhanced CT, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) were performed. Multimodal imaging showed a nodular lesion on the mesenteric side of the proximal jejunum. The lesion was closely related to the adjacent intestinal wall and showed heterogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. Contrast-enhanced MRI showed soft tissue mass-like signal features. PET/CT showed mildly increased fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in the lesion (Figure 3). This mild FDG uptake did not strongly support malignancy, but it was not specific enough to exclude GIST before surgery. Based on the overall imaging findings, GIST was considered as the leading preoperative diagnosis. This impression was mainly based on the wall-based location of the lesion, its close relationship with the adjacent jejunal wall, and its heterogeneous contrast enhancement.
The differential diagnosis also included neuroendocrine tumor, leiomyoma, inflammatory mass, and ectopic pancreas. A neuroendocrine tumor was considered because small intestinal neuroendocrine tumors may present as enhancing wall-based lesions; however, the absence of specific endocrine symptoms and the mild FDG uptake did not strongly support this diagnosis. Leiomyoma and other mesenchymal tumors could not be excluded because of the wall-based growth pattern. Inflammatory lesions were also considered because of abdominal pain, elevated CRP, and surrounding inflammatory exudation. Ectopic pancreas was also considered, but the lesion lacked typical preoperative features such as central umbilication or a duct-like structure.
Surgery was chosen because the patient had persistent abdominal pain despite anti-infective treatment, inflammatory changes were present around the lesion, and GIST or another neoplastic lesion could not be excluded by multimodal imaging. Therefore, laparoscopic resection was performed for both therapeutic management and definitive pathological diagnosis.
On February 12, 2026, the patient underwent laparoscopic resection of the small intestinal lesion under general anesthesia. Postoperative histopathology showed ectopic pancreatic tissue. The lesion measured approximately 3.2 × 2.2 × 2.0 cm. Pathological review showed mature pancreatic parenchymal structures within the lesion. Pancreatic acini, ducts, and islets were all well differentiated. The proportions of these three components were close to those seen in normal pancreatic tissue. These findings were consistent with Heinrich type I and Gaspar-Fuentes type I ectopic pancreas, corresponding to mature-type ectopic pancreas. Fat necrosis nodules were observed around the lesion, with aggregation of foamy histiocytes and a multinucleated giant cell reaction. No obvious abnormality was found at the small intestinal resection margins (Figure 4). No spindle-cell proliferation or other morphological features supporting GIST were observed on histopathological examination.
The patient recovered uneventfully after surgery. During follow-up until April 2026, she had no obvious abdominal symptoms. Because the follow-up period was short, long-term symptom control, recurrence-free status, and late postoperative complications could not be fully evaluated.
In both patients, preoperative tumor markers, serum amylase, serum lipase, liver function tests, and renal function tests were within the institutional reference ranges.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 2-months history of abdominal bloating and a 2-weeks history of persistent nausea and vomiting, accompanied by weight loss and epigastric pain. At an outside hospital, 2 consecutive endoscopic biopsies were interpreted as chronic gastritis. His symptoms progressed despite 4 weeks of standard treatment, including a proton pump inhibitor and gastric mucosal protective therapy, and gastrointestinal decompression with nasogastric nutritional support was required.
After transfer to our hospital, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed hyperplastic, erosive, and hemorrhagic mucosal changes in the gastric antrum. Repeat biopsy again demonstrated chronic inflammation without definite malignant cells (Figure 1). Because the patient had progressive obstructive symptoms and a persistent mismatch between benign biopsy results and clinical suspicion, a multidisciplinary consultation was performed. The clinical timeline is summarized in Table 1.
After written informed consent was obtained, the patient underwent F-18 FDG PET/CT followed by Ga-68 FAPI-04 PET/CT more than 48 h later. The total administered activity of F-18 FDG, calculated according to body weight, was 6.2 mCi (approximately 229 MBq), and imaging was performed 60 min after tracer injection. The total administered activity of Ga-68 FAPI-04, also calculated according to body weight, was 3.5 mCi (approximately 130 MBq), and PET/CT acquisition was also performed 60 min after injection. Both PET/CT examinations included non-contrast low-dose CT for attenuation correction and anatomical localization, without intravenous contrast administration.
Before F-18 FDG PET/CT, the patient was instructed to drink water for gastric distention; however, adequate gastric distention could not be achieved before Ga-68 FAPI-04 PET/CT because of poor tolerance. For semiquantitative analysis, the lesion was first localized on sagittal images, and a spherical 3-dimensional region of interest large enough to encompass the entire suspected tumor was placed on the corresponding axial images. SUVmax was automatically calculated by the postprocessing software. If multiple lesions were present, the lesion with the highest SUVmax was selected as the representative lesion.
F-18 FDG PET/CT showed gastric antral wall thickening with slightly increased but indistinct FDG uptake compared with the liver, with an SUVmax of 7.3 (Figure 2). In contrast, Ga-68 FAPI-04 PET/CT demonstrated intense uptake in the same gastric antrum wall, with clearer lesion delineation and an SUVmax of 19.7 (Figure 3). No distant abnormal tracer uptake suggestive of metastatic disease was identified.
Because of progressive gastric outlet obstruction, fluid imbalance, poor tolerance of oral intake, and persistent suspicion for malignancy, distal gastrectomy was performed primarily for symptom relief and definitive diagnosis. Although EUS, EUS-guided tissue acquisition, deep biopsy, or mucosal incision-assisted biopsy could have been considered after repeated negative mucosal biopsies, these procedures were not performed preoperatively in this patient because of rapidly progressive gastric outlet obstruction, persistent vomiting, poor tolerance of oral intake, and the need for timely therapeutic intervention. In addition, further repeated superficial biopsy was considered unlikely to change immediate management. Distal gastrectomy was therefore selected not only for symptom relief but also for definitive pathological diagnosis.
Intraoperative frozen section analysis suggested invasive poorly differentiated carcinoma. Final histopathology of the gastrectomy specimen confirmed poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma with partial signet-ring cell morphology, mixed Lauren type. The tumor invaded through the muscularis propria into the subserosal adipose tissue, corresponding to at least pT3 disease. Perineural invasion was present, whereas definite lymphovascular tumor emboli were not identified. The proximal resection margin was free of tumor; however, tumor infiltration was identified in the mucosal muscularis and submucosa of the distal resection margin. The omental tissue was negative for carcinoma. No regional lymph node metastasis was identified among 36 examined lymph nodes; however, carcinoma was noted in adjacent soft tissue in several nodal stations.
Immunohistochemistry showed CK7 positivity, CK20 negativity, partial MUC6 positivity, CD10 negativity, Villin negativity, HER2 negativity (score 0), p53 positivity, beta-catenin positivity, and a Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 40%. Neuroendocrine markers were negative, including synaptophysin, CD56, and chromogranin A. Mismatch repair protein expression was retained, including MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, and MSH6 (Figure 4).
The patient recovered after surgery and received postoperative XELOX chemotherapy. At the 7-months postoperative follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable without newly reported severe treatment-related adverse symptoms.

An 85-year-old woman was admitted with acute lower abdominal pain lasting 4 h. The pain was severe and distending in nature and was accompanied by nausea, two episodes of vomiting, abdominal distension, and absence of flatus or bowel movements. She had no fever or chills. The patient had a 6-month history of chronic constipation and had used glycerin suppositories with poor response. She also had a history of hypertension for more than 30 years and had been taking oral levamlodipine besylate 2.5 mg once daily. Her previous surgical history included cholecystectomy more than 20 years earlier.
On admission, her body temperature was 36.2 °C, heart rate was 96 beats/min, respiratory rate was 23 breaths/min, and blood pressure was 107/66 mmHg. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, mild rebound tenderness, muscular guarding, and decreased bowel sounds. Initial laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 24.61 mg/L and hypokalemia, with a serum potassium level of 3.31 mmol/L. Coagulation-related markers were also elevated, including fibrinogen 4.49 g/L, D-dimer 2.04 μg/mL, and fibrinogen degradation products 7.25 μg/mL. Selected perioperative laboratory findings are summarized in Table 1.
Imaging studies: Abdominal CT revealed scattered free intraperitoneal air (Figure 1a), mild colonic dilatation, mesenteric and omental edema, small-volume peritoneal and pelvic fluid collections, and increased intestinal contents. A high-density fecal mass was identified within the distal sigmoid colon, consistent with fecal impaction (Figures 1b, c). Taken together, these findings suggested hollow viscus perforation with intra-abdominal contamination, most likely involving the sigmoid colon. The CT findings were subsequently correlated with the intraoperative findings of distal sigmoid colon perforation, impacted fecal material, and feculent peritonitis.
Surgical intervention: Laparoscopic exploration was performed and revealed severe feculent peritoneal contamination. The operation was converted to limited open surgery. Intraoperatively, a 2.5 cm × 2.0 cm perforation was identified in the distal sigmoid colon, with adherent fecal material and purulent debris (Figure 2). Localized necrotic tissue at the perforation margin was debrided. The remaining inspected colon appeared viable, without diffuse ischemia or necrosis. No obvious diverticular disease, colonic mass, inflammatory bowel disease-related lesion, or other gross pathological abnormality that could account for the perforation was identified during intraoperative exploration. No bowel resection was performed. The sigmoid segment containing the perforation was exteriorized through the abdominal wall, and the debrided perforation was matured directly as a colostomy. Abdominal drains were placed. The operative time was approximately 2 h. Based on the clinical presentation, CT findings, and intraoperative findings, the diagnosis was considered probable stercoral perforation of the sigmoid colon complicated by feculent peritonitis. No histopathological confirmation was available.
Postoperative cardiology consultation was obtained. The consultation suggested that the patient’s chronic constipation might have been associated with long-term use of levamlodipine besylate. Therefore, her antihypertensive regimen was changed to valsartan 80 mg once daily to reduce the risk of medication-induced constipation.
Postoperatively, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit on postoperative day 1 for close monitoring and supportive treatment. Laboratory tests showed marked systemic inflammation, including procalcitonin 34.37 ng/mL and interleukin-6 5044.36 pg/mL, while serum lactate was 1.76 mmol/L. Antimicrobial therapy with imipenem and tigecycline was initiated. On postoperative day 2, the patient was transferred back to the Department of General Surgery. Serum β-D-glucan was <10 pg/mL. Cefoperazone-sulbactam was added on postoperative day 4. Blood cultures obtained on postoperative day 6 showed no growth. Imipenem and tigecycline were discontinued on postoperative day 8, and cefoperazone-sulbactam was continued alone. After clinical and laboratory reassessment, all antibacterial therapy was discontinued on postoperative day 13.
During hospitalization, electrolyte replacement and nutritional support were provided for hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypoalbuminemia. On postoperative day 13, the patient was conscious and clinically stable, with no abnormal discharge from the stoma. Laboratory tests showed residual anemia and inflammatory response, including hemoglobin 85 g/L and C-reactive protein 31.23 mg/L. Serum potassium was 3.43 mmol/L and albumin was 27.5 g/L. The patient was discharged in stable condition on postoperative day 14.
At the 11-week follow-up, she tolerated a regular diet, had regular bowel movements through the colostomy, and reported no abdominal pain or fever. Her general condition had improved. At the 1-year follow-up, she remained independent in daily activities, with no recurrent perforation, severe constipation, or rehospitalization. The overall clinical course is summarized in Figure 3.

The patient was a 36-year-old woman with a history of chronic spontaneous urticaria (CsU). According to a review of her outpatient records from both our hospital and an outside hospital, she had experienced recurrent wheals for more than 1 month before admission and had visited our outpatient clinic several times. She had been treated with oral antihistamines, including mizolastine 10 mg once daily and cetirizine 10 mg every night, but her urticaria remained poorly controlled. Therefore, omalizumab was initiated for antihistamine-refractory CsU. On February 6, 2025, she received her first subcutaneous injection of omalizumab 300 mg, while continuing oral mizolastine 10 mg once daily and cetirizine 10 mg every night. On February 23, 2025, 17 days after the first omalizumab dose, multiple raised, edematous erythematous papules and plaques developed on the trunk and limbs, with vesicles and bullae on the hands and feet. These lesions were accompanied by significant pain and severe pruritus. Concurrently, scattered vesicles were observed on the oral mucosa, accompanied by a sore throat that worsened upon swallowing, as well as fever, chills, and fatigue. Before this episode, the patient denied any medication use other than the treatments prescribed for urticaria.
She had a history of cervical HPV infection, bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, and chronic spontaneous urticaria.
Physical examination revealed numerous raised, edematous, erythematous papules and plaques diffusely distributed on the trunk and limbs, some appearing as purplish-red targetoid lesions. Vesicles and bullae with clear fluid and thick walls were also observed on the palms, wrists, soles, and medial aspects of both feet, some of which had ruptured and crusted. The Nikolsky sign was negative. Scattered small vesicles and erosions were present on the bilateral buccal mucosa. No abnormalities were detected on the conjunctival or genital mucosa (Figure 1).
Laboratory examinations showed an elevated absolute eosinophil count of 1.29 × 109/L (reference range: 0.02–0.52 × 109/L), an eosinophil percentage of 16.8% (reference range: 0.4–8%), and the immunoglobulin E (IgE) level was 3,557 IU/mL. Serological testing showed positivity for herpes simplex virus type I/II IgG and negativity for herpes simplex virus type I/II IgM. Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibody testing was negative. Results for the immunoglobulins and complement, antinuclear antibodies, anti-epidermal keratinocyte desmosome and basement membrane antibodies, ESR, CRP, biochemistry, coagulation, and infection screening were all within normal limits. The patient also had no history of other recent medication exposure apart from the treatment prescribed for urticaria, and the above negative infectious and autoimmune work-up made common infectious, autoimmune bullous, and alternative drug-related causes less likely. Skin biopsy pathology obtained from the left upper limb showed focal sheet-like necrotic keratinocytes in the epidermis, liquefaction degeneration of the basal cells, and intraepidermal and subepidermal blister formation containing cystic fluid and a large amount of eosinophilic infiltration (Figure 2). Sheet-like eosinophilic and lymphocytic infiltration was observed around the small vessels in the dermis. Based on the history of omalizumab treatment, the typical lesions and the histopathological findings, the diagnosis of “omalizumab-induced bullous erythema multiforme” was made. The causal relationship between omalizumab and bullous erythema multiforme was assessed using the Naranjo Adverse Drug Reaction Probability Scale. The total score was 6, indicating a probable adverse drug reaction. The detailed scoring table is provided in the Supplementary Table S1.
Initial treatment consisted of intravenous methylprednisolone at 40 mg/d combined with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 20 g/d. However, the skin lesions continued to progress, and the peripheral blood eosinophil count increased further. Subsequently, the dose of methylprednisolone was increased to 60 mg/d, but new vesicles continued to appear on the limbs. Consequently, the dose of methylprednisolone was increased to 120 mg/d, combined with oral upadacitinib at 30 mg/d. Following this, the skin lesions began to improve after 2 days, the blisters dried and crusted, and no new vesicles or bullae appeared. The treatment timeline during the patient’s hospitalization is shown in Figure 3. During systemic corticosteroid treatment, potassium chloride 0.5 g twice daily, omeprazole 20 mg once daily, and calcium carbonate 600 mg once daily were administered as supportive prophylactic medications. Complete blood counts, lipid profile, blood glucose, and electrolyte levels were monitored regularly and remained within normal ranges. No treatment emergent adverse effects related to methylprednisolone or upadacitinib were observed during hospitalization. At discharge, the patient’s condition was stable, and the corticosteroid dose was gradually tapered thereafter (Figure 4). At the 3 month follow-up after discharge, the erythematous lesions had almost completely resolved, leaving only residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and upadacitinib was reduced to 15 mg once daily. At present, the patient remains clinically stable and is taking one tablet of upadacitinib every other day.

A 78-year-old man underwent balloon-expandable transcatheter aortic valve implantation for severe aortic stenosis. Postoperatively, he developed symptomatic paroxysmal complete atrioventricular block requiring permanent pacemaker implantation. Given the patient’s history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, Bachmann bundle pacing was selected to maintain atrial synchrony and improve interatrial conduction.
A SelectSecure 3830 pacing lead (4.1 Fr, 69 cm; Medtronic, MN, USA) was delivered using a fixed-curve C315-S502 sheath (Medtronic) and positioned at the superior interatrial septum. During screw advancement, the COI was continuously monitored in real time (Figure A) using the CareLink SmartSync™ device manager (Medtronic). Current of injury was observed by unipolar sensing before screw advancement and increased gradually during the first three rotations. At five rotations, the COI jumped up abruptly, with a waveform markedly different from baseline (Figure B), suggesting stable myocardial engagement and fixation. Subsequent bipolar pacing demonstrated a paced P wave shortened by more than 10 ms compared with the intrinsic P wave, with increased amplitude and sharper morphology (Figure C), consistent with electrophysiological criteria for Bachmann bundle capture. At implantation, the atrial sensing amplitude was 1.6 mV, the pacing threshold was 0.5 V at 0.4 ms, and the lead impedance was 665 Ω. The procedure was completed without complications, and lead parameters remained stable at 4-month follow-up (Figure D). This case highlights the utility of COI-guided fixation in high-risk atrial pacing sites.

A 67-year-old male with a history of quadruple coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 10 years prior underwent coronary angiography for exertional angina. Compared to a coronary angiography performed 3 years earlier, which had shown only moderate aneurysmatic dilation of the saphenous vein graft (SVG) to the diagonal branch (Figure 1A), the current procedure revealed that the lesion had rapidly progressed into a large circular aneurysmatic formation with contrast extravasation in the midportion of the SVG to the diagonal branch (Figure 1B, Supplementary material online, Video S1). Regarding the other grafts, a patent left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to the left anterior descending artery (LAD), a patent SVG to the obtuse marginal branch, and an occluded SVG to the right coronary artery were also observed.
A computed tomography angiography was subsequently performed, which confirmed the presence of a 43×37 mm pseudoaneurysm (Figure 1 C-E, Supplementary material online, Video S2). While small or stable SGG aneurysms can occasionally be managed conservatively or via percutaneous approaches, such as covered stent deployment or coil embolization, considering the high risk of rupture and the presence of ischaemic symptoms in this case, a multidisciplinary team recommended surgical intervention, and the pseudoaneurysm was successfully resected.
Pseudoaneurysms of SVGs are a rare complication following CABG, occurring in less than 1% of patients. They may be detected incidentally during coronary angiography in asymptomatic individuals or present with symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnoea, syncope, or haemoptysis.
In contrast to arterial grafts, in which aneurysm formation is extremely rare, SVGs are more prone to progressive degenerative changes after implantation, reflected by higher rates of graft occlusion and aneurysmal dilatation. This phenomenon is largely attributed to the structural mismatch and the relatively thin wall of vein conduits exposed to systemic arterial pressures, as well as their tendency towards accelerated atherosclerotic degeneration, occasionally compounded by technical factors during graft preparation. Larger pseudoaneurysms carry significant risks of thrombosis, distal embolization, or rupture and therefore frequently require surgical or percutaneous intervention, while management decisions should be guided by rupture risk, patient comorbidities, and the need to maintain adequate myocardial revascularization.
While SVG pseudoaneurysms are documented in the literature, this case is uniquely valuable because it provides a clear, longitudinal visual record over a 3-year window. By directly contrasting the baseline mild angiographic dilation with the rapid progression into a massive pseudoaneurysm, it highlights the unpredictable nature of vein conduit degeneration and serves as a strong clinical reminder to maintain a low threshold for timely Heart Team intervention before catastrophic rupture occurs.

A 27-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of progressive low back pain radiating to the left thigh, leg, and foot. Pain intensity was reported as severe (10/10 at worst), exacerbated by physical activity. She also had a history of recurrent UTIs but denied bowel dysfunction or obvious urinary incontinence. No cutaneous lumbosacral stigmata were identified.
Physical and neurological examination were unremarkable, with intact cranial nerve function, full motor strength (5/5) in all extremities, normal sensation, and symmetric deep tendon reflexes. A voiding cystourethrogram revealed detrusor overactivity with a thick-walled bladder. These findings were later confirmed on a CT abdominal scan, which, although performed for other complaints, revealed a thickened urinary bladder wall with associated perilesional fat stranding, consistent with recurrent UTIs.
Spinal imaging revealed structural abnormalities consistent with tethered cord syndrome. CT imaging of the lumbar spine demonstrated spina bifida occulta at L5–S1 with non-fusion of the posterior vertebral elements (Fig. 1). MRI of the lumbosacral spine showed a low-lying conus medullaris terminating at the L3/L4 junction, a thickened filum terminale, and cauda equina nerve roots displaced bilaterally by the tethered cord (Fig. 2). Given her clinical symptoms, radiological findings, and recurrent UTIs with possible neurogenic bladder, surgical detethering was recommended to prevent further neurological and orthopedic sequelae, including scoliosis. A sagittal T1-weighted MRI further demonstrated the lipomatous lesion within the filum terminle and postoperative 3 months follow-up MRI showed its interval removal following detethering (Fig. 3), (see Fig. 4).

A 53-year-old male presented to our institution in December 2014 with persistent abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits. He had a 20-pack-year smoking history; however, detailed information regarding smoking cessation was unavailable, but he maintained excellent functional status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) 0). The patient's oncologic course was notable for the sequential development of four histologically distinct primary malignancies over a 10-year period (Figure 1).
First primary malignancy at the age of 53 (2014): Colonoscopy identified an ascending colonic mass, and histopathology confirmed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma, tumor size 3.5 cm single lesion, no perineural invasion, surgical margin was clear, and there was lymphovascular invasion. The patient underwent extended right hemicolectomy with lymphadenectomy, with 0 of 15 lymph nodes positive for metastasis pN0. Final staging was pT3N0M0 (stage IIA). He completed 12 cycles of adjuvant folinic acid, fluorouracil (5-FU), and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) chemotherapy due to the presence of high-risk features with lymphovascular invasion and entered structured surveillance. Follow-up included clinical evaluation, imaging studies, colonoscopy, and tumor marker assessment at regular intervals.
Second primary malignancy at the age of 58 (2017): In August 2017, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria was detected during follow-up. MRI revealed a lesion in the left renal pelvis. Radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision was performed in November 2017. Histopathology demonstrated high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma (pT1N0M0). Immunohistochemistry profile (GATA3+, CK20+, CDX2-)supported a primary urothelial carcinoma rather than metastatic colorectal carcinoma.
Interval urothelial recurrence at the age of 63 (2022): Surveillance cystoscopy in November 2022 detected an anterior urethral lesion. Histology confirmed high-grade non-invasive urothelial carcinoma (pTa), representing a urothelial recurrence rather than a new primary malignancy, managed with local excision and continued endoscopic surveillance.
Third primary malignancy at the age of 64 (2023-2024): In October 2023, surveillance CT revealed a left lower lobe pulmonary mass measuring approximately 6.4 x 4.8 cm in maximal axial dimensions. Subsequent FDG PET/CT demonstrated a markedly hypermetabolic, locally aggressive soft tissue lesion infiltrating the mediastinal pleura, encasing the left lower lobe bronchus, and exhibiting loss of intervening fat planes with the descending aorta. The lesion measured approximately 7.5 x 5.0 cm in the maximal active component, with an SUVmax of 20.5. Additionally, a hypermetabolic subcarinal lymph node measuring 1.5 cm (SUVmax 8.5) was identified, and a few ipsilateral pulmonary nodules of indeterminate significance were identified on imaging. The slight difference in lesion size measurements is considered acceptable and likely reflects differences in imaging technique and modality-based assessment. These findings were consistent with locally advanced disease (stage IIIB T4N2M0) (Figure 2).
To exclude metastatic involvement from prior colonic or urothelial primaries, immunohistochemical analysis was performed. The tumor cells were positive for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and Napsin A, and negative for CDX2 and GATA3, supporting the diagnosis of primary lung adenocarcinoma. Molecular analysis revealed an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation; the specific EGFR mutation was unavailable from the accessible records, with negative anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) and Revian oncogene segment 1 (ROS1) rearrangements. PD-L1 expression demonstrated a tumor proportion score (TPS) of 5%.
The patient subsequently underwent concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) with carboplatin and pemetrexed between February and March 2024, with a total dose of 60 Gy delivered in 30 fractions. Post-treatment FDG PET/CT demonstrated near-complete metabolic resolution with significant morphologic regression of the primary tumor with only subtle non-FDG-avid soft-tissue thickening. Moreover, there was an interval of complete resolution of the previous subcarinal nodal metastasis; the assessment was based on comparative FDG PET-CT findings rather than the formal Positron Emission Tomography Response Criteria in Solid Tumors (PERCIST) or Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) response criteria. Following a multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion involving medical oncology, radiation oncology, and cardiothoracic surgery, the disease was deemed resectable. Following concurrent chemoradiotherapy, the patient demonstrated significant treatment response and was re-evaluated by a multidisciplinary team, which considered the disease potentially resectable and recommended a left lower lobectomy (Figure 3).
Fourth primary malignancy at the age of 65 (2024): In November 2024, a suspicious subcutaneous lesion over the sternum was identified. FDG PET/CT demonstrated focal superficial uptake (SUVmax: 5.5), without additional hypermetabolic lesions (Figure 4A). Surgical excision confirmed a moderately differentiated cutaneous invasive verrucous squamous cell carcinoma, grade 1, tumor size 1 x 1 x 0.8 cm with clear margins, no perineural invasion, no lymphovascular invasion. Subsequent follow-up FDG PET/CT confirmed complete metabolic response, with no evidence of residual, recurrent, or newly developed FDG-avid disease, consistent with ongoing remission. At the latest follow-up, conducted 12 months after treatment, the patient remained clinically disease-free with no evidence of metabolically active disease on PET/CT (Figure 5).

We present the case of a 78-year-old woman, a lifelong non-smoker with no occupational exposure to respiratory toxins, with a medical history notable for minimal bilateral bronchiectasis and a surgical intervention 10 years ago for a giant pleural solitary fibrous tumor measuring 19 cm × 11 cm × 11 cm and weighing 1.5 kg. The tumor was located parietally in the posterolateral hemithorax, in contact with the right upper and lower lobes, with intramediastinal extension causing contralateral displacement and compressive effects on the esophagus and right main bronchus (Figure 1).
According to the available archival pathology report, the initial tumor showed low mitotic activity (2 mitoses/10 high-power fields), absence of cytologic atypia, and no tumor necrosis. The lesion was completely excised, with no reported residual macroscopic disease; however, detailed microscopic margin assessment was not available in the archival documentation. Based on the available parameters, a retrospective Demicco score would be estimated as 5 points.
The patient was lost to follow-up after the initial years of imaging surveillance, during which no abnormalities were detected (Figure 2).
A decade later, she presents to the emergency room reporting exertional dyspnea on moderate effort and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, with insidious onset and progressive worsening over the past month. On clinical examination, the only notable finding was absent breath sounds over the right hemithorax, without crackles or palpable superficial lymphadenopathy, and with vital signs within normal limits.
Paraclinically, pulmonary function testing revealed a moderate obstructive ventilatory impairment, with an FEV1 of 70% of the predicted value. Computed tomography revealed a new round-to-oval, heterogeneous, pleura-based mass with smooth contours, measuring 12 cm × 12 cm × 10 cm, located in the right lower lobe (Figure 3).
Bronchoscopy of the right basal subsegmental bronchi demonstrated a slight mucosal irregularity. However, biopsy could not be performed due to marked vascularization with a mildly pulsatile character, posing a significant risk of post-procedural bleeding. Cytologic evaluation of the bronchial aspirate did not reveal malignant cells, and cultures for common bacterial flora as well as acid-fast bacilli were negative. The patient was therefore referred for a CT-guided transthoracic lung biopsy.
Histopathological examination (Figure 4) revealed uniform spindle cells displaying a ‘patternless’ architecture, arranged in alternating hypercellular and hypocellular areas, surrounded by keloid-type collagen and myxoid zones. Branching ‘staghorn’-type vessels were noted, with no evidence of necrosis or local pulmonary parenchymal invasion.
Immunohistochemistry performed on the CT-guided biopsy specimen showed diffuse CD34 positivity and nuclear STAT6 expression, supporting the diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (Figure 5). Additional immunohistochemical markers, including S100, GATA3, and D2-40, were negative in tumor cells, helping to exclude neural, GATA3-expressing metastatic epithelial, and mesothelial differentiation. No necrosis or mitotic activity was identified in the biopsy material. Because core biopsy specimens may not fully capture the histological heterogeneity of SFTs, definitive risk stratification was based on the postoperative resection specimen. Final microscopic evaluation confirmed recurrent solitary fibrous tumor and identified mitotic activity (4 mitoses/10 high-power fields), while necrosis and pulmonary parenchymal invasion were absent. Consequently, the final Demicco score was 5 points, corresponding to an intermediate-risk lesion (1 point for age >55 years, 2 points for tumor size between 10 and 14.9 cm, 2 points for mitotic activity, and 0 points for absence of necrosis).
The patient underwent tumorectomy through a posterolateral thoracotomy, which revealed a multilobulated, 500 g mass with a pedicle arising from the parietal pleura and no evidence of adjacent pulmonary parenchymal invasion (Figure 6). The surgical margins were free of tumor infiltration, consistent with complete resection.
Early postoperative imaging showed satisfactory postoperative expansion of the right lung and no relevant pleural collection (Figure 7).
She was discharged in stable hemodynamic and respiratory condition, with annual imaging follow-up advised due to several high-risk predictors for recurrence, including the tumor’s considerable size, advanced age, mitotic activity, and female sex, which has been associated in some studies with increased recurrence risk.
Thus, the present case illustrates the potential for recurrence and the unpredictable clinical course of pleural SFT, underscoring the need for long-term imaging surveillance even after ostensibly curative resections and initially favorable histological findings.

A 51-year-old woman presented with rapidly progressive gait impairment. Despite remaining ambulatory until 2024 with only occasional falls, she developed progressive gait difficulty in January 2025 and became wheelchair-dependent within several months. She had no history of hypertension or diabetes mellitus; her medical history was notable only for hypothyroidism. She reported drinking alcohol three times per week over the past three years, with no prior history of regular alcohol use. There was no family history of neuropathy, gait disturbance, early wheelchair dependence, visual impairment, or other known neurological disorders. She denied visual symptoms. Physical examination revealed no clinical apparent lipomatosis or lipodystrophy.
On neurological examination, she was alert and able to cooperate, with no evidence of delirium or psychiatric symptoms. Cognitive screening revealed a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 17/30. Cranial nerve examination was otherwise unremarkable. Motor strength was preserved in the upper extremities, whereas the lower extremities showed paraplegia with severe lower-extremity contractures.
